items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dates for Reading the Megillah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dates for Reading the Megillah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the Megillah is read on the 11th, 12th, 13th, 14th, or 15th of Adar, not fewer nor more. It then details the rules for walled cities, large towns, and villages, specifying which date each reads based on the day of the week on which the 14th falls.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the general rule that the Megillah is read on the 11th through 15th of Adar, and then specifies the basic distinction: walled cities read on the 15th, villages and large towns on the 14th, with villages advancing to the day of assembly.

The Mishnah details the first case: if the 14th falls on Monday, villages and large towns read on that day, walled cities on the next day; if on Tuesday or Wednesday, villages advance to the day of assembly, large towns read on the 14th, walled cities on the 15th.

The Mishnah continues: if the 14th falls on Thursday, villages and large towns read on that day, walled cities on the next day; if on Shabbat eve, villages advance to the day of assembly, while large towns and walled cities read on the 14th.

The Mishnah concludes: if the 14th falls on Shabbat, villages and large towns advance to the day of assembly, walled cities read on the 15th; if on Sunday, villages advance to the day of assembly, large towns read on the 14th, walled cities on the 15th.

items.text: Gemara's Initial Question: Source for Multiple Dates
items.text_en: Gemara's Initial Question: Source for Multiple Dates
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that the Megillah can be read on the 11th? It initially suggests that the Sages were lenient with villages to advance to the market day, but then reframes the question to ask how the Sages could override the enactment of the Men of the Great Assembly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of reading the Megillah on the 11th, then reframes the question to address how the Sages could override the enactment of the Men of the Great Assembly.

items.text: Reframing the Question: Authority of the Sages
items.text_en: Reframing the Question: Authority of the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Men of the Great Assembly instituted all the dates, and asks: If they only instituted the 14th and 15th, how could later Sages add other dates? It then asks where in the Torah these multiple times are hinted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since the Men of the Great Assembly instituted all the reading dates, how could later Sages add the 11th and 12th without violating the rule that a court cannot annul the words of a greater court?
The Gemara resolves that indeed the Men of the Great Assembly instituted all the dates, and then asks: where in the Torah are these multiple times hinted?

items.text: First Derivation: From 'בִּזְמַנֵּיהֶם'
items.text_en: First Derivation: From 'בִּזְמַנֵּיהֶם'
items.desc_en: Rav Shemen bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan derives the multiple times from the verse 'לְקַיֵּים אֵת יְמֵי הַפּוּרִים הָאֵלֶּה בִּזְמַנֵּיהֶם', interpreting the plural 'times'. The Gemara refines the derivation, excluding the 13th as it is already a gathering day, and excluding the 16th and 17th due to the verse 'וְלֹא יַעֲבוֹר'.

sub.text: Rav Shemen bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Shemen bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Shemen bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan derives multiple reading times from the plural 'בִּזְמַנֵּיהֶם' in the verse.
The Gemara objects that the plural might be needed for its basic meaning, and answers that the verse could have used the singular 'זְמַן'.
The Gemara objects that the plural might indicate different times for different places, and answers that the verse could have used 'זְמַנָּם'.
The Gemara asks why the plural implies only two times, and answers via a verbal analogy: 'זְמַנֵּיהֶם' parallels 'זְמַנָּם' which is two.
The Gemara asks why the 12th and 13th are not included, and answers with Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak's principle that the 13th is a gathering day for all and needs no inclusion.
The Gemara asks why the 16th and 17th are not included, and answers that the verse 'וְלֹא יַעֲבוֹר' excludes them.

items.text: Second Derivation: From 'כַּיָּמִים'
items.text_en: Second Derivation: From 'כַּיָּמִים'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani derives the multiple times from the verse 'כַּיָּמִים אֲשֶׁר נָחוּ בָהֶם הַיְּהוּדִים', interpreting 'יָמִים' and 'כַּיָּמִים' to include the 11th and 12th. The Gemara then explains why each Amora did not use the other's verse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani derives the multiple reading times from the verse 'כַּיָּמִים אֲשֶׁר נָחוּ בָהֶם', interpreting 'יָמִים' and 'כַּיָּמִים' to include the 11th and 12th of Adar.
The Gemara objects that the derivation could include the 12th and 13th, but Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak answers that the 13th is already a time of assembly for all and needs no inclusion.
The Gemara further objects that the derivation could include the 16th and 17th, but the verse 'וְלֹא יַעֲבוֹר' (and it shall not pass) limits the times.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani did not derive from 'בִּזְמַנֵּיהֶם', and answers that the series 'זְמַן, זְמַנָּם, זְמַנֵּיהֶם' does not imply multiple times to him.
The Gemara asks why Rav Shemen bar Abba did not derive from 'כַּיָּמִים', and answers that that verse is written for future generations, not for the multiple times of reading.

items.text: Debate: Rabbi Akiva vs. Sages on Current Practice
items.text_en: Debate: Rabbi Akiva vs. Sages on Current Practice
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that the Mishnah's ruling is according to Rabbi Akiva, but the Sages say the Megillah is only read in its proper time. A challenge is raised from Rabbi Yehuda's statement, which seems to support the Sages' view, leading to a resolution that in the present time, due to looking at the Megillah, it is only read on its proper date.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that the Mishnah's ruling is according to Rabbi Akiva, but the Sages say the Megillah is only read in its proper time.

The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda limits the early reading to when the years are established and Israel dwells on their land, but nowadays it is only read in its proper time.
The Gemara asks: In accordance with whose opinion did Rabbi Yehuda rule? If it is according to Rabbi Akiva, even nowadays the ordinance would apply.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yehuda's ruling is according to the Sages, and at least when the years are established, the Megillah is read early, which refutes Rabbi Yochanan's statement.
An alternative version states that Rabbi Yochanan said the Sages themselves only restrict the reading nowadays, but in the ideal time the Mishnah's ruling stands.
A baraita is cited that explicitly supports the alternative version: Rabbi Yehuda says that nowadays, since people look to the Megillah, it is only read in its proper time.

items.text: Rav Ashi's Difficulty with Rabbi Yehuda's Consistency
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's Difficulty with Rabbi Yehuda's Consistency
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi raises a difficulty with Rabbi Yehuda's statement, questioning its consistency with his own views.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi raises a difficulty with Rabbi Yehuda's statement, questioning its consistency with his own views.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's statements
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's statements
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita was established as Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's opinion because of a contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's own statements. Rav Ashi explains that some teach the baraita as Rabbi Yehuda and some as Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, and due to the contradiction, the version attributing it to Rabbi Yehuda is not definitive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the baraita is established as Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's opinion.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda actually said that in the present time, since people look at it, they only read it in its proper time.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from another statement of Rabbi Yehuda, who said that in places where people enter on Monday and Thursday, they read it even in the present time.
The Gemara notes that according to the second statement, they read even in the present time, so the baraita is established as Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda.
The Gemara questions whether the contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's statements is sufficient reason to establish the baraita as Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda.
Rav Ashi explains that some teach the baraita as Rabbi Yehuda and some as Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, and due to the contradiction, the version attributing it to Rabbi Yehuda is not definitive.

items.text: Deriving the reading date for walled cities from the verse
items.text_en: Deriving the reading date for walled cities from the verse
items.desc_en: Rava derives from the verse that unwalled cities read on the 14th and walled cities on the 15th. The Gemara raises and rejects alternative interpretations: that walled cities do not read at all, that they read on both days, or that they may choose either day. The derivation is supported by the word 'their times' and the connection between remembrance and action.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source of the Mishnah's rule that walled cities read on the 15th.
Rava derives from the verse that unwalled cities (פרזים) read on the 14th, implying walled cities read on the 15th.
The Gemara objects that perhaps walled cities do not read at all, and rejects this because they are Israelites and the verse includes all from Hodu to Kush.
The Gemara suggests that walled cities might read on both the 14th and 15th, citing the verse that mentions both days.
The Gemara rejects this by noting that the repeated word 'את' separates the days, assigning each to a different group.
The Gemara suggests that walled cities might choose either day, but the verse uses 'their times' (בזמניהם) to show each has its own fixed time.
The Gemara suggests that walled cities might read on the 13th like Shushan, but this is rejected implicitly.
The Gemara asks for the source that the reading (remembrance) follows the same dates as the celebration (action), and answers with the verse linking remembrance and action.

items.text: Dispute between the Tanna of our Mishnah and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
items.text_en: Dispute between the Tanna of our Mishnah and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that our Mishnah follows a different Tanna than Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, who says walled cities from the time of Achashverosh read on the 15th. The reason for our Tanna is a gezerah shavah from the word 'perazi' connecting to the conquest of Yehoshua bin Nun.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that our Mishnah does not follow the Tanna of a baraita, namely Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha.
The baraita cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's position that walled cities from the time of Achashverosh read on the 15th.
The Gemara explains that the Tanna of our Mishnah derives his position from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on the word 'פרזי' (unwalled), linking to the conquest of Yehoshua bin Nun.

items.text: Why our Tanna rejects Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's view and the case of Shushan
items.text_en: Why our Tanna rejects Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's view and the case of Shushan
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why our Tanna does not accept Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's view, given that he has the gezerah shavah. It explains that Shushan is exceptional because a miracle occurred there, so it reads on the 15th even though it was not walled from Yehoshua's time.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why our Tanna does not adopt Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's view, given that he has the gezerah shavah (verbal analogy) of 'פרזי' 'פרזי'.

The Gemara objects: why would our Tanna reject Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's view, since he indeed has the gezerah shavah (verbal analogy)? It then clarifies that the real question is about Shushan, which fits neither the category of unwalled cities nor walled cities.
Rava answers that Shushan is exceptional because a miracle occurred there, so it reads on the 15th even though it was not walled from Yehoshua's time.

items.text: Interpreting the verse 'medinah u-medinah ve-ir va-ir'
items.text_en: Interpreting the verse 'medinah u-medinah ve-ir va-ir'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that for our Tanna, the verse distinguishes between walled cities from Yehoshua's time and from Achashverosh's time, and between Shushan and other cities. For Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, the verse is expounded as per Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, that a city and its surroundings are judged as the city, with the distance of a mil.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that for our Tanna, the verse 'medinah u-medinah ve-ir va-ir' distinguishes between walled cities from Yehoshua's time and those from Achashverosh's time.

sub.text: Gemara's question about Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.text_en: Gemara's question about Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, who already uses 'medinah u-medinah' to distinguish Shushan from other cities, what purpose does 've-ir va-ir' serve?

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha retorts that even for our Tanna, 'medinah u-medinah' is superfluous given his 'prazi' derivation, so the verse must be expounded as per Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: a city and its surroundings are judged as the city.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's clarification
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's clarification
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya (or Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba) defines the distance as a mil, using the example from Chamtan to Tiberias to illustrate the measure.

items.text: A tangential discussion about the final letters and prophecy
items.text_en: A tangential discussion about the final letters and prophecy
items.desc_en: The Gemara briefly mentions a statement about the final letters (מנצפך) being instituted by the Sages, and raises an objection from the verse that a prophet cannot innovate, citing Rav Chisda about the letters mem and samech in the tablets.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya / Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya / Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya (or Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba) states that the final letters (מנצפך) were instituted by the prophets (צופים).

The Gemara objects: how can prophets innovate letters, given the verse 'אֵלֶּה הַמִּצְוֹת' (these are the commandments) that a prophet may not innovate anything? Moreover, Rav Chisda said that the mem and samech on the tablets were miraculously standing.

items.text: The origin of open and closed parshiyot
items.text_en: The origin of open and closed parshiyot
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the open and closed paragraph breaks in the Torah were given at Sinai or established later. It concludes that they were originally given but forgotten, then reestablished by the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the open and closed parshiyot were established by a miracle, and answers that they were originally known but forgotten, then the Sages (צופים) reestablished them.
The Gemara objects that the Sages cannot innovate new Torah laws, citing the principle that no prophet may add anything new.
The Gemara resolves that the parshiyot were originally given at Sinai, then forgotten, and the Sages reestablished them.

items.text: The revelation of Targum and the Bat Kol
items.text_en: The revelation of Targum and the Bat Kol
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya or Rabbi Chiya bar Abba states that Onkelos the proselyte composed the Targum of Torah from the mouths of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, while Yonatan ben Uzziel composed the Targum of Prophets from the mouths of Chaggai, Zechariah, and Malachi. The earth shook and a Bat Kol questioned who revealed God's secrets, and Yonatan justified his action to prevent disputes. He was prevented from translating Ketuvim because it contains the end of days.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya or Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya or Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya or Rabbi Chiya bar Abba states that Onkelos the proselyte composed the Targum of Torah from the mouths of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya or Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya or Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: The same authority states that Yonatan ben Uzziel composed the Targum of Prophets from the mouths of Chaggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, and the earth shook four hundred parasangs.
A Bat Kol (heavenly voice) questions who revealed God's secrets, and Yonatan ben Uzziel justifies his action to prevent disputes.
Yonatan ben Uzziel sought to translate Ketuvim, but a Bat Kol stopped him because it contains the end of days.

items.text: The Targum of Torah was already established earlier
items.text_en: The Targum of Torah was already established earlier
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Onkelos truly composed the Targum of Torah, citing a verse from Nehemiah that implies Targum existed in Ezra's time. It resolves that the Targum was forgotten and then reestablished.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Onkelos the convert truly composed the Targum of Torah, given evidence that Targum existed earlier.

sub.text: Rav Ika bar Avin citing Rav Chananel citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Ika bar Avin citing Rav Chananel citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Ika bar Avin cites a tradition that the verse in Nehemiah describing public Torah reading includes Targum, implying it existed in Ezra's time.
The Gemara resolves that the Targum was forgotten after Ezra's time and then reestablished by Onkelos.

items.text: Why the earth shook for Targum of Prophets but not Torah
items.text_en: Why the earth shook for Targum of Prophets but not Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Targum of Torah was straightforward, but the Targum of Prophets revealed hidden meanings, as illustrated by the verse about the mourning of Hadadrimmon, which Rav Yosef explains through Targum.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the earth did not quake for the Targum of Torah but did quake for the Targum of Prophets.
The Gemara answers that the Torah's meaning is clear, while the Prophets contain both clear and obscure matters, citing a verse from Zechariah.
Rav Yosef states that without the Targum of this verse, he would not know its meaning, and he provides the Targumic interpretation identifying the mourning as that for Ahab and Josiah.

items.text: The men with Daniel and the power of mazal
items.text_en: The men with Daniel and the power of mazal
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the men who were with Daniel but did not see the vision as Chaggai, Zechariah, and Malachi. It explains that although they did not see, they were frightened because their mazal (spiritual guardian) saw the vision.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse about Daniel's vision and asks who the men were who were with him.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya / Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya / Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya (or Rabbi Chiya bar Abba) identifies the men as the prophets Chaggai, Zechariah, and Malachi.
The Gemara explains the relative superiority: the prophets were greater than Daniel in prophecy, but Daniel was greater in visionary perception.
The Gemara asks: since they did not see the vision, why were they frightened?
The Gemara answers that even though they did not see, their mazal (spiritual guardian) saw the vision, causing them to tremble.

items.text: Remedy for fear from a bad mazal
items.text_en: Remedy for fear from a bad mazal
items.desc_en: Ravina derives from the previous discussion that one who is frightened even without seeing anything is affected by his mazal. The remedy is to recite Shema, or if in a dirty place, move four cubits, or say a folk saying.

sub.desc_en: Ravina derives from the previous discussion that one who is frightened even without seeing anything is affected by his mazal, and provides remedies: reciting Shema, moving four cubits if in a dirty place, or saying a folk saying.

items.text: Priests and Levites must hear the Megillah
items.text_en: Priests and Levites must hear the Megillah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the phrase 'every family and every family' in the Megillah reading includes priestly and Levitical families, who must suspend their Temple service to hear the Megillah. A baraita supports this, and the house of Rabbi learns by kal vachomer that Torah study is also suspended for the Megillah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: now that the phrase 'every province and every city' is interpreted for a different purpose, what does the phrase 'every family and every family' come to teach?
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina answers that it includes priestly and Levitical families, who suspend their Temple service to hear the Megillah reading.
Rav Yehuda cites Rav's statement that priests in their service, Levites on their platform, and Israelites at their post all suspend their duties to hear the Megillah.
A baraita supports the same ruling: priests, Levites, and Israelites all suspend their duties to hear the Megillah.
The house of Rabbi derives by kal vachomer (a fortiori) that Torah study is also suspended for the Megillah, since Temple service is more stringent and is suspended.

items.text: The precedence of Torah study over Temple service
items.text_en: The precedence of Torah study over Temple service
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the kal vachomer by citing Joshua's prostration to the angel, which implies Torah study is more important than Temple service. The angel rebuked Joshua for neglecting both the afternoon Tamid and Torah study, and Rabbi Yochanan explains the angel's statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Temple service is indeed more stringent than Torah study, citing Joshua's prostration to the angel.
The Gemara objects that Joshua should not have prostrated at night due to danger of demons, but distinguishes because the angel identified himself as the captain of the Lord's host.
The Gemara rejects the distinction, questioning whether the angel might lie, but concludes that demons do not utter God's name in vain.
The angel rebuked Joshua for neglecting both the afternoon Tamid and Torah study, and Rabbi Yochanan explains the angel's statement.

items.text: Gemara's initial statement on the greatness of Torah study
items.text_en: Gemara's initial statement on the greatness of Torah study
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a teaching that Torah study is greater than the daily Tamid offerings, based on a verse. This sets up the discussion of priorities.

sub.text: Gemara's statement citing Rav Shmuel bar Unya
sub.text_en: Gemara's statement citing Rav Shmuel bar Unya
sub.desc_en: The Gemara teaches that Torah study is greater than the daily Tamid offerings, citing a verse.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction regarding communal vs. individual Torah study
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction regarding communal vs. individual Torah study
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves an apparent contradiction by distinguishing between communal and individual contexts. It then clarifies that the honor of Torah for an individual is stringent, but the study of Torah for an individual is light.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a communal context (דרבים) and an individual context (דיחיד).
The Gemara objects: is individual Torah study really light? It cites a baraita about mourning practices on מועד (festival days) and ראשי חודשים (New Moons), חנוכה (Hanukkah), and פורים (Purim).
Rabba bar Huna states that מועד (the festival period) does not apply in the presence of a Torah scholar, and certainly not חנוכה (Hanukkah) and פורים (Purim).
The Gemara clarifies: you are speaking of the honor of Torah (כבוד תורה), which is stringent for an individual, but the study of Torah (תלמוד תורה) for an individual is light.

items.text: Rava's established priorities: Megillah, Torah study, Temple service, and met mitzvah
items.text_en: Rava's established priorities: Megillah, Torah study, Temple service, and met mitzvah
items.desc_en: Rava states clear priorities: Megillah reading is preferable to Temple service and Torah study; met mitzvah (burial of an unattended corpse) is preferable to Torah study and Temple service, based on a baraita about a kohen and his sister.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that Megillah reading is preferable to Temple service and Torah study, based on Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina and the Sages of Rabbi's house.
Rava states that met mitzvah (burial of an unattended corpse) is preferable to Torah study and Temple service, citing the verse 'וּלְאַחוֹתוֹ' (and to his sister).

The baraita explains that the verse 'וּלְאַחוֹתוֹ' teaches that a kohen may not become impure for his sister but may become impure for a met mitzvah, establishing the priority of met mitzvah over Temple service.

items.text: Rava's unresolved query: Megillah reading vs. met mitzvah
items.text_en: Rava's unresolved query: Megillah reading vs. met mitzvah
items.desc_en: Rava raises a question: which is greater, Megillah reading (due to publicizing the miracle) or met mitzvah (due to human dignity)? He resolves it in favor of met mitzvah, citing the principle that human dignity overrides a Torah prohibition.

sub.desc_en: Rava raises an unresolved query: which is greater, Megillah reading (due to publicizing the miracle) or met mitzvah (due to human dignity)?
Rava resolves the query in favor of met mitzvah, citing the principle that human dignity overrides a Torah prohibition.

items.text: Definition of a kerakh: adjacent and visible areas
items.text_en: Definition of a kerakh: adjacent and visible areas
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi defines that a kerakh includes its surroundings: adjacent areas (even if not visible) and visible areas (even if not adjacent). The Gemara explains these cases with examples.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi defines that a kerakh (walled city) and everything adjacent to it and everything visible with it is judged as a kerakh.
A baraita clarifies that 'adjacent' applies even if not visible, and 'visible' applies even if not adjacent.
The Gemara explains that the case of 'visible even if not adjacent' is easily found, e.g., a city sitting on a mountaintop.
The Gemara asks how to find a case of 'adjacent even if not visible'.
Rabbi Yirmeya answers: a city sitting in a valley (so it is adjacent but not visible from the main city).

items.text: Further definitions of a kerakh: walled after settlement, ten batlanim, and rebuilt city
items.text_en: Further definitions of a kerakh: walled after settlement, ten batlanim, and rebuilt city
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds three more rulings: a city settled first and walled later is judged as a village; a city without ten batlanim is judged as a village; a city that was destroyed and resettled is judged as a kerakh. The Gemara clarifies the last case refers to loss of ten batlanim.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that a city settled first and walled later is judged as a village (כפר), citing the verse about a walled city (עיר חומה) which implies the wall preceded settlement.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that a city without ten בטלנין (idlers who are available for communal needs) is judged as a village, and the Gemara clarifies that this applies even if such people occasionally visit from elsewhere.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that a city that was destroyed and later resettled is judged as a kerakh (walled city), and the Gemara questions whether this refers to destroyed walls, citing a baraita of Rabbi Eliezer bar Yosei that a city is considered walled even if its walls are currently absent but existed previously.
The Gemara resolves that 'destroyed' here refers to the loss of the ten בטלנין (idlers), not the physical walls.

items.text: Beginning of an additional statement by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.text_en: Beginning of an additional statement by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite another statement by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, but the text cuts off. This section marks the start of a new teaching.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that a walled city without ten idlers is treated as a village.
The Gemara asks what new teaching Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi is conveying.
The Gemara objects that a mishna already defines a large city as having ten idlers, and fewer makes it a village.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling is necessary to teach that even if idlers happen to come from elsewhere, the city is still considered a village.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that a walled city that was destroyed and later resettled is treated as a walled city.
The Gemara asks what 'destroyed' means in this context.
The Gemara objects that if 'destroyed' means the walls were destroyed, the ruling contradicts a baraita of Rabbi Eliezer bar Yosei that a city retains its status even if the wall is gone.
The Gemara resolves that 'destroyed' means the city lost its ten idlers, and once it regains them it is treated as a city.
The Gemara begins to cite another statement by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, but the text cuts off.

items.text: Status of Lod, Ono, and Gei HaCharashim as walled cities from Joshua's time
items.text_en: Status of Lod, Ono, and Gei HaCharashim as walled cities from Joshua's time
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether these cities were walled since Joshua, given that Elpaal and Asa built them. Rabbi Elazar resolves that they were originally walled from Joshua's time, were destroyed during the concubine at Gibeah, rebuilt by Elpaal, destroyed again, and then fortified by Asa.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Lod, Ono, and Gei HaCharashim were walled cities from Joshua's time, given that Elpaal built them.
The Gemara further objects that King Asa also built these cities, contradicting the claim that they were from Joshua's time.
Rabbi Elazar resolves that the cities were originally walled from Joshua's time, were destroyed in the concubine at Gibeah incident, rebuilt by Elpaal, destroyed again, and then fortified by Asa.
The Gemara cites a verse where Asa says 'let us build these cities,' implying they existed originally, confirming Rabbi Elazar's explanation.

items.text: Women are obligated in Megillah reading
items.text_en: Women are obligated in Megillah reading
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that women are obligated to hear the Megillah because they were also part of the miracle of Purim.

sub.desc_en: רבי יהושע בן לוי (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) states that women are obligated in the reading of the Megilla because they too were part of that miracle.
רבי יהושע בן לוי (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) further states that when Purim occurs on שבת (Shabbat), one asks questions and expounds upon the subject of the day.
The Gemara questions why Purim is singled out, since the same principle applies even to יום טוב (festival days).

A ברייתא (baraita) is cited: Moses enacted that Israel should ask and expound on the subject of the day — halakhot of פסח (Passover) on Passover, of עצרת (Shavuot) on Shavuot, and of חג (Sukkot) on Sukkot.

The Gemara answers: Purim was necessary, lest you say we should decree a prohibition due to the concern of רבה (Rabba) about carrying the Megilla; therefore, רבי יהושע בן לוי (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) teaches us that expounding is permitted.

items.text: Purim on Shabbat: inquiring and expounding on the day's topic
items.text_en: Purim on Shabbat: inquiring and expounding on the day's topic
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that when Purim falls on Shabbat, one should inquire and expound on the day's topic. The Gemara questions why this is unique to Purim, as it applies to all festivals. It explains that the ruling is necessary to prevent the decree of Rabbah (that one might neglect the Megillah).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that one is obligated to read the Megilla at night and repeat it by day, citing Psalms 22:3.

items.text: Obligation to read the Megillah at night and repeat it by day
items.text_en: Obligation to read the Megillah at night and repeat it by day
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that one must read the Megillah at night and repeat it by day, citing Psalms. The Gemara initially misunderstands this as reading the Megillah at night and reviewing its Mishnah by day, but Rabbi Yirmeya clarifies that it means reading the entire Megillah twice, like one who reads a parashah and then reviews it. A supporting statement from Rabbi Chelbo in the name of Ulla Bira'ah is cited.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states the obligation to read the Megillah at night and repeat it by day, citing Psalms.
The Gemara initially misunderstands that the obligation is to read the Megillah at night and review its Mishnah by day.
Rabbi Yirmeya clarifies that the obligation is to read the entire Megillah twice, like one who reads a parashah and then reviews it.

sub.text: Rabbi Chelbo in the name of Ulla Bira'ah
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chelbo in the name of Ulla Bira'ah
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo cites Ulla Bira'ah who supports the same obligation with a different verse from Psalms.

items.text: Villagers advance reading to market day
items.text_en: Villagers advance reading to market day
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that villagers advance the reading to the market day (Monday or Thursday). Rabbi Chanina explains that the Sages were lenient with villagers to allow them to advance the reading so they could provide water and food for their brethren in the cities.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that villagers advance the reading to the market day (Monday or Thursday).
Rabbi Chanina explains that the Sages were lenient with villagers to allow them to advance the reading so they could provide water and food for their brethren in the cities.

items.text: First objection: If it's a city enactment, why not read on Monday?
items.text_en: First objection: If it's a city enactment, why not read on Monday?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the idea that the early reading for villages is a city enactment, citing a mishnah where villages read on Monday when Purim falls on Tuesday, and questions why they wouldn't read on the market day to get ten readers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the idea that the early reading for villages is a city enactment, citing a mishnah where villages read on Monday when Purim falls on Tuesday, and argues that if it were a city enactment they would read on the market day to gather ten readers, but the Sages did not institute ten.

items.text: Second objection: Thursday case
items.text_en: Second objection: Thursday case
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another objection: when Purim falls on Thursday, villages read on that day, but if it were a city enactment, they should read on the market day of the 11th, but we do not push from one market day to another.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a second objection: if Purim falls on Thursday, villages read on that day, but if it were a city enactment, they should advance to the market day of the 11th, yet we do not push from one market day to another.

items.text: Third objection: Rabbi Yehuda's statement and resolution
items.text_en: Third objection: Rabbi Yehuda's statement and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yehuda's statement that villages only read early where they gather on Mondays and Thursdays, implying the enactment is for villages, not cities. The Gemara then corrects the reason: not so they can supply water and food, but because they supply water and food to their brethren in cities.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yehuda's statement that villages only read early where they gather on Mondays and Thursdays, challenging the assumption that the enactment is for cities.
The Gemara corrects the reason: not so they can supply water and food, but because they supply water and food to their brethren in cities.

items.text: Question on mishnah's order: months vs. days
items.text_en: Question on mishnah's order: months vs. days
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishnah first lists days by month order (Monday, Thursday, etc.) and then switches to day order (Friday, Shabbat). It answers that because the cases are reversed, it lists by day order.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishnah first lists days by month order (Monday, Thursday, etc.) and then switches to day order (Friday, Shabbat).
The Gemara answers that because the cases are reversed (the mishnah's order flips), it lists by day order.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi and Tanna Kamma on Friday case
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi and Tanna Kamma on Friday case
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the mishnah's ruling for Friday as either Rabbi or Rabbi Yosei. It explains the Tanna Kamma's view that villages read on the market day, citing the verse 'each and every year' to show villages precede walled cities, and Rabbi's view that villages are not pushed from their place, with the Gemara noting the impossibility of reading on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion is expressed in the mishnah regarding the case where Purim falls on Friday, suggesting it is either Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi or Rabbi Yosei.

The Gemara cites a baraita presenting Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view: when the fourteenth occurs on Friday, villages and large towns advance to the market day, while walled cities read on Friday; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says large towns should not be deferred, and both read on Friday.

The Gemara explains the Tanna Kamma's reasoning: the verse 'each and every year' teaches that just as in every other year large towns precede walled cities, so too here large towns precede walled cities.
The Gemara objects: the verse could imply that large towns are not deferred from their place, but the Gemara rejects this because it is impossible to read on Shabbat.

The Gemara explains Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's reasoning: the verse 'each and every year' teaches that just as in every other year large towns are not deferred from their place, so too here they are not deferred.
The Gemara objects: the verse could imply that large towns precede walled cities, but the Gemara rejects this because it is impossible to read on Shabbat.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Tanna Kamma on Friday case
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Tanna Kamma on Friday case
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the baraita with Rabbi Yosei, who says walled cities do not precede villages. The Tanna Kamma argues from the verse that their times are different, while Rabbi Yosei argues that walled cities do not precede villages, with the Gemara noting the impossibility of reading on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the opinion of Rabbi Yosei is and cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosei rules that walled cities do not precede large towns, and both read on Friday.

The first tanna explains his reasoning from the verse 'בכל שנה ושנה' (in every year): just as in every year large towns read on the fourteenth and their times differ, so too here large towns read on the fourteenth and the times differ.
The Gemara objects that the verse could imply that walled cities never precede large towns, and answers that here it is impossible to fulfill all conditions.
Rabbi Yosei explains his reasoning from the same verse: just as in every year walled cities do not precede large towns, so too here they do not precede them.
The Gemara objects that the verse could imply that the times for different settlements are different, and answers that here it is impossible to fulfill all conditions.

items.text: Contradiction in Rabbi's view: villages pushed to market day
items.text_en: Contradiction in Rabbi's view: villages pushed to market day
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Rabbi elsewhere says villages pushed from their place should be pushed to the market day, but here he says they are not pushed. It resolves that there, their time is Shabbat, so since they are pushed, they are pushed; here, their time is Friday.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi (רבי) truly holds that large towns are not deferred to the market day, citing a baraita where he says that since they are already deferred from Shabbat, they should be deferred to the market day.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: in the baraita, the towns' designated time is Shabbat, so since they are already deferred, they are deferred further; here, their designated time is Friday, so they are not deferred.

items.text: Rav Helbo's statement aligned with Rabbi
items.text_en: Rav Helbo's statement aligned with Rabbi
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Helbo quoting Rav Huna that when Purim falls on Shabbat, all who are pushed are pushed to the market day, and identifies this view as following Rabbi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion is followed by Rav Helbo's statement that when Purim falls on Shabbat, all are pushed to the market day.
The Gemara objects that not everyone is pushed, since walled cities read on the next day.
The Gemara corrects the statement: anyone who is pushed is pushed to the market day.
The Gemara concludes that Rav Helbo's statement follows Rabbi's opinion.

items.text: Reason for not reading Megillah on Shabbat
items.text_en: Reason for not reading Megillah on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Megillah is not read on Shabbat: Rabbah says because not everyone is proficient, leading to a decree lest one carry it four cubits in public domain; Rav Yosef says because the poor rely on the reading for distribution. A baraita supports Rav Yosef.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the consensus that the Megillah is not read on Shabbat.
The Gemara asks for the reason why the Megillah is not read on Shabbat.
Rabbah explains that since not everyone is proficient in reading the Megillah, there is a decree lest one carry it four cubits in the public domain on Shabbat.
The Gemara notes that the same reasoning applies to the shofar and the lulav.
Rav Yosef gives an alternative reason: the poor rely on the Megillah reading to know when to collect their charity distributions.
A baraita supports Rav Yosef by stating that villages collect and distribute charity on the day of the Megillah reading.
The Gemara objects to the baraita's phrasing 'even though they said', arguing that the collection is precisely because they said so.
The Gemara corrects the baraita's wording to 'since they said', emphasizing that the poor's anticipation of the reading is the reason for the collection and distribution.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rav Asi on Megillah reading with a minyan
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rav Asi on Megillah reading with a minyan
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a statement that joy is only observed in its proper time. Rav rules that the Megillah may be read even by an individual when read in its proper time, but requires ten when read out of time. Rav Asi requires ten in both cases, and Rav deferred to Rav Asi in practice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a general principle that rejoicing is practiced only in its designated time.
Rav rules that the Megillah may be read even by an individual when read in its proper time, but requires a quorum of ten when read out of time.
Rav Asi disagrees and requires a quorum of ten in both cases, whether in its proper time or not.
The Gemara relates that in practice Rav deferred to Rav Asi's opinion and gathered ten men even when reading in its proper time.

items.text: Challenge to Rav from a statement about Purim on Shabbat
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav from a statement about Purim on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav's position by citing a statement from Rav that if Purim falls on Shabbat, the reading is on Friday. The Gemara initially interprets this to mean that out-of-time reading is like in-time, allowing individuals. It then rejects this, explaining that the statement refers to the requirement of ten for Megillah reading, and that it comes to exclude Rabbi's opinion that villages should be postponed to market day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav's position by citing a statement from Rav that if Purim falls on Shabbat, the reading is on Friday, and initially interprets this to mean that out-of-time reading is like in-time, allowing individuals.

The Gemara rejects the initial interpretation, explaining that the statement refers to the requirement of ten for Megillah reading, and that it comes to exclude Rabbi's opinion that villages should be postponed to market day.

items.text: Mishnah: Definition of a large city
items.text_en: Mishnah: Definition of a large city
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines a large city as one with ten batlanim (men who are free to attend synagogue). Fewer than that makes it a village.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines a large city as one with ten batlanim (men free to attend synagogue); fewer than that makes it a village.

items.text: Mishnah: Which observances are postponed and which are advanced
items.text_en: Mishnah: Which observances are postponed and which are advanced
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists observances that are advanced but not postponed (like Megillah for villages) and those that are postponed but not advanced (like the wood-offering of priests, Tisha B'Av, the Festival-offering, and Hakhel). It adds that even when advanced, mourning, fasting, and gifts to the poor are permitted. Rabbi Yehuda qualifies this based on market days.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for these times (Megillah) one advances and does not postpone, but for the wood-offering of priests, Tisha B'Av, the Festival-offering, and Hakhel, one postpones and does not advance.
The Mishnah adds that even when the Megillah reading is advanced, eulogizing, fasting, and giving gifts to the poor are permitted.
Rabbi Yehuda qualifies the rule: the Megillah is read on the day of assembly only in places where villagers enter town on Monday and Thursday; otherwise, it is read only in its proper time.

items.text: Gemara: Source for advancing Megillah
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for advancing Megillah
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the ten batlanim are in the synagogue. It then asks why the Megillah is advanced and not postponed, and Rabbi Abba in the name of Shmuel answers with the verse 'and it shall not pass'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita clarifying that the ten idlers mentioned in the mishna are those who sit in the synagogue.
The Gemara asks for the reason why the Megillah is advanced and not postponed.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba in the name of Shmuel answers that the verse 'and it shall not pass' (וְלֹא יַעֲבוֹר) indicates that the designated time must not pass without the reading.

items.text: Derashot about counting days and hours
items.text_en: Derashot about counting days and hours
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba in the name of Shmuel derives that one does not count days for years, but months for years. The rabbis of Caesarea in the name of Rabbi Abba derive that one does not calculate hours for months, but days for months.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba in the name of Shmuel derives from the verse 'לחדשי השנה' (for the months of the year) that one counts months for years, not days.

sub.text: Rabbis of Caesarea citing Rabbi Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbis of Caesarea citing Rabbi Abba
sub.desc_en: The rabbis of Caesarea in the name of Rabbi Abba derive from the verse 'עד חדש ימים' (until a month of days) that one calculates days for months, not hours.

items.text: Reasons for postponing Tisha B'Av, Chagigah, and Hakhel
items.text_en: Reasons for postponing Tisha B'Av, Chagigah, and Hakhel
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Tisha B'Av is postponed because one does not advance calamity. Chagigah and Hakhel are postponed because their obligation time has not yet arrived. A baraisa states that Chagigah and 'all the time of Chagigah' are postponed. The Gemara questions what 'time of Chagigah' means, and Rav Oshaya explains it refers to the Chagigah on Shabbat and the olat re'iyah even on Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reasons for postponing Tisha B'Av, Chagigah, and Hakhel: Tisha B'Av is not advanced because one does not advance calamity, and Chagigah and Hakhel are not advanced because their obligation time has not yet arrived.
A baraita states that Chagigah and 'all the time of Chagigah' are postponed, and the Gemara questions what 'time of Chagigah' means.

Rav Oshaya explains that the baraita means that the Chagigah is postponed when it falls on Shabbat, and the olat re'iyah (burnt-offering of appearance) is postponed even when it falls on Yom Tov, because the time of Chagigah is postponed.

items.text: Attribution to Beit Shammai
items.text_en: Attribution to Beit Shammai
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rav Oshaya's statement follows Beit Shammai, who hold that one brings peace-offerings on Yom Tov but not burnt-offerings, while Beit Hillel allow both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the mishna as following Beit Shammai, who permit bringing peace-offerings on Yom Tov but prohibit placing hands on them.
The Gemara contrasts Beit Shammai's view with that of Beit Hillel, who permit bringing both peace-offerings and burnt-offerings on Yom Tov and allow placing hands on them.

items.text: Rava and Rav Ashi on the extent of postponement
items.text_en: Rava and Rav Ashi on the extent of postponement
items.desc_en: Rava limits postponement to the entire festival period, citing a Mishnah. Rav Ashi extends it even to Shavuot, which is only one day, citing a Mishnah that if Shavuot falls on Shabbat, slaughter is after Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that the Festival peace-offering (חגיגה) may be postponed only for the entire festival period, not beyond, citing the Mishnah that one who did not offer it on the first day may do so throughout the festival, but after the festival passes he is no longer liable.
Rav Ashi extends the postponement even to Shavuot (עצרת), which is a one-day festival, citing the Mishnah that if Shavuot falls on Shabbat, the day of slaughter is after Shabbat.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Chanina about Rabbi planting on Purim
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Chanina about Rabbi planting on Purim
items.desc_en: The daf ends with Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina stating that Rabbi planted a sapling on Purim.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar reports in the name of Rabbi Chanina that Rabbi planted a sapling on Purim.

items.text: Opening story about Rabbi and the fasts
items.text_en: Opening story about Rabbi and the fasts
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rabbi bathed in the bathhouse of Tzippori on the seventeenth of Tammuz and sought to uproot Tisha b'Av, but the sages did not agree. Rabbi Abba bar Zavda corrects the story: Tisha b'Av fell on Shabbat and was postponed, and Rabbi said since it was postponed it should be entirely nullified, but the sages disagreed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rabbi bathed in the bathhouse of Tzippori on the seventeenth of Tammuz and sought to uproot Tisha b'Av, but the sages did not agree.
Rabbi Abba bar Zavda corrects the story: Tisha b'Av fell on Shabbat and was postponed, and Rabbi said since it was postponed it should be entirely nullified, but the sages disagreed.
The Gemara cites the verse 'טובים השנים מן האחד' (two are better than one) to support the sages' position that the fast should not be nullified.

items.text: Question about Rabbi planting on Purim
items.text_en: Question about Rabbi planting on Purim
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: How could Rabbi have planted a tree on Purim? It cites a baraita that Purim is a day of joy, feast, and holiday, prohibiting eulogy, fasting, and work. The answer is that Rabbi was born on the fourteenth and planted on the fifteenth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi could have planted a tree on Purim, citing a baraita that Purim prohibits eulogy, fasting, and work.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi was born on the fourteenth and planted on the fifteenth, which is not Purim for walled cities.

items.text: Objection based on Tiberias being walled
items.text_en: Objection based on Tiberias being walled
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Rabbi was in Tiberias, which is a walled city from the time of Joshua, so Purim is on the fifteenth, not the fourteenth. Therefore, the answer is reversed: Rabbi was born on the fifteenth and planted on the fourteenth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi was in Tiberias, which is a walled city from Joshua's time, so Purim should be on the fifteenth, contradicting the previous answer.
The Gemara gives a second answer: Rabbi was born on the fifteenth and planted on the fourteenth, reversing the earlier claim.

items.text: Uncertainty about Tiberias' status
items.text_en: Uncertainty about Tiberias' status
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether it is certain that Tiberias is walled, since Hezekiah read the Megillah there on both the fourteenth and fifteenth, indicating doubt. The Gemara resolves that Hezekiah was uncertain, but for Rabbi it was certain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether it is certain that Tiberias is walled, given that Hezekiah read the Megillah there on both the fourteenth and fifteenth, indicating doubt.
The Gemara resolves that Hezekiah was uncertain about Tiberias' status, but for Rabbi it was certain.

items.text: Permissibility of work on Purim
items.text_en: Permissibility of work on Purim
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Even if it were certain, is work permitted? It cites Megillat Ta'anit that the fourteenth and fifteenth are Purim days, forbidding eulogy and fasting, but Rava says work is only forbidden on one day. The Gemara brings a story of Rav cursing a man who planted flax on Purim, and Rabbah bar Rava says that eulogy and fasting were accepted as prohibitions, but work was not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions: Even if it were certain that Tiberias is a walled city, is work permitted on Purim? It cites Megillat Ta'anit that the 14th and 15th are Purim days, forbidding eulogy and fasting.
Rava answers that the prohibition of eulogy and fasting applies to both days, but work is forbidden only on one day.
The Gemara objects: But Rav saw a man planting flax on Purim, cursed him, and his flax did not grow, implying work is forbidden.
Rabbah bar Rava resolves that eulogy and fasting were accepted as prohibitions, but work was not accepted, so Rav's curse was for a different reason.

items.text: Proof from verses and Rav's curse explained
items.text_en: Proof from verses and Rav's curse explained
items.desc_en: The Gemara proves from the verses that initially 'yom tov' was written, but later only 'feast and joy' are mentioned, showing work was not prohibited. Rav's curse was because in his place, people had accepted the prohibition, and Rabbi's place had not accepted it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verses: initially 'שמחה ומשתה ויום טוב' (joy, feast, and holiday) was written, but later only 'משתה ושמחה' (feast and joy) appears, omitting 'יום טוב' (holiday), proving that work was not prohibited.
The Gemara explains that Rav cursed the man because in Rav's place, people had accepted the prohibition of work on Purim, whereas in Rabbi's place they had not accepted it.

items.text: Alternative answer: planting of joy
items.text_en: Alternative answer: planting of joy
items.desc_en: Alternatively, Rabbi planted a tree of joy, as per the Mishnah that during times of distress one reduces business, building, and planting, but only joyful building and planting are prohibited. The Gemara defines a joyful planting as planting royal arbors.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative answer: Rabbi indeed planted, but it was a planting of joy, as per the Mishnah.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah that during times of distress one reduces business, building, and planting, but only joyful building and planting are prohibited.
A baraita clarifies that the prohibited building is a joyful building (e.g., a wedding house for one's son) and the prohibited planting is a joyful planting (e.g., planting royal arbors).

items.text: Hezekiah's doubt about Tiberias explained
items.text_en: Hezekiah's doubt about Tiberias explained
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to Hezekiah's doubt: Is Tiberias walled? A verse lists Rakkat as Tiberias, a fortified city, but one side is the sea. The doubt is whether the sea serves as a wall for the purpose of Megillah reading, since the verse says 'which has a wall' excluding a sea wall, but the doubt is about the definition of 'walled' for Megillah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara restates Hezekiah's practice of reading the Megillah in Tiberias on both the 14th and 15th, due to doubt whether it was walled from Joshua's time.
The Gemara questions how Hezekiah could doubt Tiberias, since a verse lists Rakkat (identified as Tiberias) among fortified cities.
The Gemara explains the doubt: one side of Tiberias is a sea wall (שור דימא), not a man-made wall.
The Gemara objects: if it's a sea wall, it is certainly not a wall, citing a baraita that excludes a sea wall (שור אגר) and specifically exempts Tiberias.

The Gemara resolves: Hezekiah had no doubt about the laws of walled cities (בתי ערי חומה), but doubted regarding Megillah reading — whether the distinction between unwalled (פרזים) and walled (מוקפין) is based on visibility (מגלו) or protection (מגנו), and since the sea wall provides protection, the doubt remains.

items.text: Rav Asi's practice and Rabbi Yochanan's statement
items.text_en: Rav Asi's practice and Rabbi Yochanan's statement
items.desc_en: Rav Asi read the Megillah in Hutzal on both the fourteenth and fifteenth due to doubt about its walled status. Some say Rav Asi stated Hutzal of Beit Binyamin is definitely walled. Rabbi Yochanan recalls asking the elders about this matter.

sub.desc_en: Reports that Rav Asi read the Megillah in Hutzal on both the fourteenth and fifteenth due to doubt about its walled status.
Presents an alternative version: Rav Asi stated definitively that Hutzal of Beit Binyamin is a walled city from Joshua's time.
Rabbi Yochanan recalls that as a youth he asked the elders about this matter, implying support for the doubt.

items.text: Initial identification of place names
items.text_en: Initial identification of place names
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies Chammat with Tiberias (due to its hot springs), Rakkath with Sepphoris (because it sits high like a bank), and Kinneret with Ginosar (because its fruits are sweet like the sound of harps).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies Chammat with Tiberias (due to its hot springs), Rakkath with Sepphoris (because it sits high like a bank), and Kinneret with Ginosar (because its fruits are sweet like the sound of harps).

items.text: Rava's objection and proof from eulogies
items.text_en: Rava's objection and proof from eulogies
items.desc_en: Rava objects to identifying Rakkath with Sepphoris, citing eulogies that mention Rakkath in connection with Tiberias. He brings a eulogy for Rabbi Zeira that calls the land of Israel 'Rakkath' and mourns the loss of a precious vessel.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to identifying Rakkath with Sepphoris, citing eulogies that mention Rakkath in connection with Tiberias.
A eulogy for Rabbi Zeira calls the land of Israel 'Rakkath' and mourns the loss of a precious vessel, supporting Rava's identification of Rakkath with Tiberias.

items.text: Alternative identifications and reasons for names
items.text_en: Alternative identifications and reasons for names
items.desc_en: Rabbah identifies Chammat with Gerar's hot springs, Rakkath with Tiberias (because even its empty ones are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate), and Kinneret with Ginosar. Rabbi Yirmeya and Rava give reasons for Tiberias's name: sitting at the navel of the land and having good sight.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah rejects the earlier identifications and identifies Chammat with Gerar's hot springs, Rakkath with Tiberias (because even its empty ones are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate), and Kinneret with Ginosar.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's reason for Tiberias's name
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's reason for Tiberias's name
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya explains that Tiberias is called Rakkath, but its name Tiberias derives from its sitting at the navel of the Land of Israel.
Rava explains that Tiberias is called Rakkath, but its name Tiberias derives from its good sight.

items.text: Zeira identifies Kitron with Sepphoris
items.text_en: Zeira identifies Kitron with Sepphoris
items.desc_en: Zeira states that Kitron is Sepphoris, named because it sits on a mountain top like a bird.

sub.desc_en: Zeira identifies Kitron as Sepphoris, explaining that it is called Sepphoris because it sits on a mountain top like a bird.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and Zebulun's complaint
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and Zebulun's complaint
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Zeira's identification, noting Kitron was in Zebulun's territory and Zebulun complained about his mountainous portion. God reassured him through the חלָּזון (snail) and glass. The Gemara concludes that despite Sepphoris's bounty, Zebulun preferred fields and vineyards.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Zeira's identification of Kitron as Sepphoris, noting that Kitron was in Zebulun's territory.
The Gemara cites a verse showing Zebulun complained about his mountainous portion.
Zebulun complains to God that his brothers received fields and vineyards while he received mountains and seas.
God reassures Zebulun that all need him through the חלָּזון (snail) and glass.
Rav Yosef explains the verse: 'שְׂפוּנֵי' is the חלָּזון (snail), 'טְמוּנֵי' is tarit (a type of fish), and 'חוֹל' is white glass.
God gives Zebulun a sign that anyone who takes from him without payment will not profit from his merchandise.
The Gemara objects: if Kitron is Sepphoris, why would Zebulun complain, since Sepphoris is excellent?
The Gemara rejects the possibility that Sepphoris lacks milk and honey, citing Reish Lakish's testimony of a 16-mil by 16-mil area of milk and honey.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that Sepphoris's area is smaller than its brothers', citing Rabbah bar bar Chanah's testimony of the entire land's milk and honey area.
The Gemara concludes that despite Sepphoris's bounty, Zebulun preferred fields and vineyards, as indicated by the verse.

items.text: Ekrón as Caesarea and future redemption
items.text_en: Ekrón as Caesarea and future redemption
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu identifies 'Ekrón shall be uprooted' as Caesarea, which was a peg for Israel in Greek times. Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina interprets verses about removing blood and abominations as referring to their temples and theaters, which will become places for Torah study. Rabbi Yitzchak identifies Leshem with Pamyas and Ekron with Caesarea as a metropolis.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu identifies the verse 'Ekrón shall be uprooted' as referring to Caesarea, which served as a peg for Israel during Greek times and was later called 'Achidat Migdal Shir' after the Hasmonean victory.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina interprets the verse about removing blood and abominations as referring to Edom's temples and theaters, which will become places for public Torah study.
Rabbi Yitzchak identifies Leshem as Pamyas and Ekron as Caesarea, which was a metropolis for kings, with two versions about its role in raising or appointing kings.

items.text: Inverse relationship between Caesarea and Jerusalem
items.text_en: Inverse relationship between Caesarea and Jerusalem
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that Caesarea and Jerusalem cannot both be inhabited or destroyed simultaneously; when one is full, the other is desolate, citing verses. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak derives this from 'and nation shall prevail over nation.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a principle: Caesarea and Jerusalem cannot both be destroyed or both inhabited simultaneously; one is full when the other is desolate, citing the verse 'אמלאה החרבה' (I am filled, she is laid waste).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak derives the same inverse relationship from the verse 'ולאום מלאום יאמץ' (and one nation shall prevail over the other).

items.text: Prayers of Isaac and Jacob regarding Esau
items.text_en: Prayers of Isaac and Jacob regarding Esau
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak interprets verses about the wicked not learning righteousness as Isaac's plea for Esau to be favored, but God rejects it. He then interprets a verse as Jacob's prayer that God not grant Esau his desires, and that his schemes not succeed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak introduces a verse and presents Isaac's plea for Esau to be favored, which God rejects because Esau is wicked and does not learn righteousness.
Rabbi Yitzchak interprets another verse as Jacob's prayer that God not grant Esau his desires and that his schemes not succeed.

items.text: Opening aggadic statements about Rome and Torah study
items.text_en: Opening aggadic statements about Rome and Torah study
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents aggadic teachings: the military might of Germamia of Edom and Rome, Rabbi Yitzchak's principle that one who toils in Torah will find success, and the distinction between Torah study and business.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with an aggadic description of the military might of Germamia of Edom.
Rabbi Chama bar Chanina provides a detailed account of the number of crowned officials and governors in Germamia and Rome and their daily conflicts.
Rabbi Yitzchak states a principle: one who claims to have toiled and found Torah success is believed, but not one who claims success without toil or toil without success.

The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yitzchak's principle applies to Torah study, but for business success is from Heaven; even for Torah, sharpening understanding requires toil, but retaining learning requires heavenly assistance.

items.text: Contradiction about engaging with the wicked
items.text_en: Contradiction about engaging with the wicked
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak says not to engage with the wicked, but Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Dostai bar Matun say it is permitted. The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the wicked's personal matters and heavenly matters, or between a completely righteous person and an incomplete one, or by noting that the wicked's 'hour of good fortune' is exceptional.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that one should not engage with a wicked person whose hour is fortunate, citing verses that the wicked's ways succeed, he wins in judgment, and sees his enemies fall.

The Gemara objects: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and Rabbi Dostai bar Matun permit engaging with the wicked, and they reinterpret the verse 'אל תתחר במרעים' as warning not to be like them, not to avoid them.
The Gemara resolves: Rabbi Yitzchak's warning applies to the wicked's personal matters, while Rabbi Yochanan's permission applies to heavenly matters.

Alternatively, both refer to personal matters: Rabbi Yitzchak speaks of a completely righteous person who is not swallowed by the wicked, while Rabbi Yochanan speaks of an incomplete righteous person who is swallowed, citing Rav Huna's interpretation of the verse.
Alternatively, the case of a wicked person whose 'hour of good fortune' is exceptional is different and not subject to the general rule.

items.text: Description of the great city of Rome
items.text_en: Description of the great city of Rome
items.desc_en: Ulla describes Italy of Greece as the great city of Rome, detailing its vast size, markets, and privileges for residents and natives.

sub.desc_en: Ulla identifies Italy of Greece as the great city of Rome, describing its vast size of 300 parasangs by 300 parasangs, 365 markets, and the king dining daily in one of them.
Ulla details the privileges for residents and natives, the 3,000 bathhouses, 500 windows emitting smoke outside the wall, and the city's boundaries of sea, mountains, an iron barrier, and a marsh.

items.text: Mishnah: Megillah reading in a leap year
items.text_en: Mishnah: Megillah reading in a leap year
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the Megillah was read in Adar I and the year was intercalated, it is read again in Adar II. The only difference between Adar I and Adar II is Megillah reading and gifts to the poor.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if the Megillah was read in Adar I and the year was intercalated, it is read again in Adar II, and the only difference between the two Adars is Megillah reading and gifts to the poor.

items.text: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes which Tanna authored the Mishnah, considering the positions of Tanna Kamma, Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosi, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. It resolves the difficulty by suggesting the Mishnah follows Tanna Kamma (with gifts included) or Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel (with a missing clause about eulogies and fasts).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting that regarding the order of Torah portions, both Adars are equal.
The Gemara asks which Tanna authored the Mishnah, ruling out Tanna Kamma, Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosi, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
The baraita cites Tanna Kamma's position that all mitzvot of the second Adar apply to the first, except Megillah reading.

sub.text: Supporting baraita — Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosi
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita — Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosi
sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosi's position that one does not read the Megillah in the second Adar, as all mitzvot of the second apply to the first.

sub.text: Supporting baraita — Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita — Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in the name of Rabbi Yosi that one reads the Megillah in the second Adar, as mitzvot of the second do not apply to the first, and both agree on eulogies and fasts.
The Gemara asks how Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel differs from Tanna Kamma, since both require reading in the second Adar.

Rav Pappa explains that the difference lies in the order of Torah portions: Tanna Kamma requires them ideally in the second Adar, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel requires them in the second Adar even if already read in the first.

The Gemara re-asks which Tanna authored the Mishnah, noting that each candidate contradicts a clause: Tanna Kamma contradicts gifts, Rabbi Eliezer contradicts Megillah reading, and Rabban Shimon contradicts the order of portions.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah follows Tanna Kamma, and the mention of Megillah reading implies gifts as well, since they are linked.
The Gemara alternatively resolves that the Mishnah follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and it is missing a clause about eulogies and fasts being equal, while not dealing with the order of portions.

items.text: Halakhic ruling and scriptural basis for the dispute
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling and scriptural basis for the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. The Gemara explains that both Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel derive their positions from the verse 'year by year', with Rabbi Eliezer favoring proximity to Shevat and Rabban Shimon favoring proximity to Nisan. The reasons are given: Rabbi Eliezer avoids passing over mitzvot, while Rabban Shimon prefers connecting redemption to redemption.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel who spoke in the name of Rabbi Yosi.
Rabbi Yochanan states that both Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel derive their positions from the same verse 'year by year'.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosi interprets 'year by year' to mean Adar adjacent to Shevat.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel interprets 'year by year' to mean Adar adjacent to Nisan.
The Gemara asks: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosi's reasoning is understandable (avoiding passing over mitzvot), but what is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning?
Rabbi Tavi explains that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel prefers connecting redemption (Purim) to redemption (Passover).
Rabbi Elazar provides an alternative scriptural basis: the verse 'to establish this second letter of Purim' implies a second Adar.
The Gemara concludes that both reasons were necessary to write.

items.text: Clarification of the redundant terms 'hashnit' and 'bekhol shana v'shana'
items.text_en: Clarification of the redundant terms 'hashnit' and 'bekhol shana v'shana'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the verse uses both 'hashnit' (the second) and 'bekhol shana v'shana' (every year). Without 'hashnit', one might think the obligation applies only from the second year onward; without 'bekhol shana v'shana', one might think it applies only in the first and second years.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the redundancy of 'hashnit' and 'bekhol shana v'shana' by showing each term prevents a different mistaken inference about the obligation's scope.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei's interpretation and Esther's request to the Sages
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei's interpretation and Esther's request to the Sages
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei uses the word 'hashnit' to teach that Purim was first established in Shushan and later throughout the world. The Gemara then recounts that Esther asked the Sages to establish her holiday for future generations; they feared it would provoke the nations, but she replied that she was already recorded in the royal chronicles.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei interprets the word 'השנית' (the second).
Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda explains that the word teaches that Purim was first established in Shushan and later throughout the entire world.

Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda recounts that Esther asked the Sages to establish her holiday for future generations; they feared provoking the nations, but she replied that she was already recorded in the royal chronicles.

items.text: Esther's request to be written in the canon and the scriptural support
items.text_en: Esther's request to be written in the canon and the scriptural support
items.desc_en: A second version of the story: Esther asked the Sages to write her book for posterity. They initially refused, citing the verse 'Have I not written for you three times' (implying only the Torah, Prophets, and Writings), until they found a verse in the Torah—'Write this as a memorial in the book'—which they interpreted as including the Megillah.

sub.desc_en: Esther sends a request to the Sages to write her book for posterity.
The Sages refuse, citing the verse 'Have I not written for you three times' (Proverbs 22:20), implying only three divisions of the canon, not a fourth.
The Sages find a verse in the Torah—'Write this as a memorial in the book' (Exodus 17:14)—which they interpret as including the Megillah in the canon.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute over the interpretation of 'k'tov zot zikaron basefer'
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute over the interpretation of 'k'tov zot zikaron basefer'
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Elazar HaModa'i regarding the meaning of the verse. Rabbi Yehoshua assigns 'zot' to the Torah, 'zikaron' to Mishneh Torah, and 'basefer' to the Prophets; Rabbi Elazar HaModa'i assigns 'zot' to the Torah and Mishneh Torah, 'zikaron' to the Prophets, and 'basefer' to the Megillah.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces a dispute: Rabbi Yehoshua interprets 'k'tov zot' as what is written here (the Torah), 'zikaron' as Mishneh Torah, and 'basefer' as the Prophets.
Rabbi Elazar HaModa'i assigns 'zot' to the Torah and Mishneh Torah, 'zikaron' to the Prophets, and 'basefer' to the Megillah.

items.text: Shmuel's statement that Esther does not defile the hands and the contradiction
items.text_en: Shmuel's statement that Esther does not defile the hands and the contradiction
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel that the Book of Esther does not defile the hands (i.e., is not fully canonical). The Gemara questions this, noting that Shmuel elsewhere said Esther was composed with ruach hakodesh. The resolution: it was composed to be read, but not to be written (as a canonical book).

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name that the Book of Esther does not defile the hands, i.e., is not fully canonical.
The Gemara questions whether Shmuel holds that Esther was not composed with ruach hakodesh (divine inspiration), given that Shmuel elsewhere said it was.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: Esther was composed with ruach hakodesh to be read (as a liturgical text), but not to be written (as a canonical book that defiles the hands).

items.text: Support from a baraita about Kohelet, Shir HaShirim, and Esther
items.text_en: Support from a baraita about Kohelet, Shir HaShirim, and Esther
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Shimon states that Ruth, Shir HaShirim, and Esther all defile the hands, contradicting Shmuel. The Gemara explains that Shmuel follows Rabbi Yehoshua (who excludes Esther). A further baraita from Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya about Kohelet is cited, and the Gemara clarifies the proof from 'Al tosf al d'varav'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon dispute the status of Kohelet and Shir HaShirim, and Rabbi Shimon states that Ruth, Shir HaShirim, and Esther all defile the hands.
The Gemara explains that Shmuel follows Rabbi Yehoshua, who excludes Esther from defiling the hands.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya says Kohelet does not defile the hands because it is Solomon's wisdom, and the Sages respond with a verse from Proverbs.

The Gemara clarifies the proof from the Sages' response: the verse 'אל תוסף על דבריו' (Do not add to His words) shows that even if Solomon could have written more, he was limited by divine inspiration.

items.text: Tannaitic proofs that Esther was composed with ruach hakodesh
items.text_en: Tannaitic proofs that Esther was composed with ruach hakodesh
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Meir, and Rabbi Yosei ben Dormaskit each cite a verse from Esther to prove it was written with divine inspiration. Shmuel then offers his own proof: 'Kiyemu v'kiblu'—the Jews confirmed above what they accepted below.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer cites the verse 'ויאמר המן בלבו' (Haman said in his heart) as proof that Esther was composed with divine inspiration.
Rabbi Akiva cites the verse 'ותהי אסתר נושאת חן בעיני כל רואיה' (Esther found favor in the eyes of all who saw her) as proof.
Rabbi Meir cites the verse 'ויודע הדבר למרדכי' (the matter became known to Mordechai) as proof.
Rabbi Yosei ben Dormaskit cites the verse 'ובבזה לא שלחו את ידם' (they did not lay hands on the spoils) as proof.
