Shmuel offers his own superior proof: the verse 'קימו וקבלו' (they confirmed and accepted) indicates that the Jews confirmed above what they accepted below, showing divine inspiration.

items.text: Rava's refutation of all proofs except Shmuel's
items.text_en: Rava's refutation of all proofs except Shmuel's
items.desc_en: Rava demonstrates that each of the earlier proofs can be refuted: Rabbi Eliezer's proof is merely Haman's subjective thought; Rabbi Akiva's could be explained by each person seeing Esther as their own nationality; Rabbi Meir's could be due to Bigtan and Teresh being Tarsians; Rabbi Yosei ben Dormaskit's could be because they sent a dispatch. Only Shmuel's proof is irrefutable. Ravina adds a folk saying about a sharp pepper being better than a basket of gourds.

sub.desc_en: Rava announces that all proofs except Shmuel's have a refutation.

sub.text: Rava's refutation of Rabbi Eliezer's proof
sub.text_en: Rava's refutation of Rabbi Eliezer's proof
sub.desc_en: Rava refutes Rabbi Eliezer's proof by arguing that Haman's thought was merely his own subjective opinion.

sub.text: Rava's refutation of Rabbi Akiva's proof
sub.text_en: Rava's refutation of Rabbi Akiva's proof
sub.desc_en: Rava refutes Rabbi Akiva's proof by suggesting that each person saw Esther as their own nationality, per Rabbi Elazar's explanation.

sub.text: Rava's refutation of Rabbi Meir's proof
sub.text_en: Rava's refutation of Rabbi Meir's proof
sub.desc_en: Rava refutes Rabbi Meir's proof by suggesting that Bigtan and Teresh were Tarsians, per Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba.

sub.text: Rava's refutation of Rabbi Yosei ben Dormaskit's proof
sub.text_en: Rava's refutation of Rabbi Yosei ben Dormaskit's proof
sub.desc_en: Rava refutes Rabbi Yosei ben Dormaskit's proof by suggesting that the Jews sent a dispatch rather than refraining from plunder.
Rava concludes that Shmuel's proof is irrefutable.
Ravina adds a folk saying that one sharp pepper is better than a basket of gourds, praising Shmuel's concise proof.

items.text: Additional proofs for the permanence of Purim and the laws of mishloach manot
items.text_en: Additional proofs for the permanence of Purim and the laws of mishloach manot
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cite verses to prove Purim will never cease. Rav Yosef then derives from the verses that mishloach manot requires two portions to one person, and matanot la'evyonim requires two gifts to two people. The daf ends with a story about Rabbi Yehuda Nasi sending a gift to Rabbi Oshaya.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites the verse 'וִימֵי הַפּוּרִים הָאֵלֶּה לֹא יַעַבְרוּ מִתּוֹךְ הַיְּהוּדִים' (and these days of Purim shall not pass from among the Jews) to prove that Purim will never cease.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites the verse 'וְזִכְרָם לֹא יָסוּף מִזַּרְעָם' (and their memory shall not cease from their seed) as an additional proof that Purim will never cease.

Rav Yosef teaches a baraita deriving from the verse 'וּמִשְׁלוֹחַ מָנוֹת אִישׁ לְרֵעֵהוּ' (and sending portions one to another) that mishloach manot requires two portions to one person, and from 'וּמַתָּנוֹת לָאֶבְיוֹנִים' (and gifts to the poor) that matanot la'evyonim requires two gifts to two people.
The daf ends with a story about Rabbi Yehuda Nasi sending a gift of a leg of a third calf and a jug of wine to Rabbi Oshaya, with the continuation cut off at the end of the page.

items.text: Story of Rabbah sending gifts to Mar bar Mar
items.text_en: Story of Rabbah sending gifts to Mar bar Mar
items.desc_en: Rabbah sends a gift of dates and flour to Mar bar Mar via Abaye. Abaye comments that a peasant even if made king does not put down his basket, implying the gift was too simple. Mar bar Mar reciprocates with ginger and long pepper, and Abaye notes the exchange of sweet for sharp. Abaye then describes how he was satiated at Mar's house but still hungry after sixty dishes.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the verse about sending portions and gifts to the poor as the basis for the story.
Rabbah sends a gift of dates and flour to Mar bar Mar via Abaye, and Abaye comments that a peasant even if made king does not put down his basket, implying the gift was too simple.
Mar bar Mar reciprocates with ginger and long pepper, and Abaye notes the exchange of sweet for sharp.

sub.text: Narrative: Abaye's experience at Mar's house
sub.text_en: Narrative: Abaye's experience at Mar's house
sub.desc_en: Abaye describes how he was satiated at Mar's house but still hungry after sixty dishes.
Abaye concludes with a folk saying: the poor person is hungry but doesn't know, or relief is found after a bitter experience.

items.text: Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin exchange meals
items.text_en: Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin exchange meals
items.desc_en: A brief note that Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin would exchange their Purim meals with each other.

sub.desc_en: A brief note that Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin would exchange their Purim meals with each other.

items.text: Obligation to become intoxicated on Purim and the story of Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira
items.text_en: Obligation to become intoxicated on Purim and the story of Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira
items.desc_en: Rava states that one is obligated to become intoxicated on Purim until he cannot distinguish between 'Cursed is Haman' and 'Blessed is Mordechai'. The Gemara relates that Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira had a Purim feast together, Rabbah became drunk and killed Rabbi Zeira, then revived him through prayer. The next year, Rabbah invited him again, but Rabbi Zeira declined, saying a miracle does not happen every time.

sub.desc_en: Rava states the obligation to become intoxicated on Purim until one cannot distinguish between 'Cursed is Haman' and 'Blessed is Mordechai'.

sub.text: Story of Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira
sub.text_en: Story of Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira
sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira celebrated Purim together; Rabbah became drunk, killed Rabbi Zeira, revived him through prayer, and Rabbi Zeira declined a repeat invitation, saying a miracle does not happen every time.

items.text: Rava's ruling on the Purim feast at night and the story of Rav Ashi
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on the Purim feast at night and the story of Rav Ashi
items.desc_en: Rava rules that one who eats the Purim feast at night does not fulfill his obligation, citing the verse 'days of feasting and joy'. Rav Ashi asks Rav Kahana why the rabbis did not come, and Rav Kahana suggests they were busy with the Purim feast. Rav Ashi questions why they could not eat it at night, and Rav Kahana cites Rava's ruling. Rav Ashi then learned this ruling forty times and it became as clear as if placed in his pocket.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that one who eats the Purim feast at night does not fulfill his obligation, citing the verse 'days of feasting and joy'.
Rav Ashi, sitting before Rav Kahana, asks why the rabbis did not come.
Rav Kahana suggests that the rabbis were busy with the Purim feast.
Rav Ashi questions why they could not eat the feast at night.
Rav Kahana cites Rava's ruling that the Purim feast at night does not fulfill the obligation.
Rav Ashi learned this ruling forty times until it became as clear as if placed in his pocket.

items.text: Baraita on the difference between Yom Tov and Shabbat regarding food preparation
items.text_en: Baraita on the difference between Yom Tov and Shabbat regarding food preparation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the only difference between Yom Tov and Shabbat is the permission to prepare food for consumption (אוכל נפש) on Yom Tov. The Gemara clarifies that this excludes the preparation of utensils (מכשירי אוכל נפש). It then notes that this Mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, who permits even utensil preparation. The Gemara explains the scriptural basis for both views, and reconciles the verses by distinguishing between utensils that can and cannot be prepared before Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the only difference between Yom Tov and Shabbat is the permission to prepare food for consumption (אוכל נפש).
The Gemara clarifies that regarding the preparation of utensils (מכשירי אוכל נפש), both Yom Tov and Shabbat are equal (i.e., prohibited).
The Gemara notes that the Mishnah does not follow Rabbi Yehuda, who permits even utensil preparation on Yom Tov.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Tanna Kamma's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Tanna Kamma's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Tanna Kamma derives his position from the word 'הוּא' (it) in the verse, excluding utensils.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda derives his position from the word 'לָכֶם' (for you), which includes all your needs.
The Gemara asks how the Tanna Kamma interprets 'לָכֶם', and answers that it excludes non-Jews and dogs.
The Gemara reconciles the verses by distinguishing between utensils that can be prepared before Yom Tov (prohibited) and those that cannot (permitted).

items.text: Baraita on the difference between Shabbat and Yom Kippur regarding punishment
items.text_en: Baraita on the difference between Shabbat and Yom Kippur regarding punishment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the only difference between Shabbat and Yom Kippur is that the intentional violation of Shabbat is punishable by human court (stoning), while Yom Kippur is punishable by karet. The Gemara clarifies that this excludes the matter of monetary restitution (תשלומין), which is the same for both. It identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana, who equates Yom Kippur with Shabbat for restitution. The Gemara then discusses a related Tosefta about lashes exempting from karet, and Rava raises a contradiction: if lashes exempt from karet, then Yom Kippur's punishment would also be by human court. Rav Nachman resolves this by attributing the Mishnah to Rabbi Yitzchak, who holds that there are no lashes for those liable for karet. Rav Ashi offers an alternative resolution: the Mishnah refers to the primary punishment, not the possibility of lashes.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the only difference between Shabbat and Yom Kippur is that intentional violation of Shabbat is punished by human court (stoning), while Yom Kippur is punished by karet.
The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah excludes the matter of monetary restitution (תשלומין), which is the same for both Shabbat and Yom Kippur.
The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana, who equates Yom Kippur with Shabbat regarding exemption from monetary restitution when liable for capital punishment.

The Gemara cites a Tosefta stating that those liable for karet who receive lashes are exempt from karet, and notes that Rabbi Yochanan reports the Sages disagree with Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel on this principle.
Rava raises a contradiction: if lashes exempt from karet, then Yom Kippur's punishment would also be by human court, contradicting the Mishnah's distinction.
Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction by attributing the Mishnah to Rabbi Yitzchak, who holds that there are no lashes for those liable for karet.
Rav Ashi offers an alternative resolution: even according to the Sages, the Mishnah refers to the primary punishment, not the possibility of lashes.

items.text: Distinction between a person forbidden by vow and one forbidden from food
items.text_en: Distinction between a person forbidden by vow and one forbidden from food
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the only difference between one who is forbidden benefit from a friend and one who is forbidden food is the prohibition of stepping on his property and using vessels that are not used for food preparation. The Gemara infers that regarding vessels used for food preparation, both are equal. Rava explains that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Eliezer, who prohibits even a trivial benefit (ויתור) for one under a vow.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the only difference between one forbidden benefit from a friend and one forbidden food is stepping on property and vessels not used for food preparation.
The Gemara infers that regarding vessels used for food preparation, both are equal.
The Gemara objects that people are not particular about stepping on their property, so why is it prohibited?
Rava answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Eliezer, who prohibits even a trivial benefit (ויתור) for one under a vow.

items.text: Distinction between vows and freewill offerings
items.text_en: Distinction between vows and freewill offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the only difference between vows and freewill offerings is that one is responsible for the replacement of a vowed animal if it is lost, but not for a freewill offering. The Gemara infers that regarding the prohibition of delaying (בל תאחר), both are equal. It then cites a baraita defining a vow as saying 'upon me' and a freewill offering as saying 'this one', and Rabbi Shimon derives from a verse that responsibility applies only to what is 'upon him'. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi explains that saying 'upon me' is like carrying a burden on one's shoulder.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the only difference between vows and freewill offerings is responsibility for replacement if lost.
The Gemara infers that regarding the prohibition of delaying (בל תאחר), vows and freewill offerings are equal.
A baraita defines a vow as saying 'upon me' and a freewill offering as saying 'this one', and reiterates the difference in responsibility.
Rabbi Shimon derives from the verse 'ונרצה לו לכפר עליו' that one is responsible only for what is 'upon him'.
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi explains that saying 'עלי' (upon me) is like carrying a burden on one's shoulder, indicating personal responsibility.

items.text: Distinction between a zav with two and three sightings
items.text_en: Distinction between a zav with two and three sightings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the only difference between a zav who has two sightings and one who has three is the requirement to bring a sacrifice. The Gemara infers that regarding impurity of bedding, seat, and counting seven clean days, both are equal. It then brings a baraita of Rabbi Simai showing that two sightings are for impurity and three for a sacrifice. The Gemara raises and resolves alternative interpretations, using the verse 'from his flow' (מזובו) to limit sacrifice to some zavim. It concludes that both Rabbi Simai's teaching and the verse are necessary, and discusses the use of another verse for counting seven days.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the only difference between a zav who has two sightings and one who has three is the requirement to bring a sacrifice.
The Gemara infers that regarding impurity of bedding, seat, and counting seven clean days, both are equal.

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Simai teaches that the Torah counted two sightings and called him 'tamei', and three and called him 'tamei', establishing that two are for impurity and three for a sacrifice.
The Gemara raises an alternative interpretation: perhaps two sightings are only for impurity and not for a sacrifice, while three are for a sacrifice and not for impurity.
The Gemara rejects this by noting that before seeing three, one has already seen two, so the two cannot be exempt from impurity.
The Gemara raises another alternative: perhaps two sightings are for a sacrifice and not for impurity, while three are also for impurity.
The Gemara rejects this by citing a baraita that uses the verse 'מזובו' (from his flow) to limit the sacrifice to some zavim, specifically those with three sightings.
The Gemara raises a possible alternative reading of the verse: perhaps two sightings bring a sacrifice and three do not.
The Gemara rejects this by again noting that before seeing three, one has already seen two, so the two cannot be the exclusive cause for a sacrifice.
The Gemara concludes that both Rabbi Simai's teaching and the verse 'מזובו' are necessary, as each addresses a potential misinterpretation.
The Gemara asks: now that the verse 'מזובו' is used for this derivation, what is derived from the verse 'וכי יטהר הזב מזובו' (when the zav becomes clean from his flow)?

The Gemara answers by citing a baraita that uses the verse 'וכי יטהר הזב מזובו' to teach that the zav must cease from his flow, and 'מזובו' excludes a flow combined with a skin affliction, and 'מזובו וספר' teaches that a zav with two sightings requires counting seven clean days.
The Gemara raises a logical objection: if a zav with two sightings defiles bedding and seat, should he not require counting seven clean days?

items.text: Derivation that a zav with two sightings requires counting seven clean days
items.text_en: Derivation that a zav with two sightings requires counting seven clean days
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by citing a baraita that uses a shomeret yom keneged yom as a precedent to argue that a zav with two sightings, though impure with midras, might not require counting seven days. The verse 'mizovo' is interpreted to teach that even a partial zav (two sightings) requires counting seven clean days. Rav Pappa asks Abaye why the same word 'mizovo' is used both to include and exclude, and Abaye explains that if it were for exclusion, the verse could have been silent and derived from logic; instead, it teaches inclusion.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces a woman who observes a day against a day as a precedent: she transmits impurity to a surface designated for lying and sitting, yet does not require counting seven clean days.
The baraita concludes that despite the precedent, the verse 'מִזּוֹבוֹ וְסָפַר' (from his emission he shall count) teaches that a zav with two emissions does require counting seven clean days.
Rav Pappa asks Abaye why the same term 'מִזּוֹבוֹ' (from his emission) is used in one context to include a zav with two emissions and in another to exclude him.
Abaye answers that if the term were for exclusion, the verse could have been silent and the logic from the woman who observes a day against a day would prove otherwise.

Abaye rejects the possibility that 'מִזּוֹבוֹ' (from his emission) is needed to exclude leprosy, arguing that the verse could have simply said 'וְכִי יִטְהַר הַזָּב' (and when the zav is cleansed); thus the term must teach inclusion of a zav with two emissions.

items.text: Mishnah: Differences between metzora musgar and muchlat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Differences between metzora musgar and muchlat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the only difference between a metzora musgar (quarantined) and muchlat (confirmed) is the requirement of periah and perimah (uncovering hair and tearing garments). For one who becomes tahor from quarantine versus from confirmation, the only difference is the requirement of shaving and bringing birds.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the only difference between a metzora musgar (quarantined) and a metzora muchlat (confirmed) is the requirement of periah and perimah (uncovering hair and tearing garments).
The Mishnah states that the only difference between one who becomes tahor from quarantine and one who becomes tahor from confirmation is the requirement of shaving and bringing birds.

items.text: Gemara: Deriving that musgar and muchlat are equal regarding sending away and impurity
items.text_en: Gemara: Deriving that musgar and muchlat are equal regarding sending away and impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah implies both types of metzora are equal regarding sending away and impurity. Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak teaches a verse to show that a metzora who becomes tahor from quarantine is free from periah and perimah from the start. Rava objects with a parallel from a zav, and then offers a different derivation from the verse 'vehatzaru'a asher bo hanega'. Abaye challenges this, citing the Mishnah that they are equal regarding sending away. The Gemara resolves by interpreting 'yemei' and 'kol yemei' to include the musgar for sending away, and Abaye provides a separate verse to exclude the musgar from shaving and birds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah implies both the musgar and muchlat metzora are equal regarding sending away and impurity.
Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak teaches a verse to show that a metzora who becomes tahor from quarantine is free from periah and perimah from the start.
Rava objects with a parallel from a zav, arguing that the phrase 'וְטָהֵר' there refers to future purity from impurity, not retroactive exemption.
The Gemara applies the same logic to the metzora: the verse teaches future purity from impurity by entry, not retroactive exemption from periah and perimah.
Rava offers a different derivation from the verse 'וְהַצָּרוּעַ אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ הַנֶּגַע', excluding the musgar whose leprosy depends on days, not on his body.
Abaye challenges Rava, citing the Mishnah that they are equal regarding sending away, which contradicts Rava's exclusion of the musgar from sending away.
The Gemara resolves by interpreting 'יְמֵי' and 'כָּל יְמֵי' to include the musgar for sending away.
The Gemara asks why shaving and birds are not included for the musgar, citing the Mishnah that they are exclusive to the muchlat.
Abaye provides a separate verse to exclude the musgar from shaving and birds, since his leprosy depends on days, not on healing.

items.text: Mishnah: Differences between sefarim and tefillin/mezuzot
items.text_en: Mishnah: Differences between sefarim and tefillin/mezuzot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the only difference between sefarim (Torah scrolls) and tefillin/mezuzot is that sefarim may be written in any language, while tefillin and mezuzot may only be written in Ashurit (Hebrew square script). Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that even sefarim were only permitted to be written in Greek.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the only difference between scrolls and tefillin and mezuzot is that scrolls may be written in any language, while tefillin and mezuzot only in Ashurit; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that scrolls were only permitted in Greek.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that even sefarim were only permitted to be written in Greek.

items.text: Gemara: Resolving a contradiction about sefarim written in other languages
items.text_en: Gemara: Resolving a contradiction about sefarim written in other languages
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah implies sefarim and tefillin/mezuzot are equal regarding being sewn with sinews and imparting impurity to hands. It then raises a contradiction from a baraita that says a biblical verse written in translation or in Hebrew script does not impart impurity to hands unless written in Ashurit, on a scroll, and with ink. Rava begins to resolve the contradiction (the text cuts off).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that sefarim and tefillin/mezuzot are equal regarding being sewn with sinews and imparting impurity to hands.

The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that says a biblical verse written in translation or in Hebrew script does not impart impurity to hands unless written in Ashurit, on a scroll, and with ink.
Rava begins to resolve the contradiction (the text cuts off).

items.text: Initial contradiction: our scrolls vs. their scrolls
items.text_en: Initial contradiction: our scrolls vs. their scrolls
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a contradiction between two statements: one permits writing a scroll in any language, the other restricts it to Assyrian script. The resolution is that one refers to scrolls written for Jews (our scrolls) and the other to scrolls written for non-Jews (their scrolls).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between scrolls written for Jews (our script) and scrolls written for non-Jews (their script).

items.text: Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges the resolution: if the baraita refers to their scrolls, why does it specifically mention cases where the text is written in translation or the translation in Hebrew? Even if written in their proper languages, the requirement of Assyrian script and ink would still apply.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that if the scroll is for non-Jews, the baraita's restriction to Assyrian script and ink would still apply even to a Hebrew text written in Hebrew, so the distinction fails.

items.text: First resolution: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel vs. Sages
items.text_en: First resolution: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel vs. Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the two statements to different Tannaim: one is the Sages' view, the other is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara re-resolves the contradiction by attributing the two statements to different Tannaim: the Sages (רבנן) and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

items.text: Objection: Greek is permitted by Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Objection: Greek is permitted by Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if it is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, he permits Greek, so why would the baraita only mention translation? The Gemara offers a new resolution: the distinction is between Torah scrolls (any language) and tefillin and mezuzot (only Assyrian).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits Greek, so the distinction must be between scrolls (ספרים) and tefillin/mezuzot (תפילין ומזוזות).
The Gemara resolves: the distinction is between Torah scrolls (any language) and tefillin and mezuzot (only Assyrian).

items.text: Challenge to the second resolution
items.text_en: Challenge to the second resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the second resolution: tefillin and mezuzot require the verse 'and they shall be' (והיו) meaning they must remain as they are, so no translation is allowed. But what translation could exist in tefillin and mezuzot? Only the Torah has the Aramaic passage 'Yegar Sahaduta'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that tefillin and mezuzot require 'והיו' (they shall be) in their original language, and asks what translation could exist there.

items.text: Third resolution: Megillah vs. other scrolls
items.text_en: Third resolution: Megillah vs. other scrolls
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers a new resolution: the baraita that permits any language refers to the Megillah (because of the verse 'according to their writing and their language'), while the restrictive baraita refers to other scrolls. The Gemara then asks what translation could exist in the Megillah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara re-resolves by distinguishing between a Megillah (מגילה) and other scrolls (ספרים), then asks what translation exists in the Megillah.
The Gemara asks what translation (תרגום) could possibly exist within the Megillah that would be written as Hebrew (מקרא), challenging the applicability of the baraita's rule.

items.text: Examples of Aramaic in Megillah
items.text_en: Examples of Aramaic in Megillah
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak provide examples of Aramaic verses in the Megillah: 'and the king's command was heard' and 'and all women shall give honor to their husbands'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak each cite a verse from the Megillah that contains Aramaic translation (e.g., 'ונשמע פתגם המלך' and 'וכל הנשים יתנו יקר לבעליהן').
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers a different example: the verse 'וְכׇל הַנָּשִׁים יִתְּנוּ יְקָר לְבַעְלֵיהֶן' (and all the women shall give honor to their husbands).

items.text: Final resolution: Rabbi Yehuda and the Septuagint story
items.text_en: Final resolution: Rabbi Yehuda and the Septuagint story
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves that the restrictive baraita refers to other scrolls and follows Rabbi Yehuda, who permits only Greek. The Gemara then recounts the story of King Ptolemy who gathered 72 elders to translate the Torah into Greek, and lists the deliberate changes they made.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves that the restrictive baraita applies to other scrolls and follows Rabbi Yehuda's opinion.
The Gemara objects that the verse 'וְהָיוּ' (they shall be) requires Hebrew, and questions the permission of Greek.
The Gemara corrects the baraita to say 'books may be written in any language', and questions why the Sages' permission implies the first Tanna forbade it.
The Gemara reformulates: the Sages only permitted Greek, and Rabbi Yehuda limits that permission to a Torah scroll.
The Gemara cites the story of King Ptolemy gathering 72 elders who each independently translated the Torah into Greek with identical deliberate changes.

items.text: List of changes in the Septuagint
items.text_en: List of changes in the Septuagint
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists the specific alterations the 72 elders made when translating the Torah into Greek for King Ptolemy, including changes to avoid anthropomorphism and other issues.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins listing the first change: the elders wrote 'God created in the beginning' instead of 'In the beginning God created' to avoid implying a secondary deity.

The Gemara lists further changes: 'He finished on the sixth day and rested on the seventh' (to avoid implying God worked on Shabbat), and 'male and female He created' (singular, not 'created them' plural, to avoid polytheism).

The Gemara lists more changes: 'Come, let Me descend and confuse their language' (avoiding plural 'us'), and 'Sarah laughed among her relatives' (not 'within herself', to avoid implying she doubted God).

The Gemara lists further changes: 'for in their anger they killed an ox' (not 'a man', to avoid dishonoring Jacob's sons), and 'Moses took his wife and sons and mounted them on a carrier of men' (not 'on a donkey', to avoid anthropomorphism).

The Gemara lists the final changes: 'the dwelling of the children of Israel in Egypt and other lands was 400 years' (to avoid implying the promise to Abraham was false), and 'He sent the elect of the children of Israel' and 'to the elect of the children of Israel He did not send His hand' (to avoid implying God struck nobles).

items.text: Opening verses from the Torah translation for Ptolemy
items.text_en: Opening verses from the Torah translation for Ptolemy
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites two verses that were altered in the Greek translation of the Torah for King Ptolemy, to avoid anthropomorphism or disrespect.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites two verses from the Torah translation for King Ptolemy that were altered to avoid anthropomorphism.

items.text: The alteration regarding the hare
items.text_en: The alteration regarding the hare
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the translators omitted the hare from the list of non-kosher animals because Ptolemy's wife was named Hare, to avoid mockery.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the translators wrote 'צעירת הרגלים' (the short-legged one) instead of 'הארנבת' (the hare) because Ptolemy's wife was named Hare, to avoid mockery.

items.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling on Greek
items.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling on Greek
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits writing sacred books only in Greek. Rabbi Yochanan rules accordingly and derives it from the verse 'May God extend Yafet' – the beauty of Yafet (Greek) should dwell in the tents of Shem. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba explains that this refers to the beauty of the Greek language.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that sacred books may only be written in Greek.
Rabbi Abahu reports that Rabbi Yochanan rules the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

Rabbi Yochanan explains the rationale: the verse 'יַפְתְּ אֱלֹהִים לְיֶפֶת וְיִשְׁכֹּן בְּאׇהֳלֵי שֵׁם' (May God extend Yafet, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem) implies that the words of Yafet (Greek) should be in the tents of Shem (Israel).
The Gemara objects: why Greek specifically? Perhaps the verse refers to other descendants of Yafet like Gomer and Magog.

Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba resolves: the verse says 'יַפְתְּ' (may He beautify), meaning the beauty (יַפְיוּת) of Yafet — i.e., the Greek language, which is the most beautiful of Yafet's descendants — should dwell in the tents of Shem.

items.text: Mishnah: Differences between high priests
items.text_en: Mishnah: Differences between high priests
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the only difference between an anointed high priest and one invested with many garments is the bull brought for all commandments. The only difference between a serving high priest and a former one is the bull of Yom Kippur and the tenth of an ephah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the only difference between an anointed high priest and one invested with many garments is the bull brought for all commandments, and between a serving high priest and a former one is the bull of Yom Kippur and the tenth of an ephah.

items.text: Gemara: The Mishnah is not Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Gemara: The Mishnah is not Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's first clause (only difference is the bull) disagrees with Rabbi Meir, who holds that a priest with many garments also brings the bull. The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir derives this from the extra word 'the anointed'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's first clause implies that regarding the bull of Yom Kippur and the tenth of an ephah, the anointed priest and the one with many garments are equal.
The Gemara asserts that the Mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Meir, who holds a different position.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir says a priest with many garments brings the bull for all commandments, while the Sages say he does not.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Meir's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Meir's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Meir's reason: from the word 'משיח' (anointed) alone one might exclude the one with many garments, so the extra word 'המשיח' (the anointed) includes him.

items.text: Contradiction in the Mishnah's second clause
items.text_en: Contradiction in the Mishnah's second clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara points out that the second clause of the Mishnah (only difference for a former priest is the bull of Yom Kippur) aligns with Rabbi Meir, creating a contradiction. Rav Chisda resolves that the first clause follows the Sages and the second follows Rabbi Meir. Rav Yosef says the entire Mishnah is Rabbi's, who taught it according to different Tannaim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah's first clause was established as not following Rabbi Meir, given that the second clause aligns with Rabbi Meir's position.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir rules that a second priest appointed after a disqualification retains all high priestly duties, while Rabbi Yosei rules he is unfit for either role.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's first clause follows the Sages but the second clause follows Rabbi Meir, creating an internal contradiction.
Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction by affirming that the first clause follows the Sages and the second follows Rabbi Meir.
Rav Yosef offers an alternative resolution: the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's, who taught each clause according to different Tannaim.

items.text: Mishnah: Differences between large and small altars
items.text_en: Mishnah: Differences between large and small altars
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the only difference between a large altar (in the Mishkan) and a small altar (in private) is the Paschal lamb. The Gemara clarifies that it means similar to the Paschal lamb, and identifies the Mishnah as Rabbi Shimon's opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the only difference between a large altar (במה גדולה) and a small altar (במה קטנה) is the Paschal lamb, and gives a rule: anything that is vowed or donated may be offered on a private altar, but not fixed obligations.
The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah means only Paschal lambs, implying no other offerings are exclusive to the large altar.
The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah means 'similar to Paschal lambs' — i.e., other fixed-time communal offerings are also exclusive to the large altar.

The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as Rabbi Shimon's opinion, citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon says that the community only offered Paschal lambs and other fixed-time obligations on the large altar, but non-fixed obligations were not offered there at all.

items.text: Mishnah: Differences between Shiloh and Jerusalem
items.text_en: Mishnah: Differences between Shiloh and Jerusalem
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the differences between Shiloh and Jerusalem: in Shiloh, lesser holy offerings and second tithe could be eaten anywhere within sight, while in Jerusalem only within the walls. Most holy offerings were eaten within the curtains in both places.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the differences between Shiloh and Jerusalem regarding where lesser holy offerings and second tithe may be eaten.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that after the destruction of Shiloh, its sanctity was permitted (i.e., high places were allowed), but after Jerusalem, there is no further permission.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that after the destruction of Shiloh, its sanctity was permitted (i.e., high places were allowed), but after Jerusalem, there is no further permission.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's statement and retraction
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's statement and retraction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak says he heard that offerings may be brought at the Temple of Onias even nowadays, because its sanctity was only for its time. He later retracts due to a difficulty raised by Rav Mari, who cites a baraita that Jerusalem's sanctity is eternal.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that offerings may be brought at the Temple of Onias even nowadays, because its sanctity was only for its time (קידשה לשעתה ולא קידשה לעתיד לבוא).

The gemara supports Rabbi Yitzchak's position by citing a verse that compares Shiloh (מנוחה) to Jerusalem (נחלה), implying that just as Shiloh's sanctity was temporary, so too Jerusalem's sanctity was temporary.
The sages ask Rabbi Yitzchak if he indeed said this, and he denies it.
Rava swears by God that Rabbi Yitzchak did say it, and that he (Rava) learned it from him.
The gemara explains that Rabbi Yitzchak retracted due to a difficulty raised by Rav Mari, who cited a baraita that Jerusalem's sanctity is eternal (אין אחריה היתר).

items.text: Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Eliezer vs. Rabbi Yehoshua
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Eliezer vs. Rabbi Yehoshua
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says they made curtains for the Temple and the courtyard when building, implying the sanctity was not eternal; Rabbi Yehoshua says offerings may be brought even without a building, because the first sanctity sanctified for its time and for the future.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer reports that when building the Temple, they made curtains for the sanctuary and the courtyard, implying the sanctity was not eternal.
Rabbi Yehoshua states that offerings may be brought even without a building, because the first sanctity sanctified for its time and for the future.
The gemara infers from the dispute that Rabbi Eliezer holds the first sanctity did not sanctify for the future.

items.text: Ravina's challenge to the inference
items.text_en: Ravina's challenge to the inference
items.desc_en: Ravina challenges the Gemara's inference from Rabbi Eliezer's statement, suggesting that both Tannaim might agree that the first sanctity was eternal, and Rabbi Eliezer's curtains were only for modesty.

sub.desc_en: Ravina challenges the inference that Rabbi Eliezer holds the first sanctity did not sanctify for the future, suggesting both Tannaim might agree it did, and Rabbi Eliezer's curtains were only for modesty.

items.text: Alternative Tannaitic source: Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Alternative Tannaitic source: Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another baraita where Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yosei explicitly states that the first sanctity was only for its time, as the returnees from exile sanctified only certain cities. A contradiction is raised from another statement of his, but the Gemara resolves it by explaining that the second statement only lists which cities were sanctified, not that the first sanctity was eternal.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yosei states that the first sanctity was only for its time, as the returnees from exile sanctified only certain cities.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from another statement of Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yosei, which implies that the first sanctity was eternal.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the second statement only lists which cities were sanctified, not that the first sanctity was eternal.

items.text: Resolution of contradiction about walled cities
items.text_en: Resolution of contradiction about walled cities
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction in Rabbi Yishmael's statements about whether cities without walls are considered walled. It offers two answers: either two Tannaim disagree in Rabbi Yishmael's name, or Rabbi Elazar bar Yosei said it, interpreting 'which had no wall' to include cities that once had a wall.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two statements of Rabbi Yishmael regarding whether cities without walls are considered walled for the purpose of sanctification.
The Gemara offers the first resolution: two Tannaim disagree in the name of Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei.
The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: Rabbi Elazar bar Yosei said the statement, interpreting 'which had no wall' to include cities that once had a wall even if it no longer exists.

items.text: The principle that 'vayehi' indicates distress
items.text_en: The principle that 'vayehi' indicates distress
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi or Rabbi Yonatan states a tradition that wherever 'vayehi' appears it indicates distress. The Gemara provides many examples from Tanakh, then challenges this with counterexamples where 'vayehi' appears in joyful contexts. Rav Ashi refines the rule: 'vayehi' alone can be either, but 'vayehi bimei' always indicates distress.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Levi (or Rabbi Yonatan) states a tradition from the Men of the Great Assembly that wherever 'וַיְהִי' (vayehi) appears, it is a term of distress.
The Gemara provides many examples from Tanakh where 'וַיְהִי' (vayehi) introduces a narrative of distress, such as Haman, famine, the Tower of Babel, war, and other calamities.
The Gemara objects by citing 'וַיְהִי בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁמִינִי' (vayehi on the eighth day) of the Tabernacle dedication, which was a day of great joy.
The Gemara answers that even on that day there was distress, as Nadav and Avihu died.
The Gemara raises further counterexamples: the building of the Temple, Jacob meeting Rachel, and the days of Creation, where 'וַיְהִי' (vayehi) appears without distress.
Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction: 'וַיְהִי' (vayehi) alone can be either joyful or distressing, but 'וַיְהִי בִּימֵי' (vayehi bimei) always indicates distress.

items.text: List of five 'vayehi bimei' instances
items.text_en: List of five 'vayehi bimei' instances
items.desc_en: The Gemara enumerates the five occurrences of 'vayehi bimei' in Tanakh, confirming Rav Ashi's statement that this phrase always introduces distress.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara enumerates the five occurrences of 'וַיְהִי בִּימֵי' (and it came to pass in the days of) in Tanakh, confirming Rav Ashi's statement that this phrase always introduces distress.

items.text: Tradition about Amotz and Amaziah being brothers
items.text_en: Tradition about Amotz and Amaziah being brothers
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi transmits a tradition that Amotz and Amaziah were brothers. The Gemara explains the relevance: a modest daughter-in-law merits kings and prophets, as seen from Tamar, and this connects to Isaiah son of Amotz being a prophet.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Levi transmits a tradition that Amotz and Amaziah were brothers.
The Gemara asks what practical lesson this tradition teaches.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan explains that a modest daughter-in-law merits kings and prophets, citing Tamar as proof.
The Gemara clarifies that Tamar's modesty in her father-in-law's house, not her veiling, merited kings from David and prophets from Isaiah son of Amotz, linking back to the tradition.

items.text: Tradition that the Ark's place was not within the measured space
items.text_en: Tradition that the Ark's place was not within the measured space
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi transmits another tradition: the place of the Ark was not part of the measured dimensions of the Holy of Holies. A baraita supports this, showing that the Ark stood miraculously without occupying space.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Levi transmits a tradition that the place of the Ark was not part of the measured dimensions of the Holy of Holies.
A baraita supports this by calculating the dimensions of the Holy of Holies and the Ark, concluding that the Ark stood miraculously without occupying space.

items.text: Rabbi Yonatan's homiletical opening to Esther
items.text_en: Rabbi Yonatan's homiletical opening to Esther
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan opens the Esther narrative with a verse from Isaiah, interpreting 'name, remnant, grandson, and great-grandson' as referring to writing, language, kingdom, and Vashti. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani then opens with another verse, interpreting 'brier' as Haman, 'cypress' as Mordechai, 'nettle' as Vashti, and 'myrtle' as Esther, concluding that the reading of the Megillah is an eternal sign.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan opens the Esther narrative with a verse from Isaiah, interpreting 'name, remnant, grandson, and great-grandson' as referring to writing, language, kingdom, and Vashti.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani's homiletical opening
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani's homiletical opening
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani opens with a verse from Isaiah, interpreting 'brier' as Haman, 'cypress' as Mordechai, 'nettle' as Vashti, and 'myrtle' as Esther, concluding that the reading of the Megillah is an eternal sign.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's opening: God does not rejoice at the downfall of the wicked
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's opening: God does not rejoice at the downfall of the wicked
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi opens with a verse implying God rejoices at Israel's downfall, but the Gemara objects that God does not rejoice at the downfall of the wicked, citing the Exodus. Rabbi Yochanan explains that the angels were prevented from singing when the Egyptians drowned. Rabbi Elazar resolves: God Himself does not rejoice, but He causes others to rejoice.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi opens the section by citing a verse that seems to imply God rejoices at Israel's downfall.
The Gemara objects: Does God rejoice at the downfall of the wicked? It cites the Exodus where the angels were not allowed to sing when the Egyptians drowned, citing Rabbi Yochanan.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that when the Egyptians drowned, the angels wanted to sing but God stopped them, saying 'My handiwork is drowning in the sea, and you would sing?'
Rabbi Elazar resolves the contradiction: God Himself does not rejoice, but He causes others to rejoice, as the verse says 'יָשִׂישׂ' (He will cause joy) rather than 'יָשׂוּשׂ' (He will rejoice).

items.text: Additional homiletical openings to Esther
items.text_en: Additional homiletical openings to Esther
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana opens with a verse from Ecclesiastes, applying it to Mordechai, Haman, and Esther. Rabbah bar Ofran opens with a verse from Jeremiah, identifying the king as Vashti and the princes as Haman and his ten sons. Rav Dimi bar Yitzchak begins another opening, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana opens the Esther narrative with a verse from Ecclesiastes, applying it to Mordechai, Haman, and Esther.
Rabbah bar Ofran opens with a verse from Jeremiah, identifying the king as Vashti and the princes as Haman and his ten sons.
Rav Dimi bar Yitzchak begins another opening, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Opening verse from Ezra
items.text_en: Opening verse from Ezra
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse from Ezra that describes God's kindness before the kings of Persia, and identifies this time as the days of Haman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse from Ezra describing God's kindness before the kings of Persia and identifies this time as the days of Haman.

items.text: Seven amoraic introductions to the Megillah
items.text_en: Seven amoraic introductions to the Megillah
items.desc_en: Seven different Amoraim each open the parashah of Esther with a different biblical verse, applying it to the events of the Megillah and other historical persecutions.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa opens the parashah of Esther with the verse 'You have set man over our heads; we went through fire and water', applying 'fire' to Nebuchadnezzar, 'water' to Pharaoh, and 'You brought us out to abundance' to the days of Haman.

Rabbi Yochanan opens with the verse 'He remembered His kindness and faithfulness to the house of Israel; all the ends of the earth saw the salvation of our God', applying it to the days of Mordechai and Esther.

Reish Lakish opens with the verse 'A lion roars and a bear prowls; a wicked ruler over a poor people', identifying the lion as Nebuchadnezzar, the bear as Achashverosh (with a baraita by Rav Yosef describing Persians like bears), and the wicked ruler as Haman.

Rabbi Elazar opens with the verse 'Through laziness the rafters sink, and through idleness the house leaks', explaining that Israel's laziness in Torah study caused the Holy One (the 'rafter') to become poor (מך), citing the verse 'And if he is poor (מך) from your valuation'.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak opens with the verse 'A song of ascents: Had it not been for the Lord who was with us, let Israel say... when man rose against us', emphasizing that 'man' (not a king) refers to Haman.

Rava opens with the verse 'When the righteous increase, the people rejoice; when the wicked rule, the people groan', applying the first part to Mordechai and Esther (citing 'the city of Shushan was cheerful and glad') and the second to Haman (citing 'the city of Shushan was perplexed').
Rav Mattanah opens with the verse 'For what great nation has a God so near to them'.
Rav Ashi opens with the verse 'Or has God ever tried...'.

items.text: Interpretations of 'And it came to pass in the days of Achashverosh'
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'And it came to pass in the days of Achashverosh'
items.desc_en: Rav, Shmuel, a baraita, Rabbi Levi, and Rabbi Chiya each connect the opening phrase of Esther to different biblical verses that speak of God's enduring covenant with Israel through various exiles.

sub.desc_en: Rav opens the section by citing the verse 'וַיְהִי בִּימֵי אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ' and connects it to the verse 'וְהִתְמַכַּרְתֶּם שָׁם לְאוֹיְבֶיךָ', implying that the exile under Achashverosh was a fulfillment of that warning.
Shmuel interprets the opening phrase by citing the verse 'לֹא מְאַסְתִּים וְלֹא גְעַלְתִּים לְכַלּוֹתָם', applying each clause to a different historical exile, including the days of Haman.

A baraita supports Shmuel's approach by similarly applying the verse to different exiles, but specifies the righteous figures God raised up in each period, including Mordechai and Esther in the days of Haman.
Rabbi Levi offers a different verse, 'וְאִם לֹא תוֹרִישׁוּ אֶת יוֹשְׁבֵי הָאָרֶץ', as the scriptural basis for the opening phrase.
Rabbi Chiya concludes the section by citing the verse 'וְהָיָה כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּמִּיתִי לַעֲשׂוֹת לָהֶם אֶעֱשֶׂה לָכֶם', linking the exile to God's principle of measure-for-measure.

items.text: Etymological and homiletical interpretations of 'Achashverosh'
items.text_en: Etymological and homiletical interpretations of 'Achashverosh'
items.desc_en: Rav, Shmuel, Rabbi Yochanan, and Rabbi Chanina offer various interpretations of the name Achashverosh, linking it to Nebuchadnezzar and the suffering of Israel. The Gemara then contrasts the consistent wickedness of certain biblical figures with the consistent righteousness of others.

sub.desc_en: Rav interprets the name Achashverosh as 'brother of the head' and 'contemporary of the head', linking him to Nebuchadnezzar and citing a verse about his initial hostility.
Shmuel interprets the name as referring to the darkening of Israel's faces in his days, while Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chanina offer alternative interpretations.
The Gemara states that Achashverosh, like Esav, Datan and Aviram, and King Achaz, was consistently wicked from beginning to end.
The Gemara contrasts the wicked figures with righteous ones like Abraham, Aaron, Moses, and David, who were consistently righteous from beginning to end.

items.text: Interpretation of 'the reigning' and the extent of his kingdom
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'the reigning' and the extent of his kingdom
items.desc_en: Rav explains that Achashverosh became king on his own, with praise and criticism. Rav and Shmuel debate whether 'from Hodu to Cush' means the ends of the earth or adjacent provinces. Rav Chisda derives from the extra phrase '127 provinces' that his rule expanded over time.

sub.desc_en: Rav explains that the word 'המולך' (the reigning) indicates Achashverosh became king on his own, with two interpretations: praise that no one was worthy like him, or criticism that he was unworthy and bought the throne.

Rav and Shmuel debate whether 'from Hodu to Cush' means the ends of the earth or adjacent provinces, with one saying they are at opposite ends and the other saying they are adjacent, implying rule over the entire world.

A parallel example is brought from the verse about Solomon's rule from Tifsach to Azza, with the same debate between Rav and Shmuel about whether these are opposite ends or adjacent, implying universal rule.

Rav Chisda derives from the extra phrase '127 provinces' that Achashverosh's rule expanded over time: initially over 7, then 20, then 100, and the gemara confirms this by noting the redundancy of the phrase.

items.text: Baraita: Three kings who ruled the entire world
items.text_en: Baraita: Three kings who ruled the entire world
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that Ahab, Achashverosh, and Nebuchadnezzar each ruled the entire world, citing verses that demonstrate their universal dominion.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that three kings ruled the entire world: Ahab, Achashverosh, and Nebuchadnezzar.
The baraita cites a verse showing Ahab could swear by God's name over any nation, proving his universal rule.
The baraita cites a verse commanding all nations to serve Nebuchadnezzar, proving his universal dominion.
The baraita concludes by referencing the earlier discussion as proof that Achashverosh ruled the entire world.

items.text: Challenge: Solomon's universal rule
items.text_en: Challenge: Solomon's universal rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Solomon is not included in the list of kings who ruled the entire world. It answers that his reign was not complete, or for those who hold that a king and a commoner and a king count, Solomon had a unique aspect—he ruled over both the upper and lower realms.

items.text: Challenge: Sennacherib's universal claim
items.text_en: Challenge: Sennacherib's universal claim
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises Sennacherib, who boasted that no god could save any land from his hand. The answer is that he did not conquer Jerusalem, so his rule was not universal.

items.text: Challenge: Darius's universal dominion
items.text_en: Challenge: Darius's universal dominion
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Darius, who wrote to all peoples. The answer is that he did not rule over seven provinces, as indicated by the appointment of 120 satraps.

items.text: Challenge: Cyrus's boast
items.text_en: Challenge: Cyrus's boast
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises Cyrus, who claimed all kingdoms were given to him. The answer is that he was merely boasting.

items.text: Belshazzar's miscalculation introduced
items.text_en: Belshazzar's miscalculation introduced
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes the verse 'when the king sat' and Rava explains it means after his mind was settled. Belshazzar said that Nebuchadnezzar miscalculated, but he would calculate correctly.

items.text: Belshazzar's first calculation and its error
items.text_en: Belshazzar's first calculation and its error
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Belshazzar's calculation: 45 years of Nebuchadnezzar, 23 of Evil-Merodach, and 2 of his own total 70. He then used the Temple vessels. The Gemara derives Nebuchadnezzar's 45 years from the exiles and the 37th year of Jehoiachin's exile.

items.text: Daniel's rebuke and Belshazzar's second calculation
items.text_en: Daniel's rebuke and Belshazzar's second calculation
items.desc_en: Daniel rebuked Belshazzar for using the Temple vessels, and that night Belshazzar was killed. The Gemara then explains Belshazzar's second calculation: he counted from the exile of Babylon, subtracting 8 years, and including the reigns of Belshazzar, Darius, Cyrus, and his own, totaling 70. When he saw the 70 years had passed without redemption, he used the vessels, and Satan caused Vashti to be killed.

items.text: Analysis of Belshazzar's error and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Analysis of Belshazzar's error and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Belshazzar's calculation was actually correct, but his error was that he should have counted from the destruction of Jerusalem. The Gemara calculates the difference and notes that in his 14th year the Temple should have been built, but work was stopped. Rava explains that the years were truncated.

items.text: Chronological confusion and the 'visitation' explanation
items.text_en: Chronological confusion and the 'visitation' explanation
items.desc_en: A baraita supports the idea that the seventy-year exile was counted from the destruction of the First Temple. Rava notes that Daniel also erred in his calculation. The Gemara resolves the contradiction between verses about the completion of Babylon's seventy years and Jerusalem's desolation by explaining that the decree was only a 'visitation' (פקידה) for Cyrus to begin the rebuilding.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports that the seventy-year exile was counted from the destruction of the First Temple.
Rava notes that Daniel also erred in his calculation of the seventy years.
The Gemara raises a contradiction between verses about the completion of Babylon's seventy years and Jerusalem's desolation.
Rava resolves the contradiction by explaining that the decree was only a 'visitation' (פקידה) for Cyrus to begin the rebuilding.

items.text: Cyrus as 'Messiah' and his failure
items.text_en: Cyrus as 'Messiah' and his failure
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda explains the verse referring to Cyrus as 'His anointed' (משיחו). God complains to the true Messiah about Cyrus: God expected Cyrus to build the Temple and gather the exiles, but Cyrus only issued a proclamation allowing anyone to go up.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's teaching
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's teaching
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda explains the verse referring to Cyrus as 'His anointed' (משיחו), and God's complaint to the true Messiah that Cyrus only issued a proclamation allowing anyone to go up, rather than building the Temple and gathering the exiles.

items.text: The agreement between Persia and Media
items.text_en: The agreement between Persia and Media
items.desc_en: Rava explains the alternating order of 'Persia and Media' and 'Media and Persia' in the verses: they made a condition that if kings come from one, governors come from the other.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the alternating order of 'Persia and Media' and 'Media and Persia' by explaining that they made a mutual agreement: if kings come from one, governors come from the other.

items.text: Achashverosh wore priestly garments
items.text_en: Achashverosh wore priestly garments
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina teaches that Achashverosh wore the priestly garments at his feast, as the same phrase 'glory and splendor' (יקר תפארת) is used for the priestly garments.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina teaches that Achashverosh wore the priestly garments at his feast, based on a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between the phrase 'יקר תפארת' (glory and splendor) used here and 'לכבוד ולתפארת' (for honor and splendor) used regarding the priestly garments.

items.text: Was Achashverosh wise or foolish?
items.text_en: Was Achashverosh wise or foolish?
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate whether Achashverosh was clever or foolish. The one who says he was clever argues that he seated the distant nobles first because he could appease his own people later. The one who says he was foolish argues he should have seated his own people first so they would support him if the others rebelled.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rav and Shmuel over whether Achashverosh was clever or foolish.
Rav argues Achashverosh was clever: he seated the distant nobles first because he could appease his own people later.
Shmuel argues Achashverosh was foolish: he should have seated his own people first so they would support him if the others rebelled.

items.text: Why were the Jews of that generation deserving of destruction?
items.text_en: Why were the Jews of that generation deserving of destruction?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's students suggest the Jews were punished for enjoying Achashverosh's feast. He refutes this, arguing that only those in Shushan would have been killed, not all Jews. He explains that the decree was because they bowed to the idol, but God's punishment was only 'within' (לפנים) — not full measure — as they only bowed outwardly.

sub.text: Students of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Students of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: The students ask Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai why the Jews of that generation were deserving of destruction.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai defers, telling the students to answer first.

sub.text: Students of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Students of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: The students propose that the Jews were punished for enjoying the feast of that wicked man (Achashverosh).
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai objects that if the sin was only enjoying the feast, only those in Shushan would be killed, not all Jews worldwide.

sub.text: Students of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Students of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: The students concede and ask Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai to give his own answer.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai answers that the Jews were deserving of destruction because they bowed to the idol (Nebuchadnezzar's statue).

sub.text: Students of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Students of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: The students object that this would imply favoritism (משוא פנים), since many Jews bowed only outwardly.

Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai resolves that just as the Jews only bowed outwardly (לפנים), God punished them only outwardly (לפנים) — not with full measure, as the verse says 'for He does not afflict from His heart'.

items.text: The layout of the feast: courtyard, garden, and palace
items.text_en: The layout of the feast: courtyard, garden, and palace
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate the meaning of 'the court of the garden of the king's palace'. One says each person was seated according to their rank. The other says they were moved from the courtyard to the garden and finally to the palace because the previous areas could not contain them. A baraita adds that two openings were made.

sub.desc_en: Rav explains that each guest was seated according to their rank in the appropriate area of the palace.
Shmuel argues that the guests were moved from the courtyard to the garden and finally to the palace because the previous areas could not contain them.
A baraita adds that two openings were made from the courtyard to the garden and the palace, supporting the idea of sequential movement.

items.text: The meaning of 'Chur' and 'Karpas'
items.text_en: The meaning of 'Chur' and 'Karpas'
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate the meaning of 'Chur': one says it means 'fine white linen' (חרי חרי), the other says a white blanket was spread. Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains 'Karpas' as striped cushions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the meaning of 'Chur' in the verse.
Rav explains 'Chur' means fine white linen (חרי חרי).
Shmuel explains 'Chur' means a white blanket was spread for them.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains 'Karpas' means striped cushions.

items.text: The couches: silver or gold?
items.text_en: The couches: silver or gold?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda says each couch was made of the material appropriate for the guest. Rabbi Nechemya objects that this would cause jealousy, and explains that the couches were silver with gold legs.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse and presents Rabbi Yehuda's position that each couch was made of the material appropriate for the guest.
Rabbi Nechemya objects that assigning different materials would cause jealousy among the guests.
Rabbi Nechemya resolves the issue by explaining that all couches were silver with gold legs, ensuring uniformity.

items.text: The meaning of 'Bahat' and 'Shesh'
items.text_en: The meaning of 'Bahat' and 'Shesh'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi explains that 'Bahat' and 'Shesh' are stones that 'rub themselves' (מתחטוטות) against their owners, i.e., they are precious stones that shine.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi explains that 'Bahat' and 'Shesh' are precious stones that shine (מתחטוטות) for their owners, citing a supporting verse.

items.text: The meaning of 'Dar' and 'Socharet'
items.text_en: The meaning of 'Dar' and 'Socharet'
items.desc_en: Rav says 'Dar' means 'generation after generation' (דרי דרי). Shmuel says it is a precious stone named 'Dara' that illuminated the feast. The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that it means 'he proclaimed freedom to all merchants'.

sub.desc_en: Rav interprets 'Dar' as 'generation after generation' (דרי דרי).
Shmuel explains that 'Dar' refers to a precious stone named 'Dara' that illuminated the feast.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that 'Dar' means he proclaimed freedom to all merchants.

items.text: The vessels and the wine
items.text_en: The vessels and the wine
items.desc_en: Rava explains the unusual phrase 'vessels from vessels that are different' (מכלים שונים): a heavenly voice told them that the first vessels were destroyed because of the earlier vessels, and you are using different ones. Rav says the wine served was older than each guest.

sub.desc_en: The gemara questions the unusual spelling 'שׁוֹנִים' (different) instead of the expected 'מְשׁוּנִּים' (unusual).
Rava explains that a heavenly voice rebuked them, saying the first vessels were destroyed because of the earlier vessels, and you are using different (שׁוֹנִים) ones.
Rav interprets the phrase 'וְיֵין מַלְכוּת רָב' (royal wine in abundance) to mean each guest was served wine older than himself.

items.text: The drinking customs and the meaning of 'no coercion'
items.text_en: The drinking customs and the meaning of 'no coercion'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanan in the name of Rabbi Meir explains 'as the law' (כדת) means like the Torah's law: more eating than drinking. Rabbi Elazar explains 'no coercion' (אין אונס) means each was served wine from his own region. Rava explains 'to do according to every man's will' means according to the will of Mordechai and Haman.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks what the phrase 'as the law' (כדת) means in the context of the drinking.

sub.text: Rabbi Chanan in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chanan in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanan citing Rabbi Meir explains that 'as the law' means like the Torah's law, where eating is more than drinking.
Rabbi Elazar explains that 'no coercion' (אין אונס) means each guest was served wine from his own region.
Rava explains that 'to do according to every man's will' means according to the will of Mordechai and Haman, citing verses that describe each as 'a man' (איש).

items.text: Vashti's feast and the intention for sin
items.text_en: Vashti's feast and the intention for sin
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the verse says 'the house of the kingdom' (בית המלכות) instead of 'the house of the women' (בית הנשים) to indicate that both Achashverosh and Vashti intended for sin. The proverb says: 'He is with the gourds, and his wife is with the pumpkins' — meaning they both engaged in inappropriate behavior.

sub.desc_en: The gemara questions why the verse says 'the house of the kingdom' (בית המלכות) instead of the expected 'the house of the women' (בית הנשים).
Rava explains that both Achashverosh and Vashti intended for sin, citing the proverb 'He is with the gourds, and his wife is with the pumpkins' to indicate their mutual inappropriate behavior.

items.text: Opening word from the previous daf
items.text_en: Opening word from the previous daf
items.desc_en: The daf begins with the word 'בְּבוּצִינֵי' (with lamps), which is a continuation from the previous page.

sub.desc_en: The daf opens with the word 'בְּבוּצִינֵי' (with lamps), continuing the previous page's discussion.

items.text: The seventh day feast and Vashti's punishment
items.text_en: The seventh day feast and Vashti's punishment
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the king's heart was only good on the seventh day. Rava explains it was Shabbat, and the nations of the world speak frivolously. The Gemara describes the feast where they debated the beauty of Median and Persian women, and Achashverosh offered to show Vashti naked. The Gemara explains that Vashti was punished measure for measure for stripping Jewish women and making them work on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the king's heart was only good on the seventh day, implying it should have been good all along from the wine.
Rava answers that the seventh day was Shabbat, and while Jews speak words of Torah and praise, the nations of the world speak frivolously, so the king's heart was only good then.
The Gemara describes the feast where the guests debated the beauty of Median and Persian women, and Achashverosh offered to show Vashti naked.
The Gemara explains that Vashti was punished measure for measure for stripping Jewish women and making them work on Shabbat, as the verse indicates.

items.text: Why Vashti refused
items.text_en: Why Vashti refused
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Vashti, who was immodest, refused to come. Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina says she was afflicted with leprosy. A baraita says Gabriel made her a tail.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks: since Vashti was a licentious woman (both she and Achashverosh intended to sin), why did she refuse to come?
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina answers that leprosy broke out on her, preventing her from appearing.
A baraita adds that the angel Gabriel came and made her a tail, further disfiguring her.

items.text: The king's extreme anger
items.text_en: The king's extreme anger
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the king was so angry. Rava explains that Vashti sent a message belittling his father's drinking ability, which enraged him.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks why the king's anger burned so intensely against Vashti.

Rava explains that Vashti sent a message insulting Achashverosh's lineage, saying his father was a stableman who drank heavily without getting drunk, while Achashverosh himself became foolish with wine, which enraged him.

items.text: The king consults the sages
items.text_en: The king consults the sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the 'wise men' as the rabbis who know how to intercalate years. They are reluctant to judge Vashti, fearing the king's volatility, and advise him to consult the Ammonites and Moabites, who are settled and undisturbed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the 'wise men' as the rabbis who know how to intercalate years and set months.
The sages are reluctant to judge Vashti, fearing the king's volatility, and claim they no longer have the wisdom to judge capital cases since the destruction of the Temple.
The sages advise the king to consult the Ammonites and Moabites, who are settled and undisturbed like wine on its lees, and the king immediately summons his advisors.

items.text: The names of the princes interpreted as sacrifices
items.text_en: The names of the princes interpreted as sacrifices
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi says the entire verse about the seven princes is said with reference to the sacrifices that Israel offered. Each name is interpreted by the ministering angels as a question about whether the nations offered such sacrifices.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Levi opens by stating that the entire verse about the seven princes is said with reference to the sacrifices that Israel offered.

The ministering angels interpret each name as a question about whether the nations offered the corresponding sacrifices, such as year-old lambs (כָּרִים), two turtledoves (שְׁתֵּי תוֹרִין), an earthen altar (מִזְבֵּחַ אֲדָמָה), priestly garments (בִּגְדֵי כְהוּנָּה), blood (דָּם), meal-offerings (מְנָחוֹת), and a table (שֻׁלְחָן).

items.text: Memuchan is Haman
items.text_en: Memuchan is Haman
items.desc_en: A baraita identifies Memuchan as Haman, and explains his name means 'prepared for punishment.' Rav Kahana says this teaches that a commoner jumps to speak first.

sub.desc_en: A baraita identifies Memucan as Haman, and explains that he was called Memucan because he was prepared (מוכן) for punishment.
Rav Kahana derives from here that an ordinary person (like Haman) jumps to speak first, without proper protocol.

items.text: The first decree and the people's reaction
items.text_en: The first decree and the people's reaction
items.desc_en: Rava says that had it not been for the first letters, no enemy of Israel would have survived. The people mock the decree that every man should rule in his own house, saying even a bald man should be a governor in his own house.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that had it not been for the first letters, no enemy of Israel would have survived.
The people mock the decree that every man should rule in his own house, saying even a bald man should be a governor in his own house.

items.text: The wise and the foolish king
items.text_en: The wise and the foolish king
items.desc_en: Rabbi interprets a verse: 'Every prudent man acts with knowledge' refers to David, who sought a young woman; 'a fool spreads folly' refers to Achashverosh, who appointed officers, causing everyone to hide their daughters.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi introduces a verse from Proverbs to interpret the actions of David and Achashverosh.
Rabbi explains that 'every prudent man acts with knowledge' refers to David, who sought a young woman and everyone brought their daughters.
Rabbi explains that 'a fool spreads folly' refers to Achashverosh, who appointed officers, causing everyone to hide their daughters.

items.text: Mordechai's lineage and the dispute between tribes
items.text_en: Mordechai's lineage and the dispute between tribes
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Mordechai is called both a Yehudi and a Yemini. A baraita explains all his names are based on his attributes. Rav Nachman says Mordechai was crowned with his own merit. Rabbah bar bar Chanah says his father was from Binyamin and mother from Yehudah. The rabbis say the families argue over which tribe caused his birth. Rava says Knesset Yisrael speaks to the other side about what Yehudah and Binyamin did.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Mordechai is called both a Yehudi and a Yemini, since these indicate different tribes.
A baraita explains that all of Mordechai's names are based on his attributes, not his lineage.
The Gemara objects that the terms Yehudi and Yemini still imply lineage from Yehudah and Binyamin respectively.
Rav Nachman answers that Mordechai was crowned with his own merit, so the names reflect his qualities, not his tribal lineage.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah says Mordechai's father was from Binyamin and his mother from Yehudah, explaining both names.
The rabbis say the families of Yehudah and Binyamin argue over which tribe caused Mordechai's birth, each claiming credit.
Rava says Knesset Yisrael speaks to the other side, recounting what Yehudah and Binyamin did for her.

items.text: Opening: Why David and Saul spared their enemies
items.text_en: Opening: Why David and Saul spared their enemies
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that David spared Shimi and Saul spared Agag because their descendants (Mordechai and Haman) would later play crucial roles in the Purim story.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that David spared Shimi and Saul spared Agag because their descendants Mordechai and Haman would later play crucial roles in the Purim story.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan: Why Mordechai is called Yehudi
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan: Why Mordechai is called Yehudi
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that Mordechai was from Benjamin, but called 'Yehudi' because he denied idolatry, as anyone who denies idolatry is called a Yehudi.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asserts that Mordechai was from Benjamin but called 'Yehudi' because he denied idolatry, as anyone who denies idolatry is called a Yehudi.

items.text: Midrash on Bityah and Moses' names
items.text_en: Midrash on Bityah and Moses' names
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi expounds on the verse about Bityah, daughter of Pharaoh, and the names of her son (Moses). Each name is interpreted as a reference to Moses' deeds: he brought down manna, repaired breaches, connected Israel to God, etc.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi opens his exposition on the book of Chronicles, stating that all its words are one and we know how to interpret them.
The gemara asks why Bityah is called 'Yehudiyah' (the Jewess).
The gemara answers that she is called Yehudiyah because she denied idolatry, citing Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation that she descended to wash from her father's idols.
The gemara questions the use of 'gave birth' (ילדה) for Bityah, since she only raised Moses.
The gemara answers that the verse teaches that one who raises an orphan is considered by Scripture as if they gave birth to him.
The gemara interprets each of Moses' names (Yered, Gador, Chever, Socho, Yekutiel, Zanoach) as referring to his deeds for Israel.
The gemara explains that the repeated 'avi' (father of) indicates Moses was a father in Torah, wisdom, and prophecy.
The gemara asks why the verse calls Caleb 'Mered', since his real name is Caleb.
The Holy One, blessed be He, explains that Caleb is called Mered because he rebelled (מרד) against the spies' advice, and he married Bityah who rebelled against her father's idols.

items.text: Rava: Mordechai exiled himself
items.text_en: Rava: Mordechai exiled himself
