items.desc_en: Rava explains that the verse 'who was exiled from Jerusalem' means Mordechai exiled himself voluntarily.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves that the verse 'who was exiled from Jerusalem' means Mordechai exiled himself voluntarily.

items.text: Dispute over Esther's name: Hadassah or Esther
items.text_en: Dispute over Esther's name: Hadassah or Esther
items.desc_en: Tannaim debate whether Esther's primary name was Hadassah or Esther. Rabbi Meir says Esther was her name, and she was called Hadassah because righteous are called myrtles. Rabbi Yehuda says Hadassah was her name, and she was called Esther because she concealed her identity. Rabbi Nechemya says she was called Esther by the nations after the moon. Ben Azzai says she was medium height like a myrtle. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha says she was greenish with a thread of grace.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks why the verse calls her both Hadassah and Esther.
A baraita is cited, opening the dispute among Tannaim.
Rabbi Meir says Esther was her primary name, and she was called Hadassah because righteous people are called myrtles.
Rabbi Yehuda says Hadassah was her primary name, and she was called Esther because she concealed her identity.
Rabbi Nechemya says Hadassah was her primary name, and the nations called her Esther after the moon.
Ben Azzai says Esther was of medium height like a myrtle.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha says Esther was greenish with a thread of grace drawn over her.

items.text: Esther's parents and Mordechai taking her as a wife
items.text_en: Esther's parents and Mordechai taking her as a wife
items.desc_en: Rabbi Acha explains the redundancy in the verse about Esther's parents: her father died when she was conceived, her mother when she was born. A tradition from Rabbi Meir interprets 'for a daughter' as 'for a house' (wife), citing a proof from Nathan's parable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the redundancy of the verse stating Esther had no father or mother and then mentioning their death.
Rabbi Acha explains that the redundancy teaches that Esther's father died when she was conceived and her mother died when she was born.
A tradition in the name of Rabbi Meir interprets 'for a daughter' (לְבַת) as 'for a house' (לְבַיִת), meaning Mordechai took Esther as a wife, citing a proof from Nathan's parable.
The Gemara resolves the proof: just as in the parable 'she was like a daughter' actually means 'like a wife' because she lay in his bosom, so too here 'for a daughter' means 'for a wife'.

items.text: What Mordechai fed Esther: dispute between Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: What Mordechai fed Esther: dispute between Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rav says Mordechai fed Esther Jewish food; Shmuel says he fed her pig intestines; Rabbi Yochanan says he fed her seeds, citing a verse from Daniel.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the seven maidens served Esther to count the days of the week for Shabbat observance.
Rav says Mordechai fed Esther Jewish food.
Shmuel says Mordechai fed Esther pig intestines.
Rabbi Yochanan says Mordechai fed Esther seeds, citing a verse from Daniel.

items.text: What is 'oil of myrrh'?
items.text_en: What is 'oil of myrrh'?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba says it is stacte; Rav Huna says it is olive oil that has not reached a third of its growth. A baraisa in the name of Rabbi Yehuda says it is anpakinon, which removes hair and softens the skin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'oil of myrrh' (שמן המור) refers to.
Rabbi Chiya bar Abba identifies it as stacte (סטכת), a type of balsam oil.
Rav Huna identifies it as olive oil that has not reached a third of its growth (שמן זית שלא הביא שליש).

sub.text: Supporting baraita in the name of Rabbi Yehuda
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita in the name of Rabbi Yehuda
sub.desc_en: A baraita in the name of Rabbi Yehuda identifies it as anpakinon (אנפקינון), olive oil that has not reached a third of its growth, which removes hair and softens the skin.

items.text: Achashverosh's behavior and Esther's concealment
items.text_en: Achashverosh's behavior and Esther's concealment
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan learns from the verse that Achashverosh did not have relations during the day. Rabbi Elazar says each man saw Esther as his own nationality. Rav says Achashverosh tasted both virgin and married women. The Gemara describes how Achashverosh tried to learn Esther's lineage but failed, and Mordechai advised her not to reveal it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan deduces from the verse that Achashverosh did not have marital relations during the day, learning his praise from his disgrace.
Rabbi Elazar explains that each man saw Esther as his own nationality, and notes that the month of Tevet is when the body enjoys the body.
Rav states that Achashverosh tasted both the taste of a virgin and the taste of a married woman in Esther.
The Gemara describes how Achashverosh tried various methods to learn Esther's lineage but failed.
Mordechai advises Esther not to reveal her lineage, and she follows his counsel, as the verse states she did not tell her origins.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar begins a new drasha
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar begins a new drasha
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks about a verse, setting up the next section of the Gemara.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar introduces a new drasha by asking about the meaning of a verse.

items.text: Reward for Rachel's modesty: the birth of Saul
items.text_en: Reward for Rachel's modesty: the birth of Saul
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rachel's modesty in not exposing Leah's deception earned her the merit of having Saul descend from her. The narrative details how Rachel gave Leah the secret signs to prevent her shame, leading to Jacob marrying Leah instead.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that Rachel's modesty earned her the merit of having Saul descend from her.
The Gemara asks what modesty Rachel demonstrated, questioning the verse about Jacob telling Rachel he is her father's brother.
The Gemara explains that Jacob proposed to Rachel, and she warned him about her father's deceit, to which Jacob responded that he is a brother in deceit.
Rachel explained that her father would substitute Leah, so Jacob gave her secret signs.
Rachel gave the signs to Leah to spare her shame, and therefore she merited that Saul descended from her.

items.text: Reward for Saul's modesty: the birth of Esther
items.text_en: Reward for Saul's modesty: the birth of Esther
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Saul's modesty in not revealing his kingship to his uncle earned him the merit of having Esther descend from him. Rabbi Elazar adds a general principle: when God grants greatness, it endures for generations unless the person becomes haughty.

sub.desc_en: Identifies Saul's modesty in not disclosing his kingship as the merit that produced Esther.
Rabbi Elazar adds the principle that when God grants greatness, it endures for generations unless the person becomes haughty, citing verses.

items.text: Esther's observance of Mordechai's command
items.text_en: Esther's observance of Mordechai's command
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'And Esther did the commandment of Mordechai' to mean she showed menstrual blood to the Sages, and 'as when she was brought up with him' indicates she would rise from Ahasuerus's lap, immerse, and sit in Mordechai's lap.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya explains that Esther showed her menstrual blood to the sages, i.e. she observed niddah laws in the palace.

sub.text: Rabba bar Lima in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Lima in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Lima citing Rav explains that Esther would rise from Achashverosh's lap, immerse, and then sit in Mordecai's lap, maintaining purity.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Limah in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Limah in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Limah citing Rav interprets the second part of the verse to mean Esther would rise from Ahasuerus's lap, immerse, and sit in Mordechai's lap.

items.text: The plot of Bigtan and Teresh
items.text_en: The plot of Bigtan and Teresh
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that God caused servants to rebel against their master (Joseph) and masters to rebel against their servants (Mordechai) to fulfill the righteous's will. Rabbi Yochanan identifies Bigtan and Teresh as Tarsians who plotted to poison the king, but Mordechai, knowing 70 languages, overheard and thwarted them.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that God caused a master to rebel against his servants to fulfill the will of the righteous Joseph.
The Gemara adds that God also caused servants to rebel against their masters to perform a miracle for the righteous Mordechai.
Rabbi Yochanan identifies Bigtan and Teresh as Tarsians who plotted to poison the king, but Mordechai, knowing 70 languages, overheard them.
The Gemara describes how Mordechai offered to guard both his and the conspirator's watch, and the verse confirms they were not found at their posts.

items.text: God's healing precedes the blow for Israel
items.text_en: God's healing precedes the blow for Israel
items.desc_en: Rava explains that 'after these things' refers to God creating a remedy before the affliction. Resh Lakish elaborates that God first creates healing for Israel before striking them, unlike the nations where healing comes after the blow.

sub.desc_en: Asks what specific events 'after these things' refers to.
Rava explains that 'after these things' refers to after God created a remedy for the blow.
Resh Lakish supports Rava's answer by teaching that God first creates healing for Israel before striking them, but for the nations He strikes first and heals afterward.

items.text: Haman's joy over the lot falling in Adar
items.text_en: Haman's joy over the lot falling in Adar
items.desc_en: Rava explains Haman's initial plan to harm only Mordechai, then the Sages, then all Jews. The Tanna recounts Haman's joy when the lot fell in Adar, thinking Moses died then, unaware that Moses was both born and died on the 7th of Adar.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that Haman's contempt escalated from targeting only Mordechai, to the rabbis, and finally to all Jews.
The Tanna recounts that Haman rejoiced when the lot fell in Adar, thinking Moses died then, unaware that Moses was both born and died on the 7th of Adar.

items.text: Haman's slander against the Jews
items.text_en: Haman's slander against the Jews
items.desc_en: Rava describes Haman's cunning slander: he claims the Jews are asleep from mitzvot, are scattered, unproductive, and their laws differ from all peoples. Haman lists their distinct practices: not eating or intermarrying with others, not observing the king's laws (keeping Shabbat and holidays), and showing disrespect to the king.

sub.desc_en: Rava introduces Haman's slander, stating that Haman knew how to speak maliciously and that the Jews are 'asleep' from performing mitzvot.
Achashverosh objects that the Jews have rabbis, but Haman dismisses this by saying they are all one unified people.
Haman anticipates and refutes potential objections: the Jews are scattered and unproductive, and no province is exempt from their presence.

Haman elaborates on the Jews' distinct practices: they do not eat or intermarry with others, they observe Shabbat and holidays instead of the king's laws, and they show disrespect to the king by rejecting his touch.

items.text: The shekels as a remedy for Haman's shekels
items.text_en: The shekels as a remedy for Haman's shekels
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that God knew Haman would weigh shekels against Israel, so He preempted this by having Israel give their shekels first. This is referenced in the Mishnah about announcing the shekel donations on the first of Adar. Rabbi Abba begins a comment on the king's response to Haman.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that God, knowing Haman would weigh shekels against Israel, preempted this by having Israel give their shekels first.
The gemara cites the Mishnah that on the first of Adar they announce about the shekels, supporting Resh Lakish's statement.
Rabbi Abba begins a comment on the king's response to Haman, introducing a new point.

items.text: Mashal of Achashverosh and Haman
items.text_en: Mashal of Achashverosh and Haman
items.desc_en: A parable comparing Achashverosh and Haman to two landowners, one with a mound and one with a ditch, who each desire the other's property and eventually exchange them for free.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a mashal (parable) comparing Achashverosh and Haman to two landowners, one with a mound and one with a ditch, each wishing to acquire the other's feature.
The mashal concludes: the two eventually meet, and the ditch-owner offers to buy the mound, but the mound-owner gives it for free, paralleling Haman's offer and Achashverosh's response.

items.text: Greatness of the removal of the ring
items.text_en: Greatness of the removal of the ring
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana states that the removal of the king's ring was greater than the prophecies of 48 prophets and 7 prophetesses, as it alone brought Israel back to good.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana states that the removal of the king's ring was greater than the prophecies of 48 prophets and 7 prophetesses, as it alone brought Israel back to good.

items.text: The 48 prophets and 7 prophetesses and the novelty of Megillah
items.text_en: The 48 prophets and 7 prophetesses and the novelty of Megillah
items.desc_en: The Tanna teaches that 48 prophets and 7 prophetesses prophesied to Israel, neither adding nor subtracting from Torah except for the Megillah reading. Rabbi Chiya bar Avin in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha explains the derivation: from servitude to freedom we say song, from death to life all the more so.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna teaches that 48 prophets and 7 prophetesses prophesied to Israel, neither adding nor subtracting from Torah except for the Megillah reading.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Avin in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Avin in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Avin explains the derivation for Megillah reading: from servitude to freedom we say song, so from death to life all the more so.

items.text: Why no Hallel on Purim?
items.text_en: Why no Hallel on Purim?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Hallel is not recited on Purim, given the miracle. It answers that Hallel is not said for a miracle outside the Land of Israel, but then objects that the Exodus was outside the Land. A baraisa resolves this: before entering the Land, all lands were fit for song; after entering, they were not. Rav Nachman says reading the Megillah is itself Hallel; Rava objects that we are still servants of Achashverosh. The Gemara notes that after exile, the original fitness returns.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Hallel is not recited on Purim, given the miracle.
The Gemara answers that Hallel is not recited for a miracle that occurred outside the Land of Israel.
The Gemara objects that the Exodus was also a miracle outside the Land, yet song (Hallel) was recited.
A baraita resolves that before entering the Land, all lands were fit for song; after entering, they were not.
Rav Nachman says that reading the Megillah itself constitutes Hallel.
Rava objects that at the Exodus we could say 'servants of God, not of Pharaoh,' but on Purim we are still servants of Achashverosh.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by noting that after the exile, the original fitness for song outside the Land returns.

items.text: Many more prophets than 48
items.text_en: Many more prophets than 48
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that there were many more prophets, citing the verse about Elkanah and a baraisa that prophets were twice as many as those who left Egypt. Only prophecies needed for generations were written.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the count of 48 prophets, citing the verse about Elkanah which implies 200 prophets.
The Gemara resolves that there were indeed many more prophets, but only prophecies needed for generations were written down.

items.text: Interpretations of 'Ramataim Tzofim' and the sons of Korach
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'Ramataim Tzofim' and the sons of Korach
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani and Rabbi Chanin offer interpretations of the place name, and a Tanna explains that the sons of Korach were saved in Gehinnom.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani interprets the place name 'Ramataim Tzofim' as referring to a person from two heights that overlook each other.
Rabbi Chanin offers an alternative interpretation: a person from those who stand at the height of the world.
The gemara identifies these people as the sons of Korach, citing the verse that they did not die.

sub.text: Tanna in the name of Rabbeinu
sub.text_en: Tanna in the name of Rabbeinu
sub.desc_en: A Tanna in the name of Rabbeinu explains that a place was fortified for them in Gehinnom, and they stood upon it.

items.text: List of the seven prophetesses
items.text_en: List of the seven prophetesses
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists the seven prophetesses: Sarah, Miriam, Deborah, Channah, Avigail, Chuldah, and Esther. It provides scriptural proofs and midrashic explanations for each, including Sarah's name Yiskah, Miriam's prophecy at the Nile, Deborah's wicks and sitting under a palm, Channah's prayer about the horn, Avigail's bloodstain and nighttime judgment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who the seven prophetesses are and lists them: Sarah, Miriam, Deborah, Hannah, Abigail, Huldah, and Esther.
Rabbi Yitzchak identifies Sarah as Yiskah, explaining that she saw by divine inspiration and that all gazed upon her beauty.
Rav Nachman in the name of Rav explains that Miriam prophesied as a child that her mother would bear a savior, and later watched to see the fulfillment of her prophecy.
The Gemara explains that Deborah was called 'wife of Lappidoth' because she made wicks for the Sanctuary.
Rabbi Shimon ben Avshalom explains that Deborah sat under a palm tree to avoid seclusion with men, and an alternative explanation compares the palm's single heart to Israel's unified devotion.

The Gemara notes that Hannah said 'my horn is exalted' rather than 'my pitcher,' alluding to the enduring kingship of those anointed with a horn (David and Solomon) versus those anointed with a pitcher (Saul and Jehu).
Rav Yehuda bar Menashya interprets 'biltekha' as 'levalotekha,' teaching that God outlasts His handiwork, unlike human artisans.
The Gemara explains that 'tzur' means 'artist,' and God uniquely fashions a form within a form, endowing it with life and internal organs.

Rabba bar Shmuel explains that Abigail's descent 'by the covert of the mountain' alludes to her showing David menstrual blood at night, leading to a halakhic argument about judging capital cases at night.

items.text: Avigail's rebuke and the meaning of 'blood'
items.text_en: Avigail's rebuke and the meaning of 'blood'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Avigail's statement to David, 'Blessed be your discretion and blessed be you who have restrained me this day from coming in blood,' implies two meanings of 'blood.' It then recounts that she revealed her leg and its light traveled three parasangs, and David asked her to marry him, but she refused, referencing the incident with Bathsheba.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Avigail called David a rebel against the monarchy (מוֹרֵד בַּמַּלְכוּת) and that she blessed him for restraining him from coming in blood.
The Gemara notes that the word 'דָּמִים' (blood) implies two meanings.
The Gemara explains that Avigail revealed her leg and its light traveled three parasangs.
The Gemara recounts that David asked Avigail to marry him, she refused, referencing the incident with Bathsheba, and that this indeed later occurred.

items.text: Avigail's blessing and request
items.text_en: Avigail's blessing and request
items.desc_en: Avigail blesses David that his soul be bound in the bundle of life, and when parting, she asks him to remember her.

sub.desc_en: Avigail blesses David that his soul be bound in the bundle of life, and when parting, she asks him to remember her.

items.text: Rav Nachman's proverb about women
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's proverb about women
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites a folk saying: 'A woman with a goblin is a barrel of pitch.' Another version: 'The son of a goose goes low, and his eyes are dim.'

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites a folk saying: 'A woman with a goblin is a barrel of pitch.'
An alternative version of the proverb: 'The son of a goose goes low, and his eyes are dim.'

items.text: Why Huldah prophesied in Jeremiah's place
items.text_en: Why Huldah prophesied in Jeremiah's place
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Huldah could prophesy in the place where Jeremiah stood. The school of Rav answers that Huldah was a relative of Jeremiah, so he did not mind.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Huldah could prophesy in the place where Jeremiah stood.

sub.text: School of Rav in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: School of Rav in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: The school of Rav answers that Huldah was a relative of Jeremiah, so he did not mind her prophesying in his place.

items.text: Why Josiah sent to Huldah instead of Jeremiah
items.text_en: Why Josiah sent to Huldah instead of Jeremiah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why King Josiah sent to Huldah rather than to Jeremiah. The school of Rabbi Sheila answers that women are compassionate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why King Josiah himself sent to Huldah rather than to Jeremiah.
The school of Rabbi Sheila answers that Josiah sent to Huldah because women are compassionate.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation: Jeremiah was absent
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation: Jeremiah was absent
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says Jeremiah was not there because he had gone to bring back the ten tribes. Proof is from a verse about the Jubilee. Rav Nachman adds another proof that Josiah ruled over them.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that Jeremiah was absent from Josiah's consultation because he had gone to bring back the ten tribes.
Rabbi Yochanan proves that Jeremiah brought them back from a verse about the Jubilee, arguing that a prophet would not prophesy about the Jubilee's nullification if it were already void.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that Josiah reigned over the ten tribes, as implied by the verse about the altar at Bethel.
Rav Nachman provides another proof from a verse in Hosea that Judah also had a harvest when the captivity of the people was returned.

items.text: Esther's royal garments as holy spirit
items.text_en: Esther's royal garments as holy spirit
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets 'Esther put on royal apparel' as meaning she was clothed with the holy spirit, based on a verbal analogy with 'the spirit clothed Amasai.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse says 'Esther put on royalty' (מלכות) instead of 'royal garments' (בגדי מלכות).
The Gemara answers that 'put on royalty' means she was clothed with the holy spirit, based on a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the verse 'and the spirit clothed Amasai.'

items.text: Rav Nachman on haughty women
items.text_en: Rav Nachman on haughty women
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman says haughtiness is unbecoming for women, citing two haughty women: Deborah (who sent for Barak instead of going) and Huldah (who said 'say to the man' instead of 'say to the king').

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman opens by stating that haughtiness is unbecoming for women.
Rav Nachman cites two haughty women, Deborah and Huldah, as examples of unbecoming pride.

items.text: Huldah descended from Joshua
items.text_en: Huldah descended from Joshua
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman says Huldah was a descendant of Joshua, based on the similarity of names 'ben Harhas' and 'Timnat Heres.'

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman asserts that Huldah was a descendant of Joshua, based on the verbal analogy between 'ben Harhas' and 'Timnat Heres'.

items.text: Rav Eina's objection and resolution about Huldah's lineage
items.text_en: Rav Eina's objection and resolution about Huldah's lineage
items.desc_en: Rav Eina the Elder objects that Huldah was from Rahab's descendants, citing a tradition. Rav Nachman responds that Rahab converted and married Joshua, and Joshua had daughters even if not sons.

sub.desc_en: Rav Eina Sava objects to Rav Nachman's claim that Huldah was from Joshua's descendants, citing a baraita that lists eight prophet-priests from Rahab and Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that Huldah was also among Rahab's descendants, based on a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between 'תקוה' and 'תקות חוט השני'.

Rav Nachman resolves the objection by explaining that Rahab converted and married Joshua, and although Joshua had no sons (as the verse 'נון בנו יהושע בנו' shows), he did have daughters, so Huldah could descend from Joshua through a female line.

items.text: Identifying prophets' lineage and character
items.text_en: Identifying prophets' lineage and character
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know the fathers of prophets mentioned in Scripture. Ulla explains that if a prophet's name and his father's name are given, he is a prophet son of a prophet; if only his name, he is a prophet but not a son of a prophet. A baraita adds that if Scripture details one's lineage for praise, he is righteous son of righteous; if for disgrace, wicked son of wicked.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know the fathers of the prophets, since the prophets themselves are identified but their fathers are not.
Ulla explains that if a prophet's name and his father's name are given, he is a prophet son of a prophet; if only his name, he is a prophet but not a son of a prophet; and similarly for the city.
A baraita adds that if Scripture details one's lineage for praise, he is righteous son of righteous; if for disgrace, wicked son of wicked.

items.text: Rav Nachman identifies Malachi as Mordechai
items.text_en: Rav Nachman identifies Malachi as Mordechai
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman asserts that Malachi is Mordechai, explaining his name means 'viceroy.' A challenge is raised from a baraita listing Baruch, Seraiah, Daniel, Mordechai, Bilshan, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi as prophets in the second year of Darius, implying Malachi is distinct from Mordechai. This is a refutation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman asserts that Malachi is Mordechai, explaining that his name means 'viceroy' (משנה למלך).

A challenge is raised from a baraita that lists Baruch, Seraiah, Daniel, Mordechai, Bilshan, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi as prophets in the second year of Darius, implying Malachi is distinct from Mordechai.
The gemara concludes that this is a refutation (תיוּבתא) of Rav Nachman's identification.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha identifies Malachi as Ezra
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha identifies Malachi as Ezra
items.desc_en: A baraita records Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's view that Malachi is Ezra, while the Sages say Malachi is his name. Rav Nachman supports the former, citing Malachi's rebuke about marrying foreign women, which Ezra enforced, as recorded in Ezra 10.

sub.desc_en: A baraita records Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's view that Malachi is Ezra.
The Sages counter that Malachi is his own name, not a title for Ezra.
Rav Nachman supports Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's view, citing Malachi's rebuke about marrying foreign women, which Ezra enforced.
The gemara adds that Ezra was the one who separated the foreign wives, as recorded in Ezra 10.

items.text: Four beautiful women and their distinctive traits
items.text_en: Four beautiful women and their distinctive traits
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that four women of exceptional beauty existed: Sarah, Avigail, Rachav, and Esther. One opinion replaces Esther with Vashti. Another baraita notes that Rachav was aroused by her name, Yael by her voice, Avigail by her mention, and Michal by her sight. Rabbi Yitzchak says saying 'Rachav Rachav' immediately causes a seminal emission, but Rav Nachman objects; Rabbi Yitzchak clarifies this applies only to one who knew her.

sub.desc_en: The Sages taught that four beautiful women existed: Sarah, Avigail, Rachav, and Esther, with an alternative opinion replacing Esther with Vashti.
A second baraita lists the means by which each of four women (Rachav, Yael, Avigail, Michal) was seduced: by name, voice, mention, or sight.
Rabbi Yitzchak states that anyone who says 'Rachav Rachav' immediately experiences a seminal emission.
Rav Nachman objects that he himself says 'Rachav Rachav' and is unaffected.
Rabbi Yitzchak clarifies that his statement applies only to one who knew Rachav personally and was familiar with her.

items.text: Interpretations of Mordechai's knowledge and Esther's distress
items.text_en: Interpretations of Mordechai's knowledge and Esther's distress
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains what Mordechai understood from Esther's report: Rav says Haman surpassed Achashverosh, Shmuel says the supreme King surpassed the earthly king. On 'ותתחלחל המלכה', Rav says she became a niddah, Rabbi Yirmeya says she needed to relieve herself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Mordechai understood from the report of Esther's actions.
Rav explains that Mordechai understood that Haman had surpassed Achashverosh in power.
Shmuel explains that Mordechai understood that the supreme King (God) had surpassed the earthly king.
The Gemara asks the meaning of the word 'ותתחלחל' describing Esther's distress.
Rav explains that Esther became a niddah (menstrually impure) from the shock.
Rabbi Yirmeya explains that Esther urgently needed to relieve herself from the distress.

items.text: Hatach identified as Daniel, and Esther's message to Mordechai
items.text_en: Hatach identified as Daniel, and Esther's message to Mordechai
items.desc_en: Rav identifies Hatach as Daniel, named for being cut from greatness; Shmuel says because all royal decrees were decided by him. Rabbi Yitzchak explains Esther asked if Israel violated the five books of the Torah. The Gemara notes Mordechai did not go to Esther, teaching not to respond to a calamity. Rabbi Abba explains 'not according to law' meant previously she was forced, now willing; 'as I perished I perish' means as I am lost from my father's house, so I am lost from you.

sub.desc_en: Rav identifies Hatach as Daniel, explaining he was named for being cut from greatness.
Shmuel explains Hatach was named because all royal decrees were decided by him.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's interpretation of Esther's message
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's interpretation of Esther's message
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak explains Esther asked Mordechai if Israel violated the five books of the Torah.
The Gemara notes Mordechai did not go to Esther, teaching not to respond to a calamity.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba's explanation of Esther's response
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba's explanation of Esther's response
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba explains 'not according to law' meant previously she was forced, now willing; 'as I perished I perish' means as I am lost from my father's house, so I am lost from you.

items.text: Mordechai's actions: fasting or crossing water
items.text_en: Mordechai's actions: fasting or crossing water
items.desc_en: Rav says Mordechai passed the first day of Passover in fasting; Shmuel says he crossed a bridge over water.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the verse 'וַיַּעֲבוֹר מָרְדֳּכָי' (And Mordechai passed) as the basis for the dispute.
Rav explains that Mordechai passed the first day of Passover in fasting.
Shmuel explains that Mordechai crossed a bridge over water.

items.text: Esther's royal garment was the Holy Spirit
items.text_en: Esther's royal garment was the Holy Spirit
items.desc_en: The verse says 'Esther put on royalty' rather than 'royal garments.' Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Chanina teaches that she was clothed with the Holy Spirit, as the same verb is used for Amasai.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse says 'Esther put on royalty' instead of 'royal garments.'
Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina explains that Esther was clothed with the Holy Spirit, as the same verb 'לבשה' is used for Amasai.

items.text: Aggadic teachings of Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Chanina
items.text_en: Aggadic teachings of Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Chanina
items.desc_en: A series of teachings: (1) Never treat a commoner's blessing lightly, as Aravnah blessed David and Darius blessed Daniel. (2) Never treat a commoner's curse lightly, as Avimelech cursed Sarah, fulfilled in Isaac's blindness. (3) God's ways differ from man's: man puts water after the pot, God puts water first. (4) One who cites a teaching in its speaker's name brings redemption, as Esther cited Mordechai. (5) When a righteous person dies, he is lost only to his generation. (6) Haman's boast 'all this is worthless to me' refers to seeing Mordechai at the king's gate, as per Rav Chisda's explanation.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina teaches that one should never treat a commoner's blessing lightly, citing the examples of Aravnah blessing David and Darius blessing Daniel.
Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina teaches that one should never treat a commoner's curse lightly, citing the example of Avimelech's curse on Sarah which was fulfilled in Isaac's blindness.
Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina teaches that God's ways differ from man's: man puts water after the pot, but God puts water first, as per the verse.
Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina teaches that one who cites a teaching in its speaker's name brings redemption, as Esther cited Mordechai.
Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina teaches that when a righteous person dies, he is lost only to his generation, like a lost pearl that remains a pearl but is lost only to its owner.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Chanina, citing Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Chanina, citing Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina explains that Haman's boast 'all this is worthless to me' refers to seeing Mordechai at the king's gate, as per Rav Chisda's explanation about the contrast between Mordechai's and Haman's entries.

items.text: Introduction: Haman's boast
items.text_en: Introduction: Haman's boast
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that Haman's wealth was like a slave sold for a low price, setting the stage for his arrogance.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa introduces Haman's boast by comparing him to a slave sold for a low price.

items.text: Haman's disdain for Mordechai
items.text_en: Haman's disdain for Mordechai
items.desc_en: The verse 'And all this is worth nothing to me' teaches that Haman's treasures were engraved on his heart, but seeing Mordechai made them worthless.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse 'And all this is worth nothing to me' teaches that Haman's treasures were engraved on his heart, but seeing Mordechai made them worthless.

items.text: God as a crown for the righteous
items.text_en: God as a crown for the righteous
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina teaches that God will be a crown for every righteous person, based on a verse. The Gemara then interprets various phrases from Isaiah as referring to those who control their inclinations and engage in Torah study.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina teaches that God will be a crown for every righteous person, citing a verse from Isaiah.
The Gemara interprets the verse's phrases as referring to those who do God's will and await His glory, and limits the crown to those who make themselves like remnants.

The Gemara interprets additional phrases from the same verse as referring to those who control their inclinations, judge truthfully, overcome their evil inclination, engage in Torah debate, and attend synagogues and study halls early and late.

items.text: The Attribute of Justice questions Israel's uniqueness
items.text_en: The Attribute of Justice questions Israel's uniqueness
items.desc_en: The Attribute of Justice asks why Israel is special, and God answers that they engaged in Torah. The Gemara then cites a verse about those who stray with wine, interpreting 'paku' as Gehinnom and 'peliliyah' as judges.

sub.desc_en: The Attribute of Justice asks God why Israel is different from the nations.
God answers that Israel engaged in Torah study, unlike the nations.
The Gemara cites a verse about those who stray with wine, interpreting 'paku' as Gehinnom and 'peliliyah' as judges.

items.text: Esther's prayer and fear
items.text_en: Esther's prayer and fear
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi explains that when Esther entered the inner court, the Divine Presence departed, and she cried out 'My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?' She worried that God was judging her for calling Haman a 'dog' or an 'lion'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Levi explains that when Esther entered the inner court, the Divine Presence departed, and she cried out 'אֵלִי אֵלִי לָמָה עֲזַבְתָּנִי' (My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?), fearing that God was judging her for unintentional sins as if they were intentional.
Esther then worries that God is punishing her for calling Haman a 'כֶּלֶב' (dog) in her earlier prayer, as cited from Psalms.
Esther then rephrases her prayer, calling Haman an 'אַרְיֵה' (lion) instead of a dog, as recorded in the verse 'הוֹשִׁיעֵנִי מִפִּי אַרְיֵה' (save me from the lion's mouth).

items.text: Miracles for Esther and the length of the scepter
items.text_en: Miracles for Esther and the length of the scepter
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says three ministering angels helped Esther. Rabbi Yirmiyah and others debate how much the scepter was extended, with opinions ranging from 12 to 200 cubits.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that three ministering angels assisted Esther when she approached the king.
The gemara asks how much the scepter was extended.
Rabbi Yirmiyah gives the first opinion that the scepter was extended from 2 to 12 cubits, with alternative versions saying 16 or 24.
A baraita teaches that the scepter was extended to 60 cubits, and parallels are drawn to the arm of Pharaoh's daughter and the teeth of the wicked.
Reish Lakish reinterprets a verse to indicate that God extended the teeth of the wicked, supporting the idea of miraculous extension.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Ofran citing Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Ofran citing Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Ofran reports in the name of Rabbi Elazar a tradition that the scepter was extended to 200 cubits.

items.text: Half the kingdom: the Temple
items.text_en: Half the kingdom: the Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'half the kingdom' excludes the Temple, as it would be a divider for the kingdom.

sub.desc_en: The gemara explains that the phrase 'half the kingdom' excludes the Temple, and identifies the excluded item as the building of the Temple.

items.text: Why Esther invited Haman: multiple opinions
items.text_en: Why Esther invited Haman: multiple opinions
items.desc_en: The Tannaim and Amoraim offer various reasons for Esther's invitation: to trap him, to follow the verse about feeding an enemy, to prevent rebellion, to hide her Jewishness, to maintain prayer, to have him available, to provoke a miracle, to cause his death, because the king was fickle, or to incite jealousy. Rabbah bar Avuha learns from Elijah that she followed all opinions.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by asking why Esther invited Haman to the feast.
Rabbi Elazar says Esther set a trap for Haman, citing the verse 'let their table become a snare before them'.
Rabbi Yehoshua says Esther learned from her father's house to feed an enemy, citing Proverbs 25:21.
Rabbi Meir says Esther invited Haman to prevent him from taking counsel and rebelling.
Rabbi Yehuda says Esther invited Haman so that people would not recognize her as Jewish.
Rabbi Nechemya says Esther invited Haman so that Israel would not rely on her and neglect prayer.
Rabbi Yosei says Esther invited Haman so that he would be available to her at all times.
Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya says Esther invited Haman so that God might take notice and perform a miracle.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha says Esther planned to charm Haman so that both he and she would be killed.
Rabban Gamliel says the king was fickle, so Esther invited Haman to manipulate him.
Rabbi Eliezer HaModa'i says Esther invited Haman to incite jealousy between the king and the ministers.
Rabbah says Esther invited Haman because 'before destruction comes pride' (Proverbs 16:18).
Abaye and Rava both say Esther invited Haman to fulfill the verse 'in their heat I will set their feast' (Hosea 7:4).
Rabbah bar Avuha asked Elijah which opinion Esther followed, and Elijah replied that she followed all of them.

items.text: The number of Haman's sons
items.text_en: The number of Haman's sons
items.desc_en: Rav says Haman had 30 sons (10 died, 10 hanged, 10 beggars). The Rabbis say 70 beggars. Rami bar Abba says 208, based on the gematria of 'v'rov', but Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak corrects that it is written 'v'rov' (with a vav) which is 208.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how many sons Haman had, based on the verse 'וַיְסַפֵּר לָהֶם הָמָן אֶת כְּבוֹד עׇשְׁרוֹ וְרוֹב בָּנָיו' (and Haman recounted to them the glory of his wealth and the multitude of his sons).
Rav answers that Haman had 30 sons: 10 died, 10 were hanged, and 10 were beggars.

The Rabbis answer that the beggars among Haman's sons were 70, based on a homiletic reading of the verse 'שְׂבֵעִים בַּלֶּחֶם נִשְׂכָּרוּ' (they who were sated with bread became hired), reading 'שְׂבֵעִים' (sated) as 'שִׁבְעִים' (seventy).
Rami bar Abba answers that all of Haman's sons were 208, based on the gematria of the word 'וְרוֹב' (and multitude), which he calculates as 214.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak corrects Rami bar Abba, noting that the word is written 'וְרֹב' (with a vav and a cholam) rather than 'וְרוֹב' (with a vav and a vav), so its gematria is 208, not 214.

items.text: The king's sleepless night and the book of records
items.text_en: The king's sleepless night and the book of records
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum says the sleep of the King of the World fled; the Rabbis say both upper and lower beings were restless; Rava says it was literally Achashverosh's sleep. The king suspects a plot, remembers a kindness, and orders the book of records to be brought, which miraculously read themselves.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum interprets the verse as referring to the sleep of the King of the World (God).
The Rabbis say that both upper (angelic) and lower (human) beings were restless.
Rava insists the verse refers literally to the sleep of King Achashverosh.
The Gemara recounts Achashverosh's internal reasoning: suspecting a plot, he concludes that someone must have done him a kindness unrepaid, and orders the book of records brought.
The Gemara explains that the records read themselves miraculously, and notes the unusual wording 'וַיִּמָּצֵא כָתוּב' (and it was found written) to highlight the miracle.

items.text: The writing of the decree cannot be erased
items.text_en: The writing of the decree cannot be erased
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi cites Rabbi Sheila's homily: if a lower writing for Israel's merit cannot be erased, how much more so a heavenly writing.

items.text: Rava explains the king's question
items.text_en: Rava explains the king's question
items.desc_en: Rava interprets the verse 'No wrong was done with him' as stemming from hatred of Haman, not love of Mordechai.

items.text: The preparation was for Mordechai
items.text_en: The preparation was for Mordechai
items.desc_en: A Tanna teaches that the verse 'He prepared for him' means he prepared for Mordechai.

items.text: Haman's dialogue with the king about Mordechai
items.text_en: Haman's dialogue with the king about Mordechai
items.desc_en: The king asks who Mordechai is, and Haman feigns ignorance, then suggests minimal honor, but the king insists on full compliance.

items.text: Mordechai teaching the laws of kemitzah
items.text_en: Mordechai teaching the laws of kemitzah
items.desc_en: Haman finds Mordechai teaching the laws of kemitzah to the rabbis; Mordechai fears Haman and prays, while Haman waits.

items.text: Haman's question and Mordechai's retort
items.text_en: Haman's question and Mordechai's retort
items.desc_en: Haman asks what they were studying; they say the laws of the meal-offering. Haman boasts of his wealth, but Mordechai rebukes him as a slave whose property belongs to his master.

items.text: Haman dresses Mordechai and the barber incident
items.text_en: Haman dresses Mordechai and the barber incident
items.desc_en: Haman tells Mordechai to dress and ride; Mordechai refuses until he bathes and cuts his hair. Esther locks the bathhouses, Haman serves as barber, and Mordechai sighs, leading to Haman's confession of his lowly origins.

items.text: Mordechai mounts the horse and kicks Haman
items.text_en: Mordechai mounts the horse and kicks Haman
items.desc_en: Mordechai is too weak from fasting to mount; Haman bends down, Mordechai kicks him, and they exchange verses about not rejoicing at an enemy's fall.

items.text: Haman's daughter mistakes him for Mordechai
items.text_en: Haman's daughter mistakes him for Mordechai
items.desc_en: As Haman leads Mordechai, his daughter, thinking the rider is her father, throws a chamber pot on Haman's head; she then falls and dies.

items.text: Mordechai returns to sackcloth; Haman mourns
items.text_en: Mordechai returns to sackcloth; Haman mourns
items.desc_en: Rabbi Sheshet explains that Mordechai returned to his sackcloth and fast; Haman is described as mourning for his daughter and his own shame.

items.text: Why Haman's advisors are called 'wise men'
items.text_en: Why Haman's advisors are called 'wise men'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that anyone who speaks wisdom, even among idolaters, is called a wise man.

items.text: The tribes from which Mordechai descends
items.text_en: The tribes from which Mordechai descends
items.desc_en: Zeresh and the advisors tell Haman that if Mordechai is from certain tribes, he cannot be defeated, citing verses about Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh.

items.text: Two falls: Israel's descent and ascent
items.text_en: Two falls: Israel's descent and ascent
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai explains the double expression 'fall, you will fall' — Israel can descend to dust and ascend to the stars.

items.text: The haste of the king's eunuchs
items.text_en: The haste of the king's eunuchs
items.desc_en: The verse teaches that they brought Haman in haste.

items.text: Esther's argument about the enemy's worth
items.text_en: Esther's argument about the enemy's worth
items.desc_en: Esther tells the king that this enemy is not worth the king's loss, as he previously killed Vashti out of jealousy and now seeks to kill her.

items.text: Why the double 'and he said'
items.text_en: Why the double 'and he said'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abahu explains that initially the king spoke through an interpreter, but when Esther revealed her lineage from Saul, he spoke directly to her.

items.text: Esther's gesture toward the king
items.text_en: Esther's gesture toward the king
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says Esther initially pointed toward Ahasuerus, but an angel turned her hand toward Haman.

items.text: The king's return from the garden
items.text_en: The king's return from the garden
items.desc_en: The Gemara compares the king's rising and returning, both in anger; he finds angels disguised as men uprooting trees, who say they were commanded by Haman.

items.text: Haman falling on the bed
items.text_en: Haman falling on the bed
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says an angel threw Haman onto the bed; the king asks if he intends to assault the queen.

items.text: Harbonah's true allegiance
items.text_en: Harbonah's true allegiance
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says Harbonah was also wicked but fled when his counsel failed, as per the verse about fleeing.

items.text: Two instances of appeasement
items.text_en: Two instances of appeasement
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse mentions two appeasements: one for the King of the World and one for Ahasuerus, or alternatively for Esther and Vashti.

items.text: Joseph's gift to Benjamin
items.text_en: Joseph's gift to Benjamin
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to discuss Joseph's gift of five changes of clothing to Benjamin, questioning how Joseph could cause his brother to be distressed.

items.text: The cause of the descent to Egypt
items.text_en: The cause of the descent to Egypt
items.desc_en: Rav explains that Jacob's gift of two selas' worth of fine wool to Joseph beyond his brothers caused the chain of events leading to the descent to Egypt. Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet adds that this hinted at Mordechai, who would later emerge from Benjamin's territory wearing five royal garments.

sub.text: Rav, via Rava bar Machseya and Rav Chama bar Gurya
sub.text_en: Rav, via Rava bar Machseya and Rav Chama bar Gurya
sub.desc_en: Rav explains that Jacob's gift of two selas' worth of fine wool to Joseph beyond his brothers caused the chain of events leading to the descent to Egypt.
Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet adds that the gift hinted at Mordechai, who would later emerge from Benjamin's territory wearing five royal garments.

items.text: Joseph and Benjamin's weeping
items.text_en: Joseph and Benjamin's weeping
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets Joseph's falling on Benjamin's neck as weeping over the two Temples that would be in Benjamin's territory and destroyed. Benjamin's weeping over Joseph's neck is over the Mishkan in Shiloh, which would be in Joseph's territory and destroyed.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks how Joseph could fall on Benjamin's neck, implying multiple necks.
Rabbi Elazar explains that Joseph wept over the two Temples in Benjamin's territory, and Benjamin wept over the Mishkan in Shiloh in Joseph's territory.

items.text: Joseph's reassurance to his brothers
items.text_en: Joseph's reassurance to his brothers
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that Joseph told his brothers that just as he harbors no ill will toward Benjamin, who was not present at his sale, so too he harbors none toward them, as his mouth and heart are aligned.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that Joseph reassured his brothers that just as he harbors no ill will toward Benjamin, so too he harbors none toward them, as his mouth and heart are aligned.
The gemara notes that the verse 'for my mouth speaks to you' implies that Joseph's mouth matched his heart.

items.text: The gift of aged wine
items.text_en: The gift of aged wine
items.desc_en: Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet quoting Rabbi Elazar explains that Joseph sent his father aged wine, which is pleasing to the elderly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'from the good of Egypt' refers to.

sub.text: Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet quoting Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet quoting Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet in the name of Rabbi Elazar answers that Joseph sent aged wine, which is pleasing to the elderly.

items.text: The fox bows in its time
items.text_en: The fox bows in its time
items.desc_en: Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet quoting Rabbi Elazar applies the proverb 'When the fox is in its time, bow to it' to Joseph's brothers bowing to him. The Gemara questions the comparison of Joseph to a fox relative to his brothers, and corrects the verse to Jacob bowing to Esau.

sub.text: Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet quoting Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet quoting Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet quoting Rabbi Elazar applies the folk saying 'When the fox is in its time, bow to it' to the verse where Joseph's brothers bow to him.
The Gemara objects to comparing Joseph to a fox, asking how he is inferior to his brothers.
The Gemara corrects the application: the proverb was said about Jacob bowing to Esau, not Joseph's brothers bowing to him.

items.text: Joseph's comforting words
items.text_en: Joseph's comforting words
items.desc_en: Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet quoting Rabbi Elazar explains that Joseph spoke comforting words to his brothers, using a parable: if ten candles could not extinguish one candle, how can one candle extinguish ten?

sub.text: Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet quoting Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet quoting Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet quoting Rabbi Elazar explains that Joseph spoke comforting words to his brothers, using a parable: if ten candles could not extinguish one candle, how can one candle extinguish ten?

items.text: The meaning of 'light, joy, gladness, and honor'
items.text_en: The meaning of 'light, joy, gladness, and honor'
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda interprets the four terms in the verse: 'light' is Torah, 'joy' is the festival, 'gladness' is circumcision, and 'honor' is tefillin. A baraita adds that Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol specifies tefillin of the head.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda interprets 'light' as Torah, 'joy' as the festival, and 'gladness' as circumcision, each supported by a verse.
A baraita adds that Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol specifies 'honor' as tefillin of the head.

items.text: Reading the ten sons of Haman
items.text_en: Reading the ten sons of Haman
items.desc_en: Rav Adda from Yafo teaches that the ten sons of Haman must be read in one breath because their souls departed together. Rabbi Yochanan adds that the vav of 'Vayzata' must be extended like a beam, as they were all hanged together.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda from Yafo teaches that the ten sons of Haman must be read in one breath because their souls departed together.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that the vav of 'Vayzata' must be extended like a beam, as they were all hanged together.

items.text: The format of the Song of the Sea and the Canaanite kings
items.text_en: The format of the Song of the Sea and the Canaanite kings
items.desc_en: Rabbi Sheila of Kfar Temarta teaches that all songs in Scripture are written in a brick-and-mortar pattern (half-line over full line), except for this song (the Song of the Sea) and the song of the Canaanite kings, which are written in a mortar-and-brick pattern (full line over half line), so that their downfall has no resurgence.

sub.text: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa citing Rabbi Sheila of Kfar Temarta
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa citing Rabbi Sheila of Kfar Temarta
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Sheila states the general rule that all songs in Scripture are written in a brick-and-mortar pattern (half-line over full line).
He notes the exception: the Song of the Sea and the song of the Canaanite kings are written in a mortar-and-brick pattern (full line over half line).
He explains the reason: the unusual pattern ensures that their downfall has no resurgence.

items.text: The angel struck Haman's mouth
items.text_en: The angel struck Haman's mouth
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu explains that the verse 'the king said to Esther the queen in Shushan the capital, the Jews have killed' teaches that an angel came and struck Haman on the mouth, causing him to speak incorrectly.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu explains that an angel struck Haman on the mouth, causing him to say 'the Jews have killed' instead of 'the Jews have been killed'.

items.text: What is said in the mouth
items.text_en: What is said in the mouth
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the verse says 'he said' instead of 'she said'. Rabbi Yochanan explains that Esther told the king: what is written in the book should be said orally.

sub.desc_en: The gemara questions why the verse uses the masculine 'אָמַר' (he said) instead of the feminine 'אָמְרָה' (she said).
Rabbi Yochanan answers that Esther told the king: 'Let what is written in the book be said orally' — so the verse uses 'אָמַר' referring to the king's instruction.

items.text: The scroll requires ruling
items.text_en: The scroll requires ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum, or some say Rabbi Asi, teaches that the verse 'words of peace and truth' indicates that the scroll of Esther requires ruling like a Torah scroll.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum (or Rabbi Asi) teaches that the letter must be ruled like a Torah scroll.

items.text: Esther's word was upheld
items.text_en: Esther's word was upheld
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse says 'Esther's word was upheld' but not 'the matters of the fasts'. Rabbi Yochanan explains that the verse reads 'the matters of the fasts and their cry, and Esther's word was upheld, these days of Purim'.

sub.desc_en: The gemara questions why the verse says 'the command of Esther was fulfilled' but not 'the words of the fasts'.
Rabbi Yochanan answers by citing the full verse: 'The words of the fasts and their cry, and the command of Esther established these Purim days' — both are included.

items.text: Mordechai was accepted by most of his brothers
items.text_en: Mordechai was accepted by most of his brothers
items.desc_en: The verse says 'accepted by most of his brothers', not all, teaching that some members of the Sanhedrin separated from him.

sub.desc_en: The gemara notes that the verse says 'accepted by most of his brothers' (not all), teaching that some of the Sanhedrin separated from Mordechai.

items.text: Torah study is greater than saving lives
items.text_en: Torah study is greater than saving lives
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef proves that Torah study is greater than saving lives because Mordechai is initially listed fourth among the returnees, but later fifth, showing that his Torah study elevated him above others who were involved in saving lives.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that Torah study is greater than saving lives, as Mordechai was listed fourth initially and fifth later due to his Torah study.
Rav Yosef cites the verses showing Mordechai's position rose from fourth to fifth among the returnees, attributed to his Torah study.

items.text: Torah study is greater than building the Temple
items.text_en: Torah study is greater than building the Temple
items.desc_en: Rav, or some say Rav Shmuel bar Marta, proves that Torah study is greater than building the Temple because Ezra did not leave Baruch ben Neriah to go up to the Land of Israel while Baruch was still alive, as Torah study takes precedence.

sub.desc_en: Rav (or Rav Shmuel bar Marta) states that Torah study is greater than building the Temple, as Ezra did not leave Baruch ben Neriah to go up.

items.text: Torah study is greater than honoring parents
items.text_en: Torah study is greater than honoring parents
items.desc_en: Rabba quoting Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta proves that Torah study is greater than honoring parents because Jacob was not punished for the years he spent in the house of Ever, as Torah study takes precedence over honoring his parents.

sub.text: Rabba citing Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta
sub.text_en: Rabba citing Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta
sub.desc_en: Rabba in the name of Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta states that Torah study is greater than honoring parents, as Jacob was not punished for the years he spent in the house of Ever.

items.text: Chronological calculation of Jacob's age and the 14 years in Eber's house
items.text_en: Chronological calculation of Jacob's age and the 14 years in Eber's house
items.desc_en: The Gemara calculates the years of Ishmael and Jacob to resolve a discrepancy: Jacob told Pharaoh he was 130 years old, but the calculation from Ishmael's birth to Joseph's appointment yields only 116 years. The Gemara concludes that Jacob did not count the 14 years he spent hidden in Eber's house.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Ishmael's years are enumerated, and calculates that Ishmael was 74 when Jacob was born, leaving 63 years of Ishmael's life remaining.
A baraita teaches that Jacob was 63 when blessed, and Ishmael died that same day, as deduced from the marriage of Machalat.
The Gemara calculates that from Jacob's age at blessing (63) plus 14 years until Joseph's birth, plus Joseph's age at appointment (30), plus 7 years of plenty and 2 of famine, totals 116 years.
The Gemara objects that Jacob told Pharaoh he was 130 years old, but the calculation yields only 116 years.
The Gemara resolves that Jacob did not count the 14 years he spent hidden in Eber's house, as taught in a baraita.

items.text: Proof that Jacob was not punished and the resolution of the 22 years
items.text_en: Proof that Jacob was not punished and the resolution of the 22 years
items.desc_en: The Gemara proves that Jacob was not punished for the 14 years he spent in Eber's house, as Joseph was separated from his father for 22 years, matching the time Jacob was separated from his own father (excluding the 14 years in Eber's house). It then explains that Jacob's 20 years in Laban's house were actually 22 due to two years spent traveling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we know that Jacob was not punished for the 14 years in Eber's house?
A baraita is cited: Joseph was separated from his father for 22 years, matching the time Jacob was separated from his own father, excluding the 14 years in Eber's house.
The Gemara objects: But Jacob was only in Laban's house for 20 years, not 22.
The Gemara resolves: Jacob spent two extra years traveling, as a baraita describes his 18 months in Sukkot and 6 months in Bethel.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of reading the Megillah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of reading the Megillah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who reads the Megillah out of order, by heart, or in translation has not fulfilled the obligation. However, one may read it in a foreign language for those who speak it, and a foreigner who hears it in Hebrew has fulfilled it. Additional rules cover reading it in sections, while drowsy, while writing or correcting it, and the materials on which it must be written.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches the laws of reading the Megillah, including the importance of order, language, and the materials on which it must be written.

items.text: Gemara: Source for reading out of order being invalid
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for reading out of order being invalid
items.desc_en: Rava initially derives the invalidity of reading the Megillah out of order from the verse 'according to their writing and their time', but the Gemara objects that the verse refers to 'doing' not 'reading'. It then derives it from the juxtaposition of 'remembering' and 'doing' in the verse 'these days are remembered and done'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for reading the Megillah in order, and Rava answers by deriving it from a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between 'writing' and 'time' in the Megillah verses, while an alternative derivation links remembering to performing.
The Gemara objects that the verse uses 'doing' not 'reading', so the derivation is corrected to link 'remembering' (the Megillah theme) to 'doing' (the general mitzvah).
The Gemara objects: the verse speaks of 'doing' (עשייה), not 'reading' (קריאה), so the analogy is invalid.

The Gemara resolves: the derivation is from the verse 'these days are remembered and done' (אסתר ט:כח), which juxtaposes remembering (reading) to doing, so just as doing cannot be out of order, reading cannot be out of order.

items.text: Source that the same rule applies to Hallel
items.text_en: Source that the same rule applies to Hallel
items.desc_en: A Tanna teaches that the rule of not reading out of order applies also to Hallel, Keriat Shema, and the Amidah. The Gemara then cites various verses from which the Sages derive that Hallel must be recited in order.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna taught that the law of לא למפרע (not to read out of order) applies also to Hallel, Shema, and the Amidah prayer.

The Gemara provides sources for Hallel: Rabba cites a verse about east to west, Rav Yosef cites 'this is the day God made', Rav Avya cites 'blessed be God's name', and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites 'from now and forever'.
The baraita shows dispute between Rabbi and the Sages: Rabbi says Shema must be read in Hebrew as written, the Sages say any language, and the Gemara begins to explain Rabbi's reason.
Rav Avya cites the verse 'יהי שם ה׳ מבורך' (may the name of the Lord be blessed) as the source for the order of Hallel.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak (or alternatively Rav Acha bar Yaakov) cites the verse 'מעתה ועד עולם' (from now and forever) as the source for the order of Hallel.

items.text: Dispute regarding Keriat Shema: in order or any language
items.text_en: Dispute regarding Keriat Shema: in order or any language
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite a dispute between Rabbi and the Sages regarding whether Keriat Shema must be recited in its written order (Rabbi) or in any language (Sages), and starts to give Rabbi's reason from a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the reason for Rabbi's position that Shema must be recited in Hebrew, and the baraita begins to cite the verse.
The Gemara asks for Rabbi's reason, noting that he derives his position from a verse.

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi and the Sages on the language of Shema
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi and the Sages on the language of Shema
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the scriptural basis for Rabbi's view that Shema must be recited in Hebrew (from 've-hayu') and the Sages' view that it can be in any language (from 'shema'). It then clarifies that each side uses the other's verse for a different derivation: Rabbi uses 'shema' for audible recitation, the Sages use 've-hayu' to prevent backward recitation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating Rabbi's scriptural basis for Shema in Hebrew: the word 'והיו' (and they shall be) implies they must remain as they are (in Hebrew).
The Gemara asks: what is the Sages' scriptural basis for allowing Shema in any language?
The Gemara answers: the Sages derive from the word 'שמע' (hear) that Shema may be recited in any language you hear.
The Gemara asks: but Rabbi also has the verse 'שמע' — how does he interpret it?
The Gemara answers: Rabbi uses 'שמע' to require that one make his ears hear what his mouth utters (audible recitation).
The Gemara notes that the Sages follow the opinion that one who recites Shema without audibility has fulfilled the obligation, so 'שמע' is free for their derivation.
The Gemara asks: but the Sages also have the verse 'והיו' — how do they interpret it?
The Gemara answers: the Sages use 'והיו' to require that Shema be recited in order, not backward.
The Gemara asks: from where does Rabbi derive the prohibition against reciting Shema backward?
The Gemara answers: Rabbi derives it from the words 'דברים' and 'הדברים' (the matters — implying a specific order).
The Gemara notes that the Sages do not derive anything from the words 'דברים' 'הדברים'.

items.text: Implications for the principle of 'Torah in any language'
items.text_en: Implications for the principle of 'Torah in any language'
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether Rabbi holds that the entire Torah was said in any language, and whether the Sages hold it was said only in Hebrew. It concludes that both positions are not necessarily implied, as each verse is needed to counter a potential mistaken inference from the other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi holds that the entire Torah was said in any language, since otherwise the verse 'וְהָיוּ' would be superfluous.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'וְהָיוּ' is necessary to counter a possible inference from 'שְׁמַע' that one may recite in any language, as the Sages hold.
The Gemara asks whether the Sages hold that the entire Torah was said only in Hebrew, since otherwise the verse 'שְׁמַע' would be superfluous.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'שְׁמַע' is necessary to counter a possible inference from 'וְהָיוּ' that one must recite in Hebrew only, as Rabbi holds.

items.text: Origin of the Amidah prayer
items.text_en: Origin of the Amidah prayer
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that Shimon HaPakuli arranged the eighteen blessings before Rabban Gamliel in Yavneh, and Rabbi Yochanan says that 120 elders, including many prophets, instituted them in order.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive the source for the Amidah prayer?
A baraita is cited: Shimon HaPakuli arranged the eighteen blessings before Rabban Gamliel in Yavneh.
Rabbi Yochanan says that 120 elders, including many prophets, instituted the eighteen blessings in order.

items.text: Scriptural sources for the first blessings and their order
items.text_en: Scriptural sources for the first blessings and their order
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides verses for Avot, Gevurot, and Kedushot. It then explains why Binah follows Kedushah, and why Teshuva follows Binah. A question is raised about placing Refuah after Teshuva, and the Gemara resolves it by distinguishing between healing of ailments and healing of forgiveness.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites verses from Psalms to establish scriptural sources for the first three blessings: Avot (Patriarchs), Gevurot (Mighty Deeds), and Kedushot (Sanctifications).

The Gemara asks why the blessing of Binah (Understanding) follows Kedushah, and answers with a verse sequence showing that understanding follows sanctification, and then why Teshuva (Repentance) follows Binah, citing a verse linking understanding, return, and healing.

The Gemara objects: if the verse 'וָשָׁב וְרָפָא לוֹ' (he will return and be healed) links repentance and healing, then Refuah (Healing) should immediately follow Teshuva, but the Sages placed it later; the objection is rejected by citing a verse that places forgiveness between repentance and healing.

The Gemara resolves the objection by citing a verse from Psalms that places Geulah (Redemption) and Refuah after Selichah (Forgiveness), and explains that the healing mentioned in the earlier verse is not physical healing but the healing of forgiveness (סְלִיחָה).

items.text: Placement of Geulah, Refuah, and Birkat HaShanim
items.text_en: Placement of Geulah, Refuah, and Birkat HaShanim
items.desc_en: Rava explains that Geulah is placed seventh because redemption will occur in the seventh year. Rabbi Acha explains that Refuah is eighth because circumcision is on the eighth day and requires healing. Rabbi Alexandri explains that Birkat HaShanim is ninth, corresponding to David's plea against price manipulators in the ninth psalm.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the blessing of Geulah (redemption) was placed in the seventh position of the Amidah.
Rava explains that Geulah is placed seventh because the redemption will occur in the seventh year of the sabbatical cycle.
The Gemara objects that a baraita states the son of David comes only after the seventh year, not during it.
The Gemara resolves that the wars of the seventh year are themselves the beginning of the redemption.
The Gemara asks why the blessing of Refuah (healing) was placed in the eighth position.
Rabbi Acha explains that Refuah is eighth because circumcision, which requires healing, is performed on the eighth day.
The Gemara asks why the blessing of Birkat HaShanim (the years) was placed in the ninth position.
Rabbi Alexandri explains that Birkat HaShanim is ninth, corresponding to David's plea against price manipulators in the ninth psalm.

items.text: Order from Kibbutz Galuyot through David's coming
items.text_en: Order from Kibbutz Galuyot through David's coming
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the sequence: after Birkat HaShanim comes Kibbutz Galuyot, then judgment on the wicked, destruction of sinners, exaltation of the righteous (including converts), building of Jerusalem, and finally the coming of David.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the blessing for Kibbutz Galuyot (ingathering of the exiles) follows Birkat HaShanim (blessing of the years).
The Gemara answers with a verse (Ezekiel 36:8) linking the ingathering of exiles to the blessing of the years.
The Gemara explains that after the ingathering, judgment is executed on the wicked, citing verses from Isaiah.
The Gemara states that once judgment is done, the sinners are destroyed, including the arrogant, citing a verse.
The Gemara explains that after the sinners perish, the righteous are exalted, including righteous converts, citing Psalms and Leviticus.
The Gemara specifies that the exaltation of the righteous occurs in Jerusalem, citing a verse from Psalms.
The Gemara concludes that once Jerusalem is built, David (the Messiah) comes, citing a verse.

items.text: Order of the Amidah: why Birkat Kohanim follows Hoda'ah
items.text_en: Order of the Amidah: why Birkat Kohanim follows Hoda'ah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the sequence of the Amidah blessings by citing verses that link David, prayer, sacrifice, and thanksgiving. It then questions why the Priestly Blessing follows the thanksgiving blessing, and resolves that sacrifice and thanksgiving are one unit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses to establish the sequence: after return comes David (prayer), then sacrifice, then thanksgiving.
The Gemara asks why the Priestly Blessing is placed after the thanksgiving blessing, citing a verse where Aaron blesses after descending from the altar.
The Gemara objects that the blessing could be placed before the sacrificial service, but rejects this because the verse says 'after making' (מֵעֲשׂוֹת), not 'to make' (לַעֲשׂוֹת).
The Gemara objects that the blessing could be placed after the service but before thanksgiving, and rejects this because the verse 'זוֹבֵחַ תּוֹדָה' links sacrifice and thanksgiving.
The Gemara resolves that sacrifice and thanksgiving are one unit, so the Priestly Blessing follows both together.

items.text: Why 'Sim Shalom' follows Birkat Kohanim
items.text_en: Why 'Sim Shalom' follows Birkat Kohanim
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the blessing of peace ('Sim Shalom') follows the Priestly Blessing because the priests place God's name on Israel, and God's blessing is peace, as per the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the blessing 'Sim Shalom' (Grant Peace) was placed after the Priestly Blessing.

The Gemara answers that the Priestly Blessing places God's name on Israel, and God's blessing is peace, as the verse states 'ה׳ יְבָרֵךְ אֶת עַמּוֹ בַשָּׁלוֹם' (May the Lord bless His people with peace).

items.text: Shimon HaPakuli's role and the limit on praising God
items.text_en: Shimon HaPakuli's role and the limit on praising God
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Shimon HaPakuli re-ordered the Amidah after it was forgotten. It then discusses the prohibition of excessive praise of God, citing Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Yochanan, and Rabbi Yehuda, and concludes with a maxim about silence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since the 120 elders and prophets already established the Amidah, what did Shimon HaPakuli actually 're-order'?
The Gemara answers that the order was forgotten, and Shimon HaPakuli restored it.
Rabbi Elazar cites a verse to teach that it is forbidden to excessively praise God, as only one who can fully express His praise is worthy to speak of His might.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan (via Rabba bar bar Chana)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan (via Rabba bar bar Chana)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that one who excessively praises God is uprooted from the world, citing a verse.
Rabbi Yehuda expounds that silence is the ultimate praise, and Rav Dimi reports a Western maxim: a word is worth a sela, silence two.

items.text: Megillah must be read from a written text
items.text_en: Megillah must be read from a written text
items.desc_en: Rava derives from a verbal analogy that the Megillah must be read from a written scroll, just as the Torah was written. The Gemara clarifies that 'remember' implies oral recitation, not just mental recollection.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who reads the Megillah by heart has not fulfilled the obligation.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of this rule.

Rava derives a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'זכירה' (remembrance) used in the Megillah and in the verse about writing in a book, concluding that the Megillah must be read from a written scroll.
The Gemara objects that the word 'זכירה' might refer to mere mental recollection, not reading aloud.
The Gemara resolves that the verse 'זָכוֹר' (remember) is juxtaposed with 'לֹא תִּשְׁכָּח' (do not forget), which refers to forgetting in the heart, so 'זָכוֹר' must mean oral recitation.

items.text: Reading the Megillah in translation or Greek
items.text_en: Reading the Megillah in translation or Greek
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the case of reading the Megillah in Targum or Greek. It clarifies that if it is written in Targum and read in Targum, it is valid. Rav and Shmuel rule that Greek is valid for all, and Rabbi Acha explains that this applies when it is written in Greek.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the Mishnah's ruling that reading the Megillah in Targum is invalid, and considers whether this is simply a case of reading by heart.
The Gemara clarifies that the case is where the Megillah is written in Targum and read in Targum, yet it is still invalid.
The Gemara questions the Mishnah's allowance for reading the Megillah in Greek for those who speak Greek, given the earlier ruling that any language other than Hebrew is invalid.
Rav and Shmuel rule that the Mishnah's allowance specifically refers to Greek, not any other language.
The Gemara asks how the case of reading in Greek applies, and considers whether it is simply reading by heart.
Rabbi Acha in the name of Rabbi Elazar explains that the allowance applies when the Megillah is written in Greek.

items.text: God called Jacob 'El'
items.text_en: God called Jacob 'El'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Acha in the name of Rabbi Elazar derives from a verse that God called Jacob 'El', interpreting the verse as referring to Jacob, not the altar.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Acha in the name of Rabbi Elazar derives from the verse 'וַיִּקְרָא לוֹ אֵל אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל' that God called Jacob 'אל' (El), arguing that the verse refers to Jacob, not the altar.

items.text: Reconciling the Mishnah with Rav and Shmuel's ruling on Greek
items.text_en: Reconciling the Mishnah with Rav and Shmuel's ruling on Greek
items.desc_en: A contradiction is raised from a baraita that lists languages in which reading the Megillah is invalid. The Gemara resolves that Rav and Shmuel's ruling follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who permits only Greek, and they teach that this applies to the Megillah as well.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita listing languages in which reading the Megillah is invalid, including Greek.
The Gemara distinguishes the baraita: it refers to a Greek scroll read to Greeks, which is valid, not to a general case.
The Gemara questions why Rav and Shmuel specifically interpret the Mishnah as referring to Greek, rather than any foreign language.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah and baraita are separate; Rav and Shmuel independently ruled that Greek is valid for everyone.
The Gemara objects that the baraita explicitly limits Greek to Greeks, not to all people.
The Gemara answers that Rav and Shmuel follow Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who permits only Greek for all sacred writings.
The Gemara questions why Rav and Shmuel did not simply state the halacha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, since one might think it applies only to other books.
