The Gemara concludes that Rav and Shmuel teach that Greek is valid even for the Megillah, despite its unique requirement of 'as their writing' (כִּכְתָבָם).

items.text: A non-Hebrew speaker who hears the Megillah in Hebrew
items.text_en: A non-Hebrew speaker who hears the Megillah in Hebrew
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how an illiterate person who hears the Megillah in Hebrew fulfills the obligation if they don't understand. Ravina answers that the mitzvah is reading and publicizing the miracle, not comprehension.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a non-Hebrew speaker who hears the Megillah in Hebrew fulfills the obligation, since they do not understand the language.
Ravina answers that the mitzvah is the reading and publicizing the miracle, not comprehension, just as we ourselves do not understand every word.

items.text: Clarification of obscure terms: serugin, chaloglugot, etc.
items.text_en: Clarification of obscure terms: serugin, chaloglugot, etc.
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains several difficult words by citing the maid of Rabbi's household, a traveler, and a baraita. These include 'serugin' (intermittently), 'chaloglugot' (saffron), 'salseleha' (comb), 'yehavecha' (burden), and 'tateita' (broom).

sub.desc_en: The mishna states that if one reads the Megilla intermittently (סירוגין), he has fulfilled his obligation.
The Gemara notes that the Sages did not know the meaning of the word 'סירוגין' (intermittently).

The Sages heard the maidservant of רבי (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi)'s household say to those entering in groups: 'עד מתי אתם נכנסין סירוגין סירוגין?' (How long are you entering intermittently?), clarifying the term.
The Gemara notes that the Sages did not know the meaning of the word 'חלוגלוגות' (purslane).
The Sages heard the maidservant say to a man scattering purslane: 'עד מתי אתה מפזר חלוגלוגך?' (How long will you scatter your purslane?), clarifying the term.
The Gemara notes that the Sages did not know the meaning of the word 'סלסלה' (twirl it) in the verse 'סלסלה ותרוממך' (Exalt her and she will promote you).
The Sages heard the maidservant say to a man twirling his hair: 'עד מתי אתה מסלסל בשערך?' (How long will you twirl your hair?), clarifying the term.
The Gemara notes that the Sages did not know the meaning of the word 'יהבך' (your burden) in the verse 'השלך על ה׳ יהבך' (Cast your burden upon the Lord).
רבה בר בר חנה (Rabba bar bar Chana) recounts that an Arab traveler told him: 'שקול יהביך ושדי אגמלאי' (Take your burden and throw it on the camel), clarifying the term.
The Gemara notes that the Sages did not know the meaning of the word 'מטאטא' (broom) in the verse 'וטאטאתיה במטאטא השמד' (I will sweep it with the broom of destruction).
The Sages heard the maidservant say to her friend: 'שקולי טאטיתא וטאטי ביתא' (Take a broom and sweep the house), clarifying the term.
A ברייתא (baraita) explicitly teaches: 'קראה סירוגין – יצא' (If one reads it intermittently, he has fulfilled his obligation), confirming the mishna's ruling.

items.text: Disjointed reading and the measure of 'enough time to complete it'
items.text_en: Disjointed reading and the measure of 'enough time to complete it'
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the case of reading the Megillah in a disjointed manner (סֵירוּסִין/סֵירוּגִין). Rabbi Muna in the name of Rabbi Yehuda rules that if one paused long enough to complete the entire Megillah, he must go back to the beginning. Rav Yosef rules in accordance with Rabbi Muna. Abaye asks Rav Yosef whether 'enough time to complete it' means from where he stopped to the end or from the beginning to the end; Rav Yosef answers from the beginning to the end, otherwise you would give your words to measurements.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who reads the Megillah in a disjointed manner (סֵירוּסִין) does not fulfill the obligation.

sub.text: Rabbi Muna in the name of Rabbi Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rabbi Muna in the name of Rabbi Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Muna citing Rabbi Yehuda adds that even with a broken reading (בְּסֵירוּגִין), if one paused long enough to complete the entire Megillah, he must go back to the beginning.
Rav Yosef rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Muna's statement in the name of Rabbi Yehuda.
Abaye asks Rav Yosef whether 'enough time to complete it' (כְּדֵי לִגְמוֹר אֶת כּוּלָּהּ) means from where he stopped to the end or from the beginning to the end.
Rav Yosef answers that it means from the beginning to the end, otherwise you would give your words to measurements (נָתַתָּ דְּבָרֶיךָ לְשִׁיעוּרִין).

items.text: Dispute over the halakha of Rabbi Muna and support from Shomeret Yavam
items.text_en: Dispute over the halakha of Rabbi Muna and support from Shomeret Yavam
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding whether the halakha follows Rabbi Muna. Two versions of the tradition are given: in Sura, Rav rules in favor of Rabbi Muna and Shmuel against; in Pumbedita, Rav Kahana in the name of Rav rules in favor, and Shmuel against. Rav Bivi reverses the attributions. Rav Yosef advises to hold Rav Bivi's version because Shmuel is concerned for an individual opinion, as demonstrated by a Mishnah where Shmuel rules like Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira regarding a yevamah's sister.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba in the name of Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba in the name of Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Muna, while Shmuel rules against it, as taught in Sura.
The Gemara records the alternative version from Pumbedita: Rav Kahana in the name of Rav rules in favor of Rabbi Muna, and Shmuel against.
Rav Bivi reverses the attributions: Rav rules against Rabbi Muna, and Shmuel rules in favor.
Rav Yosef advises to hold Rav Bivi's version because Shmuel is concerned for an individual opinion.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a yevamah's sister where Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira gives a stringent individual opinion.
Shmuel rules like Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, demonstrating his tendency to follow an individual stringent opinion.

items.text: Scribe omitted letters or verses; blurred or torn letters
items.text_en: Scribe omitted letters or verses; blurred or torn letters
items.desc_en: A baraisa teaches that if a scribe omitted letters or verses and the reader read them like a translator (by heart), he fulfills his obligation. An objection is raised from a Mishnah about blurred or torn letters: if their impression is recognizable, the scroll is valid; if not, it is invalid. The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the baraisa refers to a case where the omission is in part of the scroll (and the reader fills in from memory), while the Mishnah refers to the entire scroll being defective.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that if a scribe omitted letters or verses and the reader recited them by heart like a translator, he fulfills his obligation.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about blurred or torn letters: if the impression is recognizable the scroll is valid, otherwise invalid, contradicting the lenient ruling.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the baraita about blurred letters applies to the entire scroll being defective, while the first baraita refers to a case where only part of the scroll is missing and the reader fills in from memory.

items.text: Reader omitted a verse; joining the congregation midway
items.text_en: Reader omitted a verse; joining the congregation midway
items.desc_en: A baraisa rules: if a reader omitted a verse, he should not read the entire Megillah and then the omitted verse, but rather read from that verse onward. If one enters a synagogue and finds the congregation has read half, he should not read half with them and then the other half alone, but rather read the entire Megillah from beginning to end.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that if a reader omitted a verse, he reads from that verse onward, and if one joins a congregation midway, he must read the entire Megillah from start to finish.

items.text: Definition of 'dozing' (מתנמנם)
items.text_en: Definition of 'dozing' (מתנמנם)
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the Mishnah's term 'dozing' (מתנמנם). Rav Ashi defines it as one who is neither fully asleep nor fully awake; when called, he answers but cannot recall a reasoning, yet when reminded, he remembers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the definition of 'dozing' (מתנמנם) mentioned in the Mishnah.
Rav Ashi defines a dozing person as one who is neither fully asleep nor fully awake; when called he answers but cannot recall a reasoning, yet when reminded he remembers.

items.text: Writing the Megillah from memory and the requirement to write from a written source
items.text_en: Writing the Megillah from memory and the requirement to write from a written source
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the Mishnah's case of one who writes, expounds, or corrects the Megillah: if he intended to fulfill the obligation, he fulfills it. The Gemara questions: if he writes verse by verse from memory, what intention helps? It must be that he writes from a written source. But then an objection is raised from Rav Helbo's statement that the Megillah must be entirely written. The Gemara resolves: the case is where the Megillah is before him and he reads verse by verse and writes it. This supports Rabba bar bar Chana's statement that it is forbidden to write even one letter without a written source. The Gemara suggests the case might be where it happened incidentally.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's case: if one writes the Megillah verse by verse from memory, what intention could help, since it is entirely from memory?
The Gemara answers: the case is where he writes verse by verse while reading from a written source.
The Gemara objects: how can he fulfill the obligation, since Rav Helbo ruled that the Megillah must be entirely written from a written source, even according to the lenient opinion?
The Gemara resolves: the case is where the Megillah is before him and he reads verse by verse from it and writes.
The Gemara suggests that this resolution supports Rabba bar bar Chana's statement that it is forbidden to write even one letter without a written source.
The Gemara digresses: perhaps the case is where it happened incidentally, not as a regular practice.

items.text: The prohibition to write from memory and exceptions for Rabbi Meir and in pressing circumstances
items.text_en: The prohibition to write from memory and exceptions for Rabbi Meir and in pressing circumstances
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabba bar bar Chana's statement that it is forbidden to write even one letter without a written source. An objection is raised from a story about Rabbi Meir who wrote the Megillah from memory. Rabbi Avahu answers that Rabbi Meir was exceptional because the verse 'and your eyelids will look straight before you' applied to him. Rami bar Chama asks Rabbi Yirmeya from Difti about this verse, and he explains it refers to words of Torah which are elusive but were straightened for Rabbi Meir. Rav Chisda finds Rav Chananel writing books from memory and tells him that although the entire Torah could be written from his memory, the Sages forbade it. The Gemara notes that Rabbi Meir's case was different because it was a pressing time.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabba bar bar Chana
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabba bar bar Chana
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabba bar bar Chana's statement in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that it is forbidden to write even one letter from memory.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar recounts that Rabbi Meir wrote the Megillah from memory in a pressing situation.
Rabbi Avahu answers that Rabbi Meir was exceptional because the verse 'and your eyelids will look straight before you' applied to him.

sub.text: Rami bar Chama's question to Rabbi Yirmeya miDifti
sub.text_en: Rami bar Chama's question to Rabbi Yirmeya miDifti
sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks Rabbi Yirmeya miDifti about the meaning of the verse, and he explains that it refers to words of Torah which are elusive but were straightened for Rabbi Meir.

sub.text: Story of Rav Chisda and Rav Chananel
sub.text_en: Story of Rav Chisda and Rav Chananel
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda finds Rav Chananel writing books from memory and tells him that although the entire Torah could be written from his memory, the Sages forbade it.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Meir's case was different because it was a pressing time (שעת הדחק).

items.text: Writing tefillin and mezuzot from memory and the need for ruling
items.text_en: Writing tefillin and mezuzot from memory and the need for ruling
items.desc_en: Abaye permitted the household of bar Chavu to write tefillin and mezuzot without a written source, in accordance with the tanna Rabbi Yirmeya in the name of Rabbeinu who says tefillin and mezuzot may be written without a written source and do not require ruling. The halakha is: tefillin do not require ruling, mezuzot require ruling. Both may be written without a written source because they are well-known by heart (מִיגְרָס גְּרִיסִין).

sub.desc_en: Abaye permitted the household of bar Chavu to write tefillin and mezuzot from memory.
The gemara identifies the tanna behind Abaye's ruling: Rabbi Yirmeya in the name of Rabbeinu, who says tefillin and mezuzot may be written from memory and do not require ruling.
The gemara rules: tefillin do not require ruling, mezuzot require ruling, but both may be written from memory because they are well-known by heart (מִיגְרָס גְּרִיסִין).

items.text: Explanation of terms: sam, sikra, komos
items.text_en: Explanation of terms: sam, sikra, komos
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's terms: 'sam' means a dye; 'sikra' is called 'sekarta'; 'komos' is 'koma'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins explaining the Mishnah's term 'sam' as meaning a dye.
Rabba bar bar Chana explains that 'sikra' is called 'sekarta'.
The Gemara explains that 'komos' means 'koma' (a gum resin).

items.text: Materials for writing the Megillah
items.text_en: Materials for writing the Megillah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the materials mentioned in the Mishnah for writing the Megillah: קַנְקַנְתּוֹם (a shoemaker's black ink), דִּיפְתְּרָא (a processed hide), and נְיָיר (paper). It derives from a verbal analogy that the Megillah must be written in Assyrian script and with ink, as stated in the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara defines the three materials listed in the Mishnah for writing the Megillah: קַנְקַנְתּוֹם (a shoemaker's black ink), דִּיפְתְּרָא (a salted and floured but not tanned hide), and נְיָיר (papyrus).
The Gemara cites the requirement that the Megillah be written in Assyrian script, derived from the verse 'כִּכְתָבָם וְכִזְמַנָּם' (according to their writing and their time).

The Gemara derives the requirement for ink through a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on the word 'כְּתִיבָה' (writing), linking the Megillah verse to the verse about Baruch writing Jeremiah's words 'עַל הַסֵּפֶר בַּדְּיוֹ' (on the scroll with ink).

items.text: Mishnah: Traveler's obligation
items.text_en: Mishnah: Traveler's obligation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a resident of a village who goes to a city, or a resident of a city who goes to a village, reads the Megillah according to his place if he plans to return, otherwise he reads with them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a person who travels between a village and a city reads the Megillah according to his original location if he plans to return, otherwise he reads with the locals.

items.text: Mishnah: From where does one read?
items.text_en: Mishnah: From where does one read?
items.desc_en: The Mishnah records a dispute about the minimum portion of the Megillah one must read to fulfill the obligation: Rabbi Meir says the entire Megillah, Rabbi Yehuda says from 'אִישׁ יְהוּדִי', and Rabbi Yosei says from 'אַחַר הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute about the minimum portion of the Megillah one must read: Rabbi Meir requires the entire Megillah, Rabbi Yehuda from 'אִישׁ יְהוּדִי', and Rabbi Yosei from 'אַחַר הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה'.

items.text: Rava's ruling on returning at night
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on returning at night
items.desc_en: Rava limits the Mishnah's ruling: the leniency for a city dweller to read according to his place applies only if he plans to return on the night of the 14th. He derives this from the verse calling a villager 'פָּרוּז' even if he is only a day-old villager. By logic, a city dweller (מוּקָּף) is also called such even for a day.

sub.desc_en: Rava limits the Mishnah's leniency to one who plans to return on the night of the 14th; otherwise he reads with the locals.
Rava derives his ruling from the verse, which teaches that a villager (פָּרוּז) is called such even if only a day-old villager.
The Gemara infers by logic that just as a day-old villager is called a villager, so a day-old city dweller (מוּקָּף) is called a city dweller.

items.text: Rava's ruling on a villager in a city
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on a villager in a city
items.desc_en: Rava rules that a villager who goes to a city always reads with the city dwellers, because the Sages were lenient with villagers only when they are in their place, to ensure they supply water and food to city dwellers. Abaye challenges this from a baraita, and the Gemara resolves it by emending the text.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that a villager who goes to a city always reads the Megillah with the city dwellers, because the leniency for villagers only applies when they are in their place.

Abaye challenges Rava from a baraita that seems to say a city dweller who goes to a town always reads in his own manner, which would contradict Rava's ruling, and he emends the text to read 'villager' instead of 'city dweller'.
The Gemara resolves the objection by emending the baraita to read 'reads with them', aligning it with Rava's ruling.

items.text: Derivations for the starting point
items.text_en: Derivations for the starting point
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that all the Tanna'im derive their positions from the verse 'וַתִּכְתֹּב אֶסְתֵּר הַמַּלְכָּה... אֶת כׇּל תּוֹקֶף', each interpreting 'תּוֹקֶף' differently: the strength of Achashverosh, Mordechai, Haman, or the miracle. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai adds a derivation from 'בַּלַּיְלָה הַהוּא'. Rabbi Huna brings another verse, and each Tanna explains it according to his view.

sub.desc_en: A baraita introduces a fourth opinion: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says one must read from 'בלילה ההוא' (that night).
Rabbi Yochanan states that all the Tanna'im expound the same verse 'את כל תוקף' (all the acts of power), and the one who says the whole Megilla interprets 'תוקף' as the power of Achashverosh.

The Gemara explains the remaining positions: the one who reads from 'איש יהודי' (a certain Jew) interprets 'תוקף' as Mordechai's power; from 'אחר הדברים האלה' (after these things) as Haman's power; from 'בלילה ההוא' (that night) as the power of the miracle.
Rav Huna brings an alternative derivation from the verse 'ומה ראו על ככה ומה הגיע אליהם' (what they saw concerning this matter and what befell them).

The Gemara explains the position of the one who reads the whole Megilla: 'מה ראה' refers to Achashverosh using Temple vessels, 'על ככה' because he calculated seventy years without redemption, and 'מה הגיע אליהם' that he killed Vashti.

The Gemara explains the position of the one who reads from 'איש יהודי': 'מה ראה' refers to Mordechai's zeal against Haman, 'על ככה' because Haman made himself an idol, and 'מה הגיע אליהם' that a miracle occurred.

The Gemara explains the position of the one who reads from 'אחר הדברים האלה': 'מה ראה' refers to Haman's anger at all Jews, 'על ככה' because Mordechai did not bow, and 'מה הגיע אליהם' that Haman and his sons were hanged.

The Gemara explains the position of the one who reads from 'בלילה ההוא': 'מה ראה' refers to Achashverosh bringing the book of chronicles, 'על ככה' because Esther invited Haman with him, and 'מה הגיע אליהם' that a miracle occurred.

items.text: Halakhic ruling and requirement
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling and requirement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo in the name of Rav rules that the halakha follows the one who says the entire Megillah, and even according to the one who says from 'אִישׁ יְהוּדִי', the entire Megillah must be written.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo in the name of Rav rules that the halakha follows the one who says the entire Megillah, and even according to the one who says from 'אִישׁ יְהוּדִי', the entire Megillah must be written.

items.text: Laws of sewing and writing the Megillah
items.text_en: Laws of sewing and writing the Megillah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo in the name of Rav states that the Megillah is called both 'סֵפֶר' and 'אִגֶּרֶת', implying that if sewn with linen threads it is invalid, but if with three sinew threads it is valid, provided they are spaced. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel says that one who reads from a Megillah written among the Writings has not fulfilled his obligation, unless it is missing or extra. The Gemara then recounts an incident with Levi bar Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo in the name of Rav states that the Megillah is called both 'סֵפֶר' (book) and 'אִגֶּרֶת' (letter), implying that if sewn with linen threads it is invalid.
The second part of Rav's statement: the Megillah is called 'אִגֶּרֶת' (letter), so if one inserts three sinew threads it is valid.
Rav Nachman adds a condition: the three sinew threads must be spaced (triangulated) along the seam.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that one who reads from a Megillah written among the Writings (Ketuvim) has not fulfilled his obligation.
Rava qualifies Shmuel's ruling: this applies only if the Megillah is not missing or extra in any detail, but if it is missing or extra, the concern does not apply.
The Gemara begins recounting an incident involving Levi bar Shmuel reading the Megillah before Rav Yehuda.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's three statements and the cave of Moses and Elijah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's three statements and the cave of Moses and Elijah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who reads from a megillah written among other scrolls does not fulfill his obligation, and this was taught specifically regarding a congregation. He also states that the remnant of stitching is a halakhah from Sinai, and that even a tiny remnant of the cave where Moses and Elijah stood would prevent anyone from standing due to the divine light. Finally, he explains that God showed Moses the minutiae of Torah and scribes, including the reading of the megillah.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who reads from a megillah written among other scrolls does not fulfill his obligation.
The Gemara clarifies that the ruling was taught specifically regarding a congregation.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the remnant of stitching is a halakhah from Sinai.
The Gemara clarifies that the rule applies only to prevent the scroll from tearing.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that even a tiny remnant of the cave where Moses and Elijah stood would prevent anyone from standing due to the divine light.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that God showed Moses the minutiae of Torah and scribes, including the reading of the megillah.

items.text: Mishnah: Who is disqualified from reading the megillah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Who is disqualified from reading the megillah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that everyone is fit to read the megillah except for a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor. Rabbi Yehuda validates a minor.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that everyone is fit to read the megillah except for a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor.
Rabbi Yehuda validates a minor for reading the megillah.

items.text: Gemara's initial identification of the Mishnah's author
items.text_en: Gemara's initial identification of the Mishnah's author
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who taught that a deaf-mute is disqualified even after the fact. Rav Mattanah suggests it is Rabbi Yosei, who holds that one who recites Shema without hearing it does not fulfill the obligation. The Gemara rejects the possibility that it is Rabbi Yehuda, because the Mishnah compares the deaf-mute to an imbecile and a minor, who are disqualified even after the fact.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who taught that a deaf-mute is disqualified even after the fact.
Rav Mattanah identifies the Mishnah's author as Rabbi Yosei, who holds that one who recites Shema without hearing it does not fulfill the obligation.
The Gemara objects that perhaps it is Rabbi Yehuda, who only disqualifies לכתחילה (the ideal standard) but permits בדיעבד (after the fact).
The Gemara rejects the objection, arguing that the Mishnah compares the deaf-mute to an imbecile and a minor, who are disqualified even after the fact.

items.text: Refining the attribution: Rabbi Yehuda and the minor
items.text_en: Refining the attribution: Rabbi Yehuda and the minor
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that since the Mishnah's latter clause says Rabbi Yehuda validates a minor, the first clause cannot be Rabbi Yehuda. It then considers that the entire Mishnah might be Rabbi Yehuda, with a missing detail: the disqualification applies only to a minor who has not reached the age of training, but one who has reached it is even initially permitted, and Rabbi Yehuda validates such a minor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that perhaps the first clause (disqualifying a deaf person) and the second clause (Rabbi Yehuda validating a minor) are each according to their own reasoning, not necessarily from the same Tanna.
The Gemara rejects the objection: since the latter clause explicitly says Rabbi Yehuda validates a minor, it implies the first clause (which disqualifies a minor) is not Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara questions whether the entire Mishnah could be Rabbi Yehuda, noting the contradiction: the first clause disqualifies a minor while the latter validates him.

The Gemara resolves that the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Yehuda, but it is missing a detail: the disqualification applies only to a minor who has not reached the age of training (חינוך), while one who has reached it is even initially permitted, and Rabbi Yehuda validates such a minor.

items.text: Contradictory baraitot and final difficulty
items.text_en: Contradictory baraitot and final difficulty
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier assumption that the Mishnah is Rabbi Yehuda and applies only after the fact, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda's son permits a deaf-mute who speaks but does not hear to separate terumah initially. It then brings another baraita about blessing after meals in the heart, which fits neither Rabbi Yehuda nor Rabbi Yosei, showing the difficulty of consistent attribution.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier assumption that the Mishnah is Rabbi Yehuda and applies only after the fact (בדיעבד).

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda's son permits a deaf-mute who speaks but does not hear to separate תרומה (priestly portion) לכתחילה (the ideal standard), showing difficulty with the earlier attribution.
The Gemara brings another baraita about blessing after meals in the heart, which fits neither Rabbi Yehuda nor Rabbi Yosei, demonstrating the difficulty of consistent attribution.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's view on Shema
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's view on Shema
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that Rabbi Yehuda's statement in the Mishnah (that one may read the Megillah from dawn) is only post-facto, but then resolves that it is even initially. It then reconciles a contradiction between Rabbi Yehuda's own opinion and that of his teacher, concluding that the baraita attributed to him actually reflects Rabbi Meir's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda's statement in the Mishnah applies even לכתחילה (the ideal standard), and distinguishes between his own view and that of his teacher.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya that one must read the Shema audibly, while Rabbi Meir says that intent of the heart is what matters.
The Gemara concludes that even if Rabbi Yehuda follows his teacher's view, the baraita taught by Yehuda bar Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi is actually Rabbi Meir's opinion.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's proof from a minor and the response
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's proof from a minor and the response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda brings a proof from his own childhood experience of reading the Megillah above Rabbi Tarfon, but the Sages reject it because a minor cannot serve as evidence. Rabbi then brings a similar proof from his youth, and the Sages respond with a double objection: he was a minor, and even if an adult, he was a permissive authority.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda brings a baraita citing his own childhood experience of reading the Megillah above Rabbi Tarfon and the elders in Lod, as proof that a minor may read the Megillah.
The Sages reject Rabbi Yehuda's proof, arguing that a minor's action cannot serve as halachic evidence.
Rabbi (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) brings a similar baraita from his own youth, where he read the Megillah above Rabbi Yehuda.
The Sages reject Rabbi's proof with a double objection: he was a minor, and even if an adult, he was a permissive authority (מַתִּיר) whose lenient practice cannot be cited as evidence.

The Gemara clarifies that the Sages' response to Rabbi contained two distinct objections: first, he was a minor; second, even if an adult, he was a permissive authority (מַתִּיר) whose lenient practice cannot be cited as evidence.

items.text: Mishnah: Daytime-only mitzvot
items.text_en: Mishnah: Daytime-only mitzvot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists several mitzvot that must be performed during the day: reading the Megillah, circumcision, immersion, sprinkling, and the immersion of a shomeret yom keneged yom. All are valid if done from dawn onward.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists mitzvot that must be performed during the day: reading the Megillah, circumcision, immersion, sprinkling, and the immersion of a shomeret yom keneged yom, all valid from dawn onward.

items.text: Source for Megillah reading by day
items.text_en: Source for Megillah reading by day
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'and these days are remembered and done' that the reading must be by day, not night. This challenges Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who requires both a night and day reading; the Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers to the daytime reading.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that Megillah reading must be by day, and cites the verse 'וְהַיָּמִים הָאֵלֶּה נִזְכָּרִים וְנַעֲשִׂים' (and these days are remembered and done) to derive that it is performed by day, not night.
The Gemara raises an objection against Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who requires reading the Megillah both at night and by day, from the verse that implies only daytime reading.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's derivation refers only to the daytime reading, not the nighttime one, so Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's requirement remains valid.

items.text: Sources for circumcision, immersion, and sprinkling
items.text_en: Sources for circumcision, immersion, and sprinkling
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses for circumcision (Leviticus 12:3) and for sprinkling and immersion (Numbers 19:19), noting that immersion is juxtaposed to sprinkling, thus both must be by day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse for circumcision (Leviticus 12:3) to prove it must be performed by day.
The Gemara cites the verse for sprinkling (Numbers 19:19) and notes that immersion is juxtaposed to sprinkling, so both must be by day.

items.text: The unique case of shomeret yom keneged yom
items.text_en: The unique case of shomeret yom keneged yom
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the shomeret yom keneged yom is singled out, as all immersions require daytime. It explains that one might have thought she could immerse at night, based on a comparison to a zav's first emission, which is like a ba'al keri and allows daytime immersion. The verse 'all the days of her flow' prevents daytime immersion, but one might think she could immerse at night after partial guarding; the Mishnah teaches that she needs a full day of counting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the shomeret yom keneged yom is singled out, as all immersions require daytime.
The Gemara explains that one might have thought she could immerse at night, based on a comparison to a zav's first emission, which is like a ba'al keri and allows daytime immersion.

The Gemara resolves that the verse 'all the days of her flow' prevents daytime immersion, but one might think she could immerse at night after partial guarding; the Mishnah teaches that she needs a full day of counting.

items.text: Defining the boundaries of day and night
items.text_en: Defining the boundaries of day and night
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the source for the rule that counting the Omer is done during the day. Rava derives from Genesis 1:5 that once light begins to dawn, it is called 'day'. Rabbi Zeira brings a proof from Nehemiah 4:15-16 that the day extends from dawn until nightfall, and that the night is for guarding.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the rule that counting the Omer is performed during the day.
Rava derives from Genesis 1:5 that once light begins to dawn, it is called 'day'.
The Gemara objects that if the same logic applied to night, it would incorrectly define night as beginning at dusk, but we know night only begins after the stars appear.
Rabbi Zeira brings a proof from Nehemiah 4:15-16 that the day extends from dawn until nightfall, and the night is for guarding.
The Gemara explains the additional verse: it precludes the possibility that the workers started early or finished late, showing that day is from dawn to nightfall.

items.text: Mishnah: List of daytime and nighttime mitzvot
items.text_en: Mishnah: List of daytime and nighttime mitzvot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists all mitzvot that are valid only during the day (Megillah reading, Hallel, shofar, lulav, Musaf prayer, additional offerings, various vidduyim, semikhah, shechitah, tenufah, etc.) and those valid only during the night (omer cutting, burning fats and limbs). The general rule: a mitzvah whose time is during the day is valid all day; one whose time is at night is valid all night.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing all mitzvot that are valid only during the day, beginning with Megillah reading and continuing through various Temple and ritual acts.

The Mishnah concludes by listing mitzvot valid only at night (omer cutting, burning fats and limbs) and states the general rule: a daytime mitzvah is valid all day, a nighttime mitzvah is valid all night.

items.text: Gemara: Scriptural sources for each daytime mitzvah
items.text_en: Gemara: Scriptural sources for each daytime mitzvah
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides a verse for each mitzvah listed in the Mishnah to prove that it must be performed during the day. For Megillah: 'והימים האלה נזכרים ונעשים'. For Hallel: 'ממזרח שמש עד מבואו'. For lulav: 'ולקחתם לכם ביום הראשון'. For shofar: 'יום תרועה יהיה לכם'. For Musaf: 'דבר יום ביומו'. For vidduy parim: a gezerah shavah from Yom Kippur. For vidduy ma'aser: 'היום הזה ה' אלהיך מצוך'. For semikhah and shechitah: 'ביום זבחכם'. For tenufah: 'ביום הניפכם את העומר'. For hagashah: linked to tenufah. For melikah, kemitzah, haktarah, and hazayah: 'ביום צוותו את בני ישראל'. For sotah: a gezerah shavah from 'תורה' to 'תורה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that each mitzvah listed in the Mishnah must be performed during the day?

sub.text: Gemara's answer for Megillah and Hallel
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer for Megillah and Hallel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses: for Megillah, 'והימים האלה נזכרים ונעשים' (these days are remembered and done); for Hallel, 'ממזרח שמש עד מבואו' (from the rising of the sun to its setting), and Rabbi Yosei adds 'זה היום עשה ה׳' (this is the day the Lord has made).

sub.text: Gemara's answer for lulav, shofar, Musaf, and Musaf prayer
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer for lulav, shofar, Musaf, and Musaf prayer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses: for lulav, 'ולקחתם לכם ביום הראשון' (you shall take for yourselves on the first day); for shofar, 'יום תרועה יהיה לכם' (a day of sounding the shofar shall be for you); for Musaf, 'דבר יום ביומו' (the matter of the day in its day); and the Sages equated Musaf prayer with Musaf offerings.

sub.text: Gemara's answer for vidduy parim and vidduy ma'aser
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer for vidduy parim and vidduy ma'aser
sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives vidduy parim (confession over the bulls) via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'כפרה' (atonement) from Yom Kippur, where atonement is performed by day; and for vidduy ma'aser (confession of tithes), it cites the verse 'היום הזה ה׳ אלהיך מצוך' (this day the Lord your God commands you).

sub.text: Gemara's answer for semikhah, shechitah, and tenufah
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer for semikhah, shechitah, and tenufah
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses: for semikhah (leaning) and shechitah (slaughter), the verse 'ביום זבחכם' (on the day of your sacrifice); for tenufah (waving), 'ביום הניפכם את העומר' (on the day you wave the omer).

sub.text: Gemara's answer for hagashah, melikah, kemitzah, haktarah, and hazayah
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer for hagashah, melikah, kemitzah, haktarah, and hazayah
sub.desc_en: The Gemara links hagashah (bringing near) to tenufah via a juxtaposition in the sotah passage; and for melikah (pinching), kemitzah (taking a handful), haktarah (burning), and hazayah (sprinkling), it cites 'ביום צוותו את בני ישראל' (on the day He commanded the children of Israel).

The Gemara derives sotah (the suspected adulteress) via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'תורה' (Torah) from the verse 'על פי התורה אשר יורוך ועל המשפט' (according to the Torah they teach you and the judgment).

items.text: Introduction of the principle: day and night validity
items.text_en: Introduction of the principle: day and night validity
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by citing the Mishnah's rule that a mitzvah whose time is during the day is valid all day, and one whose time is at night is valid all night. It then lists examples: the red heifer, the beheaded heifer, the purification of a leper, the cutting of the omer, and the burning of fats and limbs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating the principle that a mitzvah whose time is during the day is valid all day, and one whose time is at night is valid all night.

The Gemara cites Devei Rabbi Yannai's derivation that the beheaded heifer (עגלה ערופה) is valid only by day because atonement (כפרה) is written regarding it, like sacrifices, and the purification of a leper is derived from the verse 'This shall be the law of the leper on the day of his purification.'

The Gemara adds that the omer cutting is valid all night because reaping and counting are at night and bringing is by day, and the burning of fats and limbs is valid all night from the verse 'All night until morning.'

items.text: Clarification of 'this is the rule' for day mitzvot
items.text_en: Clarification of 'this is the rule' for day mitzvot
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'this is the rule' comes to include for day mitzvot. It answers that it includes the arrangement and removal of the showbread, according to Rabbi Yosei, who says that if one removed the old bread in the morning and arranged the new bread in the evening, it is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'this is the rule' comes to include for day mitzvot.
The Gemara answers that it includes the arrangement and removal of the showbread, according to Rabbi Yosei.

A baraita cites Rabbi Yosei's ruling that if one removed the old bread in the morning and arranged the new bread in the evening, it is invalid, and the verse requires the table to never be without bread.

items.text: Clarification of 'this is the rule' for night mitzvot
items.text_en: Clarification of 'this is the rule' for night mitzvot
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'this is the rule' comes to include for night mitzvot. It answers that it includes the eating of the Paschal lamb, and not according to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, who derives from a verse that the eating is only until midnight.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'this is the rule' for night mitzvot comes to include.
The Gemara answers that it includes the eating of the Paschal lamb, and not according to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.
A baraita cites Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, who derives from a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) that the Paschal lamb must be eaten only until midnight.

items.text: Mishnah: Megillah reading and Torah reading on various days
items.text_en: Mishnah: Megillah reading and Torah reading on various days
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who reads the Megillah may stand or sit, and if one or two read it, they have fulfilled the obligation. It then lists the number of aliyot for different days: three on Monday, Thursday, and Shabbat Minchah; four on Rosh Chodesh and Chol Hamoed; five on Yom Tov; six on Yom Kippur; and seven on Shabbat. It also notes that on days with Musaf but not Yom Tov, four read, and that one may add readers on Shabbat and Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah begins a new chapter with the title 'הקורא למפרע' (one who reads out of order).
The Mishnah rules that one who reads the Megillah may stand or sit, and one or two readers fulfill the obligation; blessings depend on local custom.
The Mishnah states that on Monday, Thursday, and Shabbat Minchah, three people read from the Torah, with no additions or haftarah, and only the first and last recite blessings.
The Mishnah rules that on Rosh Chodesh and Chol Hamoed, four people read, with no additions or haftarah, and only the first and last recite blessings.

The Mishnah gives a general rule: on days with Musaf but not Yom Tov, four read; on Yom Tov, five; on Yom Kippur, six; on Shabbat, seven; one may add readers and recite haftarah, and only the first and last recite blessings.

items.text: Gemara: Standing while reading the Torah
items.text_en: Gemara: Standing while reading the Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the requirement to stand while reading the Torah, citing Rabbi Avahu who derives from the verse 'And you, stand here with Me' that even God, as it were, stands. It then brings a baraita that from Moses until Rabban Gamliel, people learned Torah standing, but after his death, sickness came and they learned sitting. Finally, it resolves a contradiction between verses about Moses standing or sitting on the mountain, with various opinions: Rav says standing to learn and sitting to review; Rabbi Chanina says leaning; Rabbi Yochanan says 'sitting' means delaying; and Rava says easy matters standing, difficult ones sitting.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna states that unlike the Megilla, reading the Torah requires standing.
The Gemara asks: From where are these matters derived?
Rabbi Avahu answers that the verse 'ואתה פה עמד עמדי' (And you, stand here with Me) implies that even God, as it were, stands.
Rabbi Avahu further derives from the same verse that a teacher should not sit on a couch while his student sits on the ground.

The Sages taught in a baraita that from Moses until Rabban Gamliel they studied Torah standing, but after his death sickness came and they studied sitting, fulfilling the mishna that honor for Torah ceased.
The Gemara raises a contradiction: one verse says 'ואשב בהר' (And I sat on the mount) and another says 'ואנכי עמדתי בהר' (And I stood on the mount).
Rav resolves: Moses stood to learn and sat to review.
Rabbi Chanina says Moses was neither standing nor sitting but leaning.
Rabbi Yochanan says 'ישיבה' (sitting) is merely an expression of delaying, as in 'ותשבו בקדש' (and you dwelled in Kadesh).
Rava says Moses studied easy matters standing and difficult matters sitting.

items.text: Return to Mishnah: one or two readers
items.text_en: Return to Mishnah: one or two readers
items.desc_en: The Gemara briefly returns to the Mishnah's statement that if one or two read the Megillah, they have fulfilled the obligation, setting up further discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that if one or two read the Megillah, they have fulfilled the obligation.

items.text: Rules for reading and translating Torah, Prophets, Hallel, and Megillah
items.text_en: Rules for reading and translating Torah, Prophets, Hallel, and Megillah
items.desc_en: A baraita states that for Torah reading, one reads and one translates, but not two translators; for Prophets, one reads and two may translate; for Hallel and Megillah, even ten readers and ten translators are allowed. The Gemara explains that because the Megillah is beloved, people pay attention and listen.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states the rules for reading and translating Torah, Prophets, Hallel, and Megillah, specifying the number of readers and translators permitted for each.
The Gemara explains that the reason for the leniency with Megillah is that because it is beloved, people pay attention and listen.

items.text: Blessings before and after the Megillah reading
items.text_en: Blessings before and after the Megillah reading
items.desc_en: Abaye distinguishes between the blessing after the Megillah (which is optional depending on custom) and the blessing before (which is obligatory, based on the principle that all mitzvot require a blessing before performance). The Gemara then discusses the specific texts of the blessings, with Rava and Rav Pappa offering formulations.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that in a place where it is customary to recite a blessing after the Megillah, one should do so.

Abaye distinguishes that the Mishnah's leniency applies only to the blessing after the Megillah, but the blessing before is obligatory, citing Shmuel's principle that all מצות (commandments) require a blessing before performance.
The Gemara questions how the word 'עוֹבֵר' (passes) implies doing something before the act.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a verse where 'וַיַּעֲבֹר' (passed) means going before, proving the linguistic point.
Abaye and an alternative source offer additional verses where 'עָבַר' (passed) clearly means going before.
The Gemara asks what blessing is recited before the Megillah reading.
Rav Sheshet mi-Katrazya came before Rav Ashi and recited the blessing 'עַל מִקְרָא מְגִלָּה' (on reading the Megillah).
The Gemara asks what blessing is recited after the Megillah reading.
The Gemara presents the standard text of the blessing after the Megillah, which praises God for avenging Israel.
Rava proposes an alternative conclusion to the blessing: 'הָאֵל הַמּוֹשִׁיעַ' (the God who saves).
Rav Pappa rules that we include both formulations: 'הַנִּפְרָע לְיִשְׂרָאֵל מִכָּל צָרֵיהֶם הָאֵל הַמּוֹשִׁיעַ' (who avenges Israel from all their enemies, the God who saves).

items.text: The three readers on Monday, Thursday, and Shabbat Minchah correspond to what?
items.text_en: The three readers on Monday, Thursday, and Shabbat Minchah correspond to what?
items.desc_en: Rav Asi says the three readers correspond to Torah, Prophets, and Writings; Rava says they correspond to Priests, Levites, and Israelites. The Gemara then asks about the ten verses minimum, with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, Rav Yosef, Rabbi Levi, and Rabbi Yochanan offering different correspondences (ten idlers, Ten Commandments, ten praises in Psalms, ten utterances of creation). The Gemara resolves that 'Bereishit' itself is an utterance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the three readers on Monday, Thursday, and Shabbat Minchah correspond to.
Rav Asi answers that the three readers correspond to Torah, Prophets, and Writings.
Rava answers that the three readers correspond to Priests, Levites, and Israelites.
The Gemara cites Rav Shimi's baraita that one may not read fewer than ten verses in the synagogue, and 'וַיְדַבֵּר' (And the Lord spoke) counts toward the minimum.
The Gemara asks what the ten verses correspond to.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi answers that the ten verses correspond to the ten idlers (בטלנין) in the synagogue.
Rav Yosef answers that the ten verses correspond to the Ten Commandments given to Moses at Sinai.
Rabbi Levi answers that the ten verses correspond to the ten praises (הילולין) that David said in the book of Psalms.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the ten verses correspond to the ten utterances (מאמרות) by which the world was created.
The Gemara asks which are the ten utterances, noting that only nine instances of 'וַיֹּאמֶר' (And He said) appear in the creation account.
The Gemara resolves that 'בְּרֵאשִׁית' (In the beginning) itself is considered an utterance, as it is written 'בִּדְבַר ה׳ שָׁמַיִם נַעֲשׂוּ' (By the word of the Lord the heavens were made).

items.text: Praise for the first, middle, and last reader who reads four verses
items.text_en: Praise for the first, middle, and last reader who reads four verses
items.desc_en: Rava states that the first, middle, and last reader who reads four verses are praiseworthy. The Gemara provides reasons: the first because of the mitzvah of the first (from the Temple treasury), the middle because the middle lamp of the Menorah is praiseworthy, and the last because of the principle of ascending in holiness. Rav Pappa praises someone who read first with four verses.

sub.desc_en: Rava declares that the first, middle, and last reader who reads four verses are praiseworthy.

sub.text: Supporting baraita for the first reader
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for the first reader
sub.desc_en: The Gemara supports the praise for the first reader by citing a Mishnah about the Temple treasury, where the first basket is used first because of the principle of מצוה בראשון (the mitzvah of the first).

sub.text: Supporting baraita for the middle reader
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for the middle reader
sub.desc_en: The Gemara supports the praise for the middle reader by citing a baraita about the Menorah's middle lamp facing the Shechinah, and Rabbi Yochanan's inference that the middle is praiseworthy.

sub.text: Supporting principle for the last reader
sub.text_en: Supporting principle for the last reader
sub.desc_en: The Gemara supports the praise for the last reader by invoking the principle of מעלין בקודש (ascending in holiness), and adds that Rav Pappa praised someone who read first with four verses.

items.text: The opener and closer bless; current practice of all blessing
items.text_en: The opener and closer bless; current practice of all blessing
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the one who opens the reading blesses before it, and the one who closes blesses after. The Gemara explains that nowadays everyone blesses both before and after due to a rabbinic decree for those who enter and leave.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the one who opens the reading blesses before it, and the one who closes blesses after it.
The Gemara explains that nowadays everyone blesses both before and after due to a rabbinic decree for those who enter and leave.

items.text: How to read the Rosh Chodesh portion with eight verses
items.text_en: How to read the Rosh Chodesh portion with eight verses
items.desc_en: Ulla bar Rav asks Rava how to read the Rosh Chodesh portion, which has eight verses, given the rules about not leaving fewer than three verses. The Gemara considers options: reading 2-3-3 leaves two verses, which is insufficient; reading 4-4 leaves seven, but the next portions (Shabbat and Rosh Chodesh) have two and five verses respectively, creating a problem. The discussion is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Ulla bar Rav asks Rava how to read the Rosh Chodesh portion, which has eight verses, given the constraints.

The Gemara considers options: reading 2-3-3 leaves two verses (insufficient), reading 4-4 leaves seven verses, but the next portions have two and five verses, creating a problem, and the discussion is cut off.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and initial question
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and initial question
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one does not begin a Torah portion with fewer than three verses. The Gemara raises a problem: if a portion has only five verses, and two readers read three and two respectively, two verses remain for the next reader, violating the rule.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule that one does not begin a Torah portion with fewer than three verses, and the Gemara raises a problem: if a portion has five verses and two readers read three and two respectively, two verses remain for the next reader, violating the rule.

items.text: Support from a baraita and further difficulty
items.text_en: Support from a baraita and further difficulty
items.desc_en: A baraita about the first day of creation is cited, where 'Bereishit' is read by two and 'Yehi Rakia' by one. The Gemara questions how 'Bereishit' can be read by two when it has five verses, contradicting the rule of not reading fewer than three verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about the first day of creation, where 'Bereishit' is read by two and 'Yehi Rakia' by one.
The Gemara questions how 'Bereishit' can be read by two when it has five verses, contradicting the rule of not reading fewer than three verses.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel's dispute: doleg vs. posek
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel's dispute: doleg vs. posek
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate how to handle the situation: Rav says to skip (doleg) to the next portion, while Shmuel says to break (posek) the portion. Their reasons are explained: Rav holds that one may not break a verse that Moses did not break, while Shmuel is concerned about those entering and leaving.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rav and Shmuel dispute the method: Rav says doleg (skip) and Shmuel says posek (break the verse).
The Gemara explains that Rav holds one may not break a verse that Moses did not break.

The Gemara objects that Rabbi Chananya reported Rabbi Chanina the Great only allowed breaking verses for children learning, and the Gemara answers that there too it was unavoidable, so here too it is unavoidable.
The Gemara explains that Shmuel rejects skipping due to a גזירה (decree) for those entering and leaving.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought that describes how to read a six-verse portion by two readers, and a five-verse portion by one. The Gemara challenges both Rav and Shmuel, but resolves that the baraita deals with a case where it is possible to read without skipping or breaking.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited describing how to read a six-verse portion by two readers and a five-verse portion by one, with a dispute about the second reader's continuation.
The Gemara objects: according to Rav who allows skipping (דּוֹלֵג) or Shmuel who allows breaking (פּוֹסֵק), why does the baraita not simply use those methods?
The Gemara resolves: the baraita deals with a case where it is possible to read without skipping or breaking, so those methods are unnecessary.

items.text: Ruling of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and discussion on leaving verses
items.text_en: Ruling of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and discussion on leaving verses
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules like the 'Yesh Omrim' that one may not leave fewer than three verses at the end of a portion. The Gemara questions why this is necessary, and explains that it prevents people from leaving during the reading.

sub.text: Rabbi Tanchum citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Tanchum citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules like the 'Yesh Omrim' that one may not leave fewer than three verses at the end of a portion.
The Gemara asks: this ruling is obvious, since if the Yesh Omrim are stringent about starting, they should certainly be stringent about leaving.
The Gemara explains: one might have thought that leaving is less problematic because people entering are common but people leaving are not, so the ruling teaches that the same concern applies.
The Gemara digresses to ask why the Tanna Kamma forbids leaving but not starting, and answers that one who enters can simply wait for the next reading.

items.text: Final halakhic ruling: doleg
items.text_en: Final halakhic ruling: doleg
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rava sends a query to Rav Yosef about the halakha, and the response is that one should skip (doleg), and the middle reader also skips.

sub.text: Rabba son of Rava to Rav Yosef
sub.text_en: Rabba son of Rava to Rav Yosef
sub.desc_en: Rabba son of Rava sent to Rav Yosef: what is the הלכה (binding law)? Rav Yosef replied: the law is to skip (דולג), and the middle reader skips.
Rav Yosef responds that the halakha (הלכה) is to skip (דולג), and the middle reader also skips.

items.text: Question about fast day readings
items.text_en: Question about fast day readings
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how many aliyot are read on a public fast day, comparing to Rosh Chodesh and Chol HaMoed which have four due to the additional sacrifice. A baraita is cited but found inconclusive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how many aliyot are read on a public fast day, considering whether it follows Rosh Chodesh and Chol HaMoed (four due to the additional sacrifice) or is different because there is no sacrifice, only an additional prayer.
A baraita is cited that lists readings for various occasions, but the Gemara finds it inconclusive because the first clause implies three for a fast day while the second clause implies four.

items.text: Story of Rav in Babylon and inference about fast day aliyot
items.text_en: Story of Rav in Babylon and inference about fast day aliyot
items.desc_en: Rav visits Babylon on a fast day, reads from the Torah, but does not recite the blessing after. The Gemara initially thinks this shows he expected another reader, but concludes Rav read as a priest, and the story does not resolve the question about the number of aliyot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story: Rav visited Babylon on a public fast day, read from the Torah, opened with a blessing, concluded without a blessing, and everyone fell on their faces except Rav.
The Gemara asks: Since Rav read as an Israelite, why did he conclude without a blessing? Is it not because he expected another reader after him, implying that on a fast day there are four aliyot?
The Gemara rejects the inference: Rav read as a priest, not as an Israelite, as Rav Huna also read among the priests.
The Gemara objects: Rav Huna reading among priests is understandable because even the great priests of Eretz Yisrael deferred to him, but Rav had Shmuel, a priest, who was greater than him.
The Gemara answers: Shmuel himself deferred to Rav, and Rav only showed him honor in his presence, not in his absence, so when Rav read, Shmuel was not present to take precedence.
The Gemara provides supporting evidence: if Rav had read as an Israelite, why would he have recited the opening blessing? It must be that he read as a priest, following the later enactment.
The Gemara objects: if so, why did he not recite the concluding blessing? The Gemara answers that the case is different because where Rav sat, people would enter (and he did not want to interrupt).

items.text: Proof from the Mishnah's rule
items.text_en: Proof from the Mishnah's rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that on a public fast day and Tisha B'Av, three people read from the Torah, based on the Mishnah's rule that any day with cessation of work (like a public fast) has three readers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the previous proof does not resolve the issue.
The Gemara brings a Mishnah rule: any day with cessation of work, like a public fast and Tisha B'Av, has three readers, while days without it have four.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative version
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative version
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi challenges the proof by citing a different version of the Mishnah that says any day with Musaf but not a festival has four readers, implying that includes public fasts and Tisha B'Av.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects that the Mishnah's version he knows (any day with Musaf but not a festival has four readers) includes public fasts and Tisha B'Av, undermining the proof.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of Rav Ashi's Mishnah
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of Rav Ashi's Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions which Tanna holds the view in Rav Ashi's Mishnah, concluding it is neither the first Tanna nor Rabbi Yosei, based on a baraita about readings on different days of the week.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna's view underlies Rav Ashi's Mishnah.
The Gemara answers that it is neither the first Tanna nor Rabbi Yosei, citing a baraita about readings on different days of the week.

items.text: Resolution: the rule is a mnemonic
items.text_en: Resolution: the rule is a mnemonic
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the rule 'this is the principle' is merely a mnemonic to distinguish between festivals and intermediate days, and then lists the number of readers for each occasion based on its sanctity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: the baraita's rule 'this is the principle' contradicts the mishnah's formulation.
The Gemara answers that the baraita's rule comes to include Rosh Chodesh and Chol HaMoed, not fasts.
The Gemara objects: the mishnah already explicitly states that on Rosh Chodesh and Chol HaMoed four read, so the rule is redundant.
The Gemara resolves that the rule is merely a mnemonic to distinguish between festivals and intermediate days, and then lists the number of readers for each occasion based on its sanctity.

items.text: Rav's conduct on a fast day
items.text_en: Rav's conduct on a fast day
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates that when Rav visited Babylonia on a public fast day, he read from the Torah but did not prostrate, and explains that the floor was made of stone, which is prohibited for prostration except in the Temple.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that when Rav visited Babylonia on a public fast day, he read from the Torah but did not prostrate with the congregation.
The Gemara asks why Rav did not prostrate.
The Gemara explains that the floor was made of stone, and cites a baraita and Ulla's statement that the Torah only prohibited prostration on a stone floor outside the Temple.

items.text: Explanations for Rav's behavior
items.text_en: Explanations for Rav's behavior
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers several explanations for why Rav alone did not prostrate: he was before the congregation, he did not want to trouble them, he performed full prostration (spreading hands and feet), and he was a distinguished person who should not prostrate unless answered like Joshua.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rav alone did not prostrate, since the stone floor prohibition would apply to everyone.
The Gemara answers that Rav was before the congregation and did not want to trouble them by going elsewhere to prostrate.
The Gemara alternatively explains that Rav performed full prostration (פישוט ידים ורגלים, spreading hands and feet), which is the prohibited form, and he would not deviate from his practice.
The Gemara further explains that a distinguished person (אדם חשוב) is different, as Rabbi Elazar taught that such a person may not prostrate unless answered like Joshua bin Nun.

items.text: Definitions of prostration types
items.text_en: Definitions of prostration types
items.desc_en: A baraita defines three types of prostration: kiddah (on the face), keriah (on the knees), and hishtachava'ah (spreading hands and feet), each with biblical prooftexts.

sub.desc_en: The baraita defines three types of prostration: קִידָּה (on the face), כְּרִיעָה (on the knees), and הִשְׁתַּחֲוָאָה (spreading hands and feet), each with a biblical prooftext.

items.text: Levi's injury and lesson
items.text_en: Levi's injury and lesson
items.desc_en: Levi performed kiddah before Rabbi and became lame, illustrating that one should not be overly bold in prayer, as Rabbi Elazar said that a great person who did so was injured, and that was Levi.

sub.desc_en: Levi performed קידָּה (prostration on the face) before Rabbi and became lame.
The gemara asks: Did the prostration itself cause his injury, given Rabbi Elazar's teaching that a great person who spoke boldly toward Heaven was injured, and that person was Levi?
The gemara resolves: Both the bold speech and the prostration together caused his injury.
Rav Chiyya bar Avin adds that he saw Abaye (perform a similar prostration), implying the lesson was not universally applied.

items.text: Rava's practice regarding the additional aliyah
items.text_en: Rava's practice regarding the additional aliyah
items.desc_en: Rava would pray for an additional aliyah, setting the stage for the discussion of the Mishnah's numbers.

sub.desc_en: The gemara notes that Rava would pray for an additional aliyah (עלייה), introducing the context for the Mishnah's discussion of aliyah numbers.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions which Tanna authored the Mishnah's numbers (5 for Yom Tov, 6 for Yom Kippur, 7 for Shabbat), noting it is neither Rabbi Yishmael nor Rabbi Akiva as per a baraisa. Rava resolves by citing a Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael who allows adding, and explains the contradiction between the two versions of Rabbi Yishmael's position as two different Tanna'im.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna authored the Mishnah's numbers, noting it is neither Rabbi Yishmael nor Rabbi Akiva.
The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yishmael, the allowance to add is problematic, and if it follows Rabbi Akiva, the numbers six and seven are reversed.
Rava resolves that the Mishnah follows a Tanna from the school of Rabbi Yishmael who allows adding to the numbers.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction between the two versions of Rabbi Yishmael's position by attributing them to two different Tanna'im.

items.text: Attributing the baraisa about arrival and departure times
items.text_en: Attributing the baraisa about arrival and departure times
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who authored the baraisa about arriving early and leaving late on Yom Tov, Yom Kippur, and Shabbat, suggesting it might be Rabbi Akiva who has an extra person, but concludes it could even be Rabbi Yishmael due to the lengthy order of the day.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks who is the Tanna of a baraita that describes different arrival and departure times for festivals, Yom Kippur, and Shabbat.
The gemara suggests it might be Rabbi Akiva, who has an extra person, but concludes it could even be Rabbi Yishmael, as the day's order is longer.
The Gemara concludes it could even be Rabbi Yishmael, because the lengthy order of the day accounts for the extra time.

items.text: Symbolic meaning of three, five, and seven
items.text_en: Symbolic meaning of three, five, and seven
items.desc_en: A dispute between Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani and Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi (or others) about what the numbers three, five, and seven correspond to: one says the priestly blessing, another says the three gatekeepers, five of the king's confidants, and seven of the king's courtiers. Rav Yosef teaches the latter interpretation, and Abaye questions why he hadn't explained it earlier.

sub.desc_en: The other disputant says the numbers correspond to the three gatekeepers, five of the king's confidants, and seven of the king's courtiers (from the Book of Esther).
Rav Yosef explicitly teaches the interpretation that the numbers correspond to the gatekeepers, confidants, and courtiers.
Abaye asks Rav Yosef: until now, why didn't you explain this interpretation to us?
Rav Yosef responds: I didn't know you needed it; if you had asked me, wouldn't I have told you?

items.text: The six of Yom Kippur and the seven of Shabbat
items.text_en: The six of Yom Kippur and the seven of Shabbat
items.desc_en: Yaakov the heretic asks Rav Yehuda what the six aliyot of Yom Kippur correspond to, and Rav Yehuda answers they correspond to the six on Ezra's right and six on his left, citing a verse. The Gemara notes that the verse lists seven names, but explains that Zechariah and Meshullam are the same person, with Meshullam being a nickname.

sub.desc_en: Yaakov the heretic asks Rav Yehuda what the six aliyot of Yom Kippur correspond to.
Rav Yehuda answers that they correspond to the six on Ezra's right and six on his left, citing the verse listing the names.
The Gemara objects that the verse lists seven names, not six.
The Gemara resolves that Zechariah and Meshullam are the same person, with Meshullam being a nickname meaning 'perfect in his deeds'.

items.text: Who may be counted among the seven aliyot
items.text_en: Who may be counted among the seven aliyot
items.desc_en: A baraisa teaches that everyone may be counted among the seven aliyot, even a minor or a woman, but the Sages said a woman should not read from the Torah due to the dignity of the congregation.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that everyone, including a minor and a woman, counts toward the seven aliyot, but the sages said a woman should not read from the Torah due to communal dignity.

items.text: Whether the maftir counts among the seven aliyot
items.text_en: Whether the maftir counts among the seven aliyot
items.desc_en: A dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba: one says the maftir counts among the seven, the other says not. The one who says it does not count cites Ulla's reason that the maftir reads from the prophet due to the honor of the Torah, so it does not count. An objection is raised from a baraisa requiring 21 verses for the haftarah, which would be 24 if the maftir counted, but the Gemara deflects because the maftir's reading is for the honor of the Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: does the מפטיר (maftir) count toward the quorum of seven readers?

sub.text: Rav Huna and Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rav Huna and Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba dispute: one says the מפטיר (maftir) counts because he reads from the Torah.
The other opinion follows Ulla, who says the מפטיר (maftir) reads from the prophet only due to the honor of the Torah, so he does not count toward the seven.
The Gemara objects from a ברייתא (baraita) requiring twenty-one verses for the הפטרה (haftarah), which would be twenty-four if the מפטיר (maftir) were an extra reader.
The Gemara deflects the objection, explaining that since the מפטיר (maftir) reads only for the honor of the Torah, the minimum verse count remains twenty-one.

items.text: Conclusion of the discussion on reading fewer than ten verses
items.text_en: Conclusion of the discussion on reading fewer than ten verses
items.desc_en: Rava challenges the earlier assertion that one cannot read fewer than twenty-one verses, citing the case of "your burnt offerings" which has fewer. The Gemara distinguishes between a place with a translator and without, citing Rav Shmuel bar Abba's testimony about Rabbi Yochanan and the baraita of Rav Tachlifa bar Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a corresponding verse is also not required when reading fewer than ten verses.
Rava objects by citing the case of 'עוֹלוֹתֵיכֶם סְפוֹ' (your burnt offerings), which has fewer than twenty-one verses, and the Gemara distinguishes that there the topic concludes.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Abba's testimony and baraita of Rav Tachlifa bar Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Abba's testimony and baraita of Rav Tachlifa bar Shmuel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether without a concluding topic one cannot stop, and cites Rav Shmuel bar Abba's testimony about Rabbi Yochanan and the baraita of Rav Tachlifa bar Shmuel, which distinguishes between a place without a translator (where one may stop at ten verses) and with a translator (where one may stop at fewer).

items.text: Mishnah: List of rituals requiring ten
items.text_en: Mishnah: List of rituals requiring ten
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists several communal rituals that require a minyan of ten: reciting the Shema with its blessings, passing before the ark, the priestly blessing, reading from the Torah, reading from the Prophets, the mourners' stand and sit, the mourners' blessing and consolation, the wedding blessing, and the invitation to bless God by name. It adds that for land valuation, nine Israelites and a priest suffice, and similarly for a person valued by vow.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists communal rituals that require a minyan of ten: reciting the Shema with its blessings, passing before the ark, priestly blessing, Torah reading, haftarah, the mourners' and grooms' blessings, and zimmun with God's name; and adds that for land valuation nine Israelites and a priest suffice, and similarly for a person.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of ten from the verse
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of ten from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the requirement of ten. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan cites the verse "and I shall be sanctified among the children of Israel" — anything involving sanctity requires no fewer than ten. The derivation is through a series of verbal analogies: "among" from "among the congregation" and "congregation" from "the evil congregation" (the spies), where the congregation is ten.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the scriptural source for the requirement of ten for matters of sanctity.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan derives from the verse 'וְנִקְדַּשְׁתִּי בְּתוֹךְ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל' (I will be sanctified among the children of Israel) that any matter of sanctity requires no fewer than ten.

The Gemara explains the derivation through a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) using 'תּוֹךְ' (among) and 'עֵדָה' (congregation), linking to the ten spies in the verse 'עַד מָתַי לָעֵדָה הָרָעָה הַזֹּאת' (How long shall this evil congregation be).

items.text: Explanation of the mourners' stand and sit
items.text_en: Explanation of the mourners' stand and sit
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the mourners' stand and sit requires ten because one must say "stand, honored ones, stand" and "sit, honored ones, sit," and with fewer than ten it is not proper conduct.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the ritual of 'מעמד ומושב' (standing and sitting) requires ten because saying 'עִמְדוּ יְקָרִים עֲמוֹדוּ, שְׁבוּ יְקָרִים שֵׁבוּ' (Stand, honored ones, stand; sit, honored ones, sit) with fewer than ten is not proper conduct (אורח ארעא).

items.text: Definition of mourners' blessing and wedding blessing
items.text_en: Definition of mourners' blessing and wedding blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines the mourners' blessing as the blessing of Rechava. Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that the mourners' blessing requires ten, and the mourners are not counted in the minyan; the wedding blessing requires ten, and the bridegroom is counted.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation with Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation with Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'ברכת אבלים' (the mourners' blessing) is the 'ברכת רחבה' (the broad blessing), and cites Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the mourners' blessing requires ten with the mourners not counting, while the grooms' blessing requires ten with the grooms counting.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that the mourners' blessing requires ten and the mourners are not counted, while the wedding blessing requires ten and the bridegroom is counted.

items.text: Explanation of the invitation to bless by name
items.text_en: Explanation of the invitation to bless by name
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the invitation to bless God by name requires ten because one must say "let us bless our God," and with fewer than ten it is not proper conduct.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that zimmun with God's name (saying 'נְבָרֵךְ לֵאלֹהֵינוּ' — Let us bless our God) requires ten because fewer than ten is not proper conduct.

items.text: Source for land requiring nine and a priest
items.text_en: Source for land requiring nine and a priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the rule that land valuation requires nine Israelites and a priest. Shmuel answers that ten priests are written in the relevant passage; one is for the law itself, one is to exclude, and the rest constitute multiple exclusions which come to include, teaching that nine Israelites and one priest suffice. The Gemara raises a difficulty: why not five priests and five Israelites?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the rule that land valuation requires nine Israelites and a priest.

Shmuel explains that ten priests are written in the passage; one is for the law itself, one is to exclude, and the rest constitute multiple exclusions which come to include, teaching that nine Israelites and one priest suffice.
The Gemara raises a difficulty: why not five priests and five Israelites?

items.text: Explanation of a person valued by vow
items.text_en: Explanation of a person valued by vow
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a person can be like land. Rabbi Abahu explains that it refers to one who says "my valuation is upon me," as taught in a baraita: one who says "my valuation is upon me" is assessed like a slave, and a slave is compared to land, as it is written "and you shall bequeath them to your children after you as an inheritance."

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a person can be considered like land (קרקע) for valuation, asking: is a person holy?

Rabbi Avahu answers that it refers to one who says 'דְּמֵי עָלַי' (my monetary value is upon me), and cites a baraita that such a person is appraised like a slave, and a slave is equated to land through the verse 'וְהִתְנַחַלְתֶּם אוֹתָם לִבְנֵיכֶם אַחֲרֵיכֶם לָרֶשֶׁת אֲחוּזָּה' (You shall bequeath them to your children after you as an inheritance).

items.text: Mishnah: Rules for the Torah reader
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rules for the Torah reader
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who reads from the Torah should not read fewer than three verses, and should not read to the translator more than one verse at a time.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who reads from the Torah must read no fewer than three verses, and may not read more than one verse to the translator.
