items.text: Opening Mishnah: Rules for reading from the Prophets
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Rules for reading from the Prophets
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that three verses are read from the Prophets, and if they are three separate passages, each is read individually. One may skip within the Prophets but not within the Torah, provided the translator does not pause.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that three verses are read from the Prophets; if they are three separate passages, each is read individually; one may skip within the Prophets but not within the Torah, provided the translator does not pause.

items.text: Gemara's question: What do the three verses correspond to?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: What do the three verses correspond to?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the three verses from the Prophets correspond to, and Rav Asi answers that they correspond to the Torah, Prophets, and Writings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what do these three verses correspond to?
Rav Asi answers that they correspond to Torah, Prophets, and Writings.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's rule with examples
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's rule with examples
items.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates on the Mishnah's rule, providing examples of three separate passages from Isaiah where each is read individually.

sub.desc_en: A baraita elaborates: one may not read more than one verse to the translator in the Torah, but in the Prophets three verses, and if they are three separate passages, each is read individually, citing examples from Isaiah.
Examples of three-verse paragraphs from Isaiah are cited to illustrate the rule.

items.text: Contradiction and resolution regarding skipping in the Torah
items.text_en: Contradiction and resolution regarding skipping in the Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah says one may not skip in the Torah, yet a baraita allows skipping from 'Acharei Mot' to 'Ach Ba'asor'. Abaye resolves this by distinguishing between skipping within one topic (permitted) and between two topics (forbidden), with the condition that the translator does not pause.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah forbids skipping in the Torah, yet a baraita allows skipping from 'Acharei Mot' to 'Ach Ba'asor'.
Abaye initially resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a case where the translator pauses (forbidden) and where he does not pause (permitted).
The Gemara objects: the Mishnah explicitly states that skipping in the Torah is absolutely forbidden, implying no exception even when the translator does not pause.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between skipping within one topic (permitted) and between two topics (forbidden), with the condition that the translator does not pause.

items.text: Additional baraita: Skipping between prophets
items.text_en: Additional baraita: Skipping between prophets
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one may not skip from one prophet to another, but within the Book of the Twelve Prophets one may skip, provided one does not skip from the end of the book to the beginning.

sub.desc_en: Another baraita adds: one may not skip from one prophet to another, but within the Book of the Twelve Prophets one may skip, provided one does not skip from the end of the book to its beginning.

items.text: Mishnah: Who may lead the service?
items.text_en: Mishnah: Who may lead the service?
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the one who reads the haftarah also leads the prayers and recites the priestly blessing. A minor may do so with his father or teacher's assistance, but a minor cannot lead certain parts. A person with a physical defect (poche'ach) or a blind person (somei) has restrictions, with Rabbi Yehuda adding that one who never saw light may not lead the Shema.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the one who reads the haftarah also leads the Shema, passes before the ark, and lifts his hands for the priestly blessing; if he is a minor, his father or teacher passes before the ark in his place.
The Mishnah rules that a minor may read from the Torah and translate, but may not lead the Shema, pass before the ark, or lift his hands.
The Mishnah rules that a person with exposed limbs (פּוֹחֵחַ) may lead the Shema and translate, but may not read from the Torah, pass before the ark, or lift his hands.
The Mishnah rules that a blind person may lead the Shema and translate, but Rabbi Yehuda adds that one who never saw the luminaries in his life may not lead the Shema.

items.text: Gemara: Reasons for disqualification and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara: Reasons for disqualification and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates the reason why a blind person cannot lead the Shema: Rav Pappa says it is due to honor (of God), while Rabbah bar Shimi says it is to avoid suspicion. The Gemara questions both reasons regarding a minor, and concludes that the concern is the honor of the father or teacher.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the reason that the one who reads the haftara is honored with these other roles?
Rav Pappa answers: It is due to a desire to grant him honor.
Rabbah bar Shimi answers: It is due to a concern that they will come to quarrel.
The Gemara asks: What is the practical difference between these two reasons?
The Gemara answers: There is a practical difference where the one who passes before the ark does so free of charge.
The Gemara objects from the mishna: If the reason is due to concern for quarreling, would a minor engage in quarreling?
The Gemara objects: If the reason is due to honor, does a minor have honor that is slighted?
The Gemara resolves: Rather, according to Rav Pappa it is a display of honor to his father and his teacher.

items.text: Transition from previous daf
items.text_en: Transition from previous daf
items.desc_en: The Gemara connects the previous discussion to the current one, noting that here too there is a concern for the honor of one's father and teacher.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara connects the previous discussion to the current one, noting that here too there is a concern for the honor of one's father and teacher.

items.text: Minor who can uncover himself may read the Torah?
items.text_en: Minor who can uncover himself may read the Torah?
items.desc_en: Ulla bar Rav asks Abaye whether a minor who can uncover himself may read the Torah. Abaye responds by comparing it to a naked person, who is disqualified due to communal honor, and concludes that the minor is also disqualified for the same reason.

sub.text: Ulla bar Rav's question to Abaye
sub.text_en: Ulla bar Rav's question to Abaye
sub.desc_en: Ulla bar Rav asks Abaye whether a minor who is a פוחח (one whose garments are not properly arranged) may read from the Torah.
Abaye responds by drawing an analogy to a naked person, who is disqualified due to public dignity, and applies the same reasoning to a minor פוחח.

items.text: Blind person leading the Shema and the dispute with Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Blind person leading the Shema and the dispute with Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a blind person may lead the Shema. A baraita reports that the Sages told Rabbi Yehuda that many have expounded on the Merkavah without seeing it. Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between understanding and pleasure, while the Rabbis, following Rabbi Yosei, argue that a blind person does derive pleasure from light, as illustrated by a story of a blind person carrying a torch.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that a blind person may lead the Shema prayer.
A baraita is cited where the Sages told Rabbi Yehuda that many have expounded on the Divine Chariot without seeing it, challenging his objection to a blind person leading prayer.
Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes: there, understanding depends on the heart's intuition and one can intend and know; here, the issue is pleasure (הנאה) from light, which a blind person lacks.

sub.text: Rabbis' objection with Rabbi Yosei's support
sub.text_en: Rabbis' objection with Rabbi Yosei's support
sub.desc_en: The Rabbis argue that a blind person does have pleasure, citing Rabbi Yosei's story of a blind man who carried a torch to be seen and saved from hazards.
Rabbi Yosei recounts a story of a blind person carrying a torch, who explains that the light helps others see him and save him from pitfalls, thorns, and thistles.

items.text: Mishnah: Priest with blemishes or dyed hands may not raise his hands
items.text_en: Mishnah: Priest with blemishes or dyed hands may not raise his hands
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a priest with blemishes on his hands may not perform the Priestly Blessing. Rabbi Yehuda adds that one with dyed hands is also disqualified because people will stare at him.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a priest with blemishes on his hands may not perform the Priestly Blessing, and Rabbi Yehuda adds that one with dyed hands is also disqualified because people will stare at him.

items.text: Gemara: Specific disqualifications for Priestly Blessing
items.text_en: Gemara: Specific disqualifications for Priestly Blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates on the Mishnah, listing specific blemishes and conditions that disqualify a priest: blotched, crooked, or bent hands; people from certain cities due to pronunciation; a priest with a thick voice; a zablugan (one with a certain eye condition); and a blind person in one eye. In each case, if the condition is common in the city, it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that the blemishes mentioned in the Mishnah refer to the face, hands, and feet.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that a priest with blotched hands may not perform the Priestly Blessing.
A baraita supports Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling regarding blotched hands.
The baraita adds that crooked or bent hands also disqualify a priest from the Priestly Blessing.
Rav Assi rules that priests from Haifa and Beit She'an may not perform the Priestly Blessing due to their pronunciation.
A baraita supports Rav Assi, listing cities whose residents mispronounce letters and are therefore disqualified from leading prayer.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya's statement to Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya's statement to Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya tells Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi that if he were a Levite, his thick voice would disqualify him from the platform.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi's report to his father
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi's report to his father
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi reports Rabbi Chiyya's comment to his father, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rejects Rabbi Chiyya's criticism, arguing that a thick voice could cause mispronunciation of the verse 'וְחִכִּיתִי לַה׳' (I wait for the Lord), leading to blasphemy.
Rav Huna rules that a priest with a zablugan (a certain eye condition) may not perform the Priestly Blessing.
The Gemara objects that there was a zablugan in Rav Huna's neighborhood who performed the Priestly Blessing.
The Gemara resolves that the zablugan was a well-known resident of his city, making it permissible.
A baraita supports Rav Huna's ruling with the same exception for a well-known resident.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that a priest blind in one eye may not perform the Priestly Blessing.
The Gemara objects that there was a one-eyed priest in Rabbi Yochanan's neighborhood who performed the Priestly Blessing.
The Gemara resolves that the one-eyed priest was a well-known resident of his city, making it permissible.
A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling with the same exception for a well-known resident.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that a priest with dyed hands may not perform the Priestly Blessing.
A baraita adds that if most people in the city have dyed hands due to their occupation, it is permitted.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Rules for prayer leader and tefillin
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Rules for prayer leader and tefillin
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who refuses to lead the prayer in colored garments may not lead in white, and similar rules for sandals. The Gemara explains the concern for heresy. It then discusses the law that tefillin must be square, and Rav Papa clarifies that the Mishnah refers to a round shape like a nut.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who refuses to lead the prayer in colored garments may not lead in white, and similarly for sandals.
The Mishnah continues with rules about tefillin: round ones are dangerous and lack merit, placing them on the forehead or palm is heresy, and gilding them is the way of outsiders.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah forbids leading prayer in colored garments, and answers that we suspect heresy may have been cast upon him.
The Gemara cites the tradition that tefillin must be square as a law from Sinai, and Rava adds that this applies to their stitching and diagonal.
Rav Papa clarifies that the Mishnah's 'round' tefillin refers to a shape like a nut, not a perfect sphere.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Prohibited formulations
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Prohibited formulations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists several expressions that are censured: 'May the good bless you' (a heretical formulation), 'Your mercy reaches the bird's nest', 'May Your name be mentioned for good', and 'We give thanks, we give thanks' (repetition implying two powers). Also, one who uses euphemisms for forbidden relations or misinterprets the verse about Molech is silenced.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing prohibited formulations: 'May the good bless you' (a heretical expression), 'Your mercy reaches the bird's nest', 'May Your name be mentioned for good', and 'We give thanks, we give thanks' (repetition implying two powers), all of which are silenced.
The Mishnah continues: one who uses euphemisms for forbidden relations or misinterprets the verse about Molech is silenced with a rebuke.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's prohibitions
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's prohibitions
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why 'We give thanks, we give thanks' and 'May Your name be mentioned for good' are problematic, citing the obligation to bless for bad as for good. It then questions the reason for prohibiting 'Your mercy reaches the bird's nest', presenting two Amoraitic opinions: one says it casts jealousy on creation, the other says it implies God's attributes are mercy rather than decrees.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains why 'We give thanks, we give thanks' and 'May Your name be mentioned for good' are problematic, citing the obligation to bless for bad as for good.
The Gemara asks why the phrase 'Your mercy reaches the bird's nest' is prohibited.
One Amora (Rabbi Yosei bar Avin) says the phrase is prohibited because it casts jealousy on the acts of creation.
The other Amora (Rabbi Yosei bar Zevida) says the phrase is prohibited because it implies God's attributes are mercy rather than decrees.

items.text: Story of a prayer leader before Rabbah
items.text_en: Story of a prayer leader before Rabbah
items.desc_en: A prayer leader before Rabbah used the phrase 'You had mercy on the bird's nest' in a prayer, and Rabbah praised him. Abaye objected that the Mishnah says to silence such a person. The Gemara explains that Rabbah was only testing Abaye's sharpness.

sub.desc_en: A prayer leader before Rabbah used the phrase 'You had mercy on the bird's nest' in a prayer, and Rabbah praised him.
Abaye objects that the Mishnah explicitly says to silence such a prayer leader.
The Gemara explains that Rabbah was only testing Abaye's sharpness, not actually approving the prayer.

items.text: Story of a prayer leader before Rabbi Chanina
items.text_en: Story of a prayer leader before Rabbi Chanina
items.desc_en: A prayer leader before Rabbi Chanina added extra praises to God. Rabbi Chanina rebuked him, explaining that even the three standard praises are only recited because Moses and the Great Assembly instituted them; adding more is like praising a king with silver coins when he has gold.

sub.desc_en: A prayer leader descended before Rabbi Chanina and recited an extended list of praises for God.

Rabbi Chanina rebukes the leader, arguing that even the three standard praises are only said because Moses and the Great Assembly instituted them, and adding more is like praising a king with silver coins when he has gold.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina on fear of Heaven and a parable
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina on fear of Heaven and a parable
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that everything is in Heaven's hands except fear of Heaven, citing a verse. The Gemara questions whether fear is a small matter, and answers that relative to Moses it is small, illustrated by a parable about a large or small vessel.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that everything is in Heaven's hands except fear of Heaven, citing the verse 'ועתה ישראל מה ה' אלהיך שואל מעמך כי אם ליראה'.
The Gemara questions whether fear of Heaven is implied to be a small matter from the verse.
The Gemara answers that relative to Moses it is a small matter, illustrated by a parable: a large vessel one possesses seems small, while a small vessel one lacks seems large.

items.text: Repeating 'Shema' and the rule of repetition
items.text_en: Repeating 'Shema' and the rule of repetition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira says that saying 'Shema, Shema' is like saying 'Modim, Modim' and is silenced. An objection is raised from a baraita that one who repeats Shema is merely 'disgraced', not silenced. The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing between repeating a phrase and repeating a whole verse. Rav Pappa questions whether repetition might be for intent, and Rava responds harshly.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira rules that one who says 'שמע שמע' (Shema, Shema) is treated like one who says 'מודים מודים' (Modim, Modim) and is silenced.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that one who repeats the Shema is merely 'disgraced' (מגונה), not silenced, contradicting Rabbi Zeira's ruling.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between repeating a single phrase (מילתא מילתא), which is silenced, and repeating an entire verse (פסוקא פסוקא), which is merely disgraced.
Rav Pappa asks Rava whether repeating the Shema might be permissible if the first recitation lacked intent (כוונה) and the second is meant to fulfill the obligation.
Rava responds harshly, saying that if one did not have intent the first time, he should be struck with a blacksmith's hammer until he does have intent, implying that repetition is not a remedy.

items.text: Explanations of the Mishnah's last two cases
items.text_en: Explanations of the Mishnah's last two cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'one who uses euphemisms for forbidden relations' refers to calling them 'his father's shame' or 'his mother's shame'. Regarding the verse about Molech, the school of Rabbi Yishmael says it speaks of an Israelite who has a child with a gentile woman for idolatry.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who uses euphemisms for forbidden relations is silenced.
Rav Yosef teaches that the euphemisms refer to calling them 'his father's shame' and 'his mother's shame'.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael explains that the verse about Molech speaks of an Israelite who has a child with a gentile woman for idolatry.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on which biblical passages are read and translated
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on which biblical passages are read and translated
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists passages that are read but not translated (e.g., Reuben's act, the second calf story, priestly blessing, David and Amnon) and those that are read and translated (Tamar, first calf). The Gemara elaborates with a baraita listing passages that are read and translated, and discusses whether the creation story might be problematic due to inquiries about what is above and below.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists passages that are read but not translated: Reuben's act, the second calf story, the priestly blessing, and the story of David and Amnon.

The Mishnah adds that one does not conclude with the Merkavah (Ezekiel's chariot vision), though Rabbi Yehudah permits it, and Rabbi Eliezer forbids concluding with 'Hoda et Yerushalayim' (Ezekiel 16).

A baraita elaborates that there are categories of passages: some are read and translated, some read but not translated, and some neither read nor translated, and it provides a mnemonic for those that are read and translated.
The Gemara questions why the creation story is listed as read and translated, since one might think it should be restricted due to concerns about inquiries into what is above and below.

items.text: Opening: the Mishnah's ruling on reading and translating Lot's story
items.text_en: Opening: the Mishnah's ruling on reading and translating Lot's story
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling that the story of Lot and his daughters is read and translated is not obvious; one might have thought we should refrain out of respect for Abraham, so the Mishnah teaches that it is permitted.

items.text: The story of Lot and his daughters
items.text_en: The story of Lot and his daughters
items.desc_en: The Gemara confirms that the story of Lot and his daughters is read and translated, dismissing the concern that it might dishonor Abraham.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the story of Lot and his two daughters is read and translated.
The Gemara asks why this is not obvious, since it is a biblical narrative.
The Gemara explains that the ruling is needed to counter a concern that reading it might dishonor Abraham, so it teaches that it is permitted.

items.text: The story of Tamar and Judah
items.text_en: The story of Tamar and Judah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the story of Tamar and Judah is read and translated, and that Judah's confession is actually to his credit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the story of Tamar and Judah is read and translated.
The Gemara asks why this is not obvious.
The Gemara explains that one might have thought to avoid reading it out of respect for Judah, but the story is actually read because Judah's confession is to his credit.

items.text: The first story of the Golden Calf
items.text_en: The first story of the Golden Calf
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the first account of the Golden Calf is read and translated, and that it actually serves as atonement for Israel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the first account of the Golden Calf is read and translated.
The Gemara asks why this is not obvious, since it is a biblical narrative.
The Gemara explains that one might have thought to avoid reading it out of respect for Israel, but it is read because it serves as atonement for them.

items.text: Curses and blessings, warnings and punishments
items.text_en: Curses and blessings, warnings and punishments
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that passages of curses and blessings, as well as warnings and punishments, are read and translated, despite concerns that they might dishearten the congregation or lead to sin out of fear.

sub.desc_en: The Tosefta states that the passages of curses and blessings are read and translated.
The Gemara asks why this ruling is not obvious.
The Gemara explains that one might have thought the curses would dishearten the congregation, so the Tosefta teaches that they are still read and translated.
The Tosefta states that the passages of warnings and punishments are read and translated.
The Gemara asks why this ruling is not obvious.
The Gemara explains that one might have thought people would act out of fear rather than love, so the Tosefta teaches that they are still read and translated.

items.text: Stories of Amnon and Tamar, Absalom, and the concubine in Gibeah
items.text_en: Stories of Amnon and Tamar, Absalom, and the concubine in Gibeah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that these stories are read and translated, despite potential dishonor to David or Benjamin.

sub.desc_en: The Tosefta states that the incident of Amnon and Tamar and the incident of Absalom are read and translated.
The Gemara asks: This is obvious, why would one think otherwise?
The Gemara explains that one might have thought to be concerned for the honor of David, but the Tosefta teaches that it is read and translated.
The Tosefta states that the incident of the concubine in Gibeah is read and translated.
The Gemara asks: This is obvious, why would one think otherwise?
The Gemara explains that one might have thought to be concerned for the honor of the tribe of Benjamin, but the Tosefta teaches that it is read and translated.

items.text: The passage 'Make known to Jerusalem her abominations'
items.text_en: The passage 'Make known to Jerusalem her abominations'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that this passage is read and translated, contrary to Rabbi Eliezer's view, citing a story where Rabbi Eliezer rebuked someone for reading it, and the man was found to be of flawed lineage.

sub.desc_en: The Tosefta states that the passage 'Make known to Jerusalem her abominations' is read and translated.
The Gemara asks why this ruling is not obvious.
The Gemara explains that the ruling is needed to exclude the opinion of רבי אליעזר (Rabbi Eliezer), who forbade reading this passage.
A baraita recounts an incident where a man read this passage before רבי אליעזר (Rabbi Eliezer), who rebuked him, and the man was found to have a stain of illegitimacy.

items.text: Passages read but not translated: Reuben, second Golden Calf
items.text_en: Passages read but not translated: Reuben, second Golden Calf
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists passages that are read but not translated: the story of Reuben (with a story about Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel), and the second account of the Golden Calf (from 'And Moses said' until 'And Moses saw').

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing passages that are read but not translated, beginning with the story of Reuben.

sub.text: Story about Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Story about Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a story where Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel instructed the translator not to translate the story of Reuben, and the sages praised him.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's warning about responses
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's warning about responses
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one must be careful in his responses, because Aaron's response to Moses led heretics to err, as it says 'And I cast it into the fire, and out came this calf.'

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one must be careful in his responses, because Aaron's response to Moses led heretics to err, as it says 'And I cast it into the fire, and out came this calf.'

items.text: The Priestly Blessing is read but not translated
items.text_en: The Priestly Blessing is read but not translated
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Priestly Blessing is read but not translated because it contains the Tetragrammaton.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the Priestly Blessing is read but not translated.
The Gemara asks for the reason why the Priestly Blessing is not translated.
The Gemara answers that it is because the verse contains the Tetragrammaton (implied by the word 'יִשָּׂא' which is part of the blessing).

items.text: The story of David and Amnon
items.text_en: The story of David and Amnon
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction: the story of Amnon and Tamar is read and translated when it says 'Amnon son of David', but not when it says 'Amnon' alone.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that the story of David and Amnon is neither read nor translated.
The Gemara raises a contradiction: earlier it was said that the story of Amnon and Tamar is read and translated.
The Gemara resolves: when it says 'Amnon son of David' it is read and translated, but when it says 'Amnon' alone it is not.

items.text: Euphemistic substitutions for lewd terms
items.text_en: Euphemistic substitutions for lewd terms
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that all derogatory terms in Scripture are read euphemistically, e.g., 'yishgalenah' is read as 'yishkavenah', etc. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha says 'lemachara'ot' is read as is, because it is a disgrace to idolatry.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating the general rule that all derogatory terms in Scripture are read euphemistically, and lists examples such as 'יִשְׁגָּלֶנָּה' read as 'יִשְׁכָּבֶנָּה' and others.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha adds that the term 'לְמַחֲרָאוֹת' is read as is, because it is a disgrace to idolatry.

items.text: Permissible mockery of idolatry
items.text_en: Permissible mockery of idolatry
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that all mockery is forbidden except mockery of idolatry, citing verses. Rabbi Yannai and Rav Huna bar Manoach in the name of Rav Acha bar Rav Ika add that one may tell a gentile to take his idol and put it in a certain place. Rav Ashi adds that one may disparage a bad reputation and praise a good one.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that all mockery is forbidden except mockery of idolatry, citing verses about the fall of Bel and Nebo.
Rabbi Yannai adds a supporting verse from Hosea, interpreting 'כבודו' (his glory) as 'כבידו' (his dung) to mock the idol.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Manoach citing Rav Acha bar Rav Ika
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Manoach citing Rav Acha bar Rav Ika
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Manoach in the name of Rav Acha bar Rav Ika permits a Jew to tell a gentile to take his idol and place it in a certain place (a euphemism for a latrine).
Rav Ashi adds that one may disparage a person with a bad reputation and praise one with a good reputation, and whoever praises the latter will be blessed.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter and beginning of the next Mishnah
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter and beginning of the next Mishnah
items.desc_en: The daf concludes with the end of the chapter ('Hadran alach haKoreh et haMegillah omed') and the beginning of the next Mishnah about selling a town square to buy a synagogue, etc.

sub.desc_en: The gemara concludes the chapter with the standard 'Hadran alach' formula.
The Mishnah begins the new chapter, listing the hierarchy of selling communal property to ascend in sanctity.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Hierarchy of sales
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Hierarchy of sales
items.desc_en: The Mishnah establishes a rule that one may sell a synagogue item only to purchase a holier item, and similarly for the proceeds. It lists the order: books, Torah scrolls, scrolls, covers, ark, synagogue, and city square.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the hierarchy of synagogue item sales: one may sell a less holy item to purchase a holier one, and the same rule applies to the proceeds.

items.text: Gemara: Status of the city square
items.text_en: Gemara: Status of the city square
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana quotes Rabbi Yochanan that the Mishnah's ruling about the square is only according to Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei, but the Sages hold the square has no sanctity. The Gemara explains Rabbi Menachem's reasoning: people pray there on fast days, while the Sages dismiss this as occasional.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the Mishnah's case of townspeople who sold their city square.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the Mishnah's ruling is only according to Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei, but the Sages hold the square has no sanctity.
The Gemara asks for Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei's reasoning.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei holds the square has sanctity because people pray there on fast days and during the ma'amadot (stationary groups).

sub.text: Gemara's statement of the Sages' view
sub.text_en: Gemara's statement of the Sages' view
sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Sages reject this reasoning, considering the prayer there merely an occasional occurrence (אקראי בעלמא) that does not confer sanctity.

items.text: Distinction between village and city synagogues
items.text_en: Distinction between village and city synagogues
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quotes Rabbi Yonatan that the Mishnah's permission to sell a synagogue for an ark applies only to village synagogues, but city synagogues, built with public funds, cannot be sold. Rav Ashi adds that a synagogue in Mata Mechasya, though visited by outsiders, can be sold because they come only on his account.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a synagogue may be sold to purchase an ark.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan distinguishes between village synagogues, which may be sold, and city synagogues built with public funds, which cannot be sold because they belong to the public.
Rav Ashi adds that the synagogue of Mata Mechasya, though visited by outsiders, can be sold because they come only on his account.

items.text: Objection from the synagogue of Tursiyim
items.text_en: Objection from the synagogue of Tursiyim
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda recounts that the synagogue of Tursiyim in Jerusalem was sold to Rabbi Eliezer, who used it for his needs. This challenges the rule that city synagogues cannot be sold. The Gemara answers that it was a small synagogue built by them, not a public one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda recounts that the synagogue of Tursiyim in Jerusalem was sold to Rabbi Eliezer, challenging the rule that city synagogues cannot be sold.
The Gemara answers that it was a small synagogue built by them, not a public one belonging to the city.

items.text: Debate on Jerusalem's impurity and tribal division
items.text_en: Debate on Jerusalem's impurity and tribal division
items.desc_en: Another objection is raised: synagogues in Jerusalem should be impure from leprosy if they are like city synagogues, but a baraita says they are impure. The Gemara resolves that the dispute is whether Jerusalem was divided among the tribes: the first Tanna holds it was not, so synagogues are like villages; Rabbi Yehuda holds it was divided, so they are like cities.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that Jerusalem is not impure from leprosy, implying synagogues there should be impure, but Rabbi Yehuda limits this to the Temple site only.
The Gemara questions why synagogues and study halls in Jerusalem would be impure from leprosy, given that they should be like city synagogues.
The Gemara resolves the dispute: the first Tanna holds Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes, so synagogues are like villages; Rabbi Yehuda holds it was divided, so they are like cities.

items.text: Supporting Tannaitic disputes on Jerusalem's division
items.text_en: Supporting Tannaitic disputes on Jerusalem's division
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings two Tannaitic sources: one describes the tribal portions of Judah and Benjamin in the Temple, implying division; another states that houses in Jerusalem cannot be rented because they are not owned by individuals, implying no division. This supports the earlier dispute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that the dispute about Jerusalem's division is also reflected in a dispute between Tannaim.
A baraita describes the Temple's division between Judah and Benjamin, implying that Jerusalem was divided among the tribes.
Another baraita states that houses in Jerusalem cannot be rented because they are not owned by individuals, implying that Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes.

items.text: Abaye's lesson and Rava's condition for sale
items.text_en: Abaye's lesson and Rava's condition for sale
items.desc_en: Abaye derives a lesson in etiquette from the baraita about guests taking hides. Rava states that the Mishnah's rule applies only when the seven town leaders did not sell with the townspeople's consent, but if they did, even a synagogue can be sold for any purpose.

sub.desc_en: Abaye derives a lesson in etiquette (אורח ארעא) from the baraita: a guest should leave a hide or a skin for his host.
Rava qualifies the Mishnah's rule: it applies only when the seven town leaders did not sell with the townspeople's consent, but if they did, even a synagogue can be sold for any purpose.

items.text: Opening ruling on using a synagogue for drinking beer
items.text_en: Opening ruling on using a synagogue for drinking beer
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that using a synagogue for drinking beer is permitted. This sets the stage for the discussion on the permissible uses of a synagogue.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that using a synagogue for drinking beer is permitted.

items.text: Ravina's question about planting a synagogue courtyard
items.text_en: Ravina's question about planting a synagogue courtyard
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether he may plant a courtyard that belonged to a synagogue. Rav Ashi instructs him to sell it to seven communal leaders in the presence of the townspeople and then plant it.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether he may plant a courtyard that belonged to a synagogue.
Rav Ashi instructs Ravina to sell the courtyard to seven communal leaders in the presence of the townspeople and then plant it.

items.text: Rami bar Abba's dilemma about demolishing an old synagogue
items.text_en: Rami bar Abba's dilemma about demolishing an old synagogue
items.desc_en: Rami bar Abba wants to demolish an old synagogue to reuse its materials for a new one. He questions whether Rav Chisda's ruling—that one may not demolish a synagogue until building another—applies here. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna both prohibit it.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Abba, while building a new synagogue, questions whether Rav Chisda's rule against demolishing an old synagogue before building a new one applies when he intends to reuse the old materials for the new building.

sub.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna's prohibition
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna's prohibition
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna each prohibit Rami bar Abba from demolishing the old synagogue, applying Rav Chisda's ruling to this case as well.

items.text: Rava's distinction between exchange/sale and rental/mortgage of a synagogue
items.text_en: Rava's distinction between exchange/sale and rental/mortgage of a synagogue
items.desc_en: Rava rules that exchanging or selling a synagogue is permitted, but renting or mortgaging it is forbidden because its sanctity remains. He adds that the same applies to its bricks, but only for an old synagogue; a new one has no sanctity. Even according to the opinion that designation is significant, this case is different because it is like spun wool awaiting weaving.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that exchanging or selling a synagogue is permitted, but renting or mortgaging it is forbidden because its sanctity remains.
Rava extends the same rule to the bricks of an old synagogue, but notes that a new synagogue has no sanctity.
The Stam clarifies that even according to the opinion that designation is significant, this case is different because it is like spun wool awaiting weaving.

items.text: Dispute about giving a synagogue as a gift
items.text_en: Dispute about giving a synagogue as a gift
items.desc_en: Rav Acha and Ravina disagree about whether a synagogue may be given as a gift. One prohibits it, arguing that its sanctity cannot be nullified; the other permits it, reasoning that the recipient's benefit makes it equivalent to a sale.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina regarding whether a synagogue may be given as a gift.
The one who prohibits argues that the sanctity of the synagogue cannot be nullified by a gift.
The one who permits argues that since the recipient benefits, the gift is equivalent to a sale, which nullifies the sanctity.

items.text: Baraita on disposal of sacred and mitzvah objects
items.text_en: Baraita on disposal of sacred and mitzvah objects
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that objects used for mitzvot (e.g., sukkah, lulav) may be discarded, while objects used for sanctity (e.g., Torah covers, tefillin) must be hidden (genizah). It lists examples of each category.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by distinguishing between objects used for mitzvot (commandments), which may be discarded, and objects used for sanctity (קדושה), which must be hidden (גניזה), listing examples of each category.

items.text: Rava's rulings on secondary sanctity of furniture and covers
items.text_en: Rava's rulings on secondary sanctity of furniture and covers
items.desc_en: Rava initially thought a chair used for a Torah scroll is merely a secondary vessel, but upon seeing that a Torah scroll is placed on it, he deems it sacred. Similarly, a curtain used to wrap a Torah scroll is sacred. He also rules that a worn-out chest may be made into a small chest but not a chair, and a worn-out curtain may be used for books but not for chumashim.

sub.desc_en: Rava initially thought a chair used for a Torah scroll is merely a secondary vessel (תשמיש דתשמיש) and therefore permitted for mundane use.
Upon seeing that a Torah scroll is placed on the chair, Rava revises his view and deems it a sacred vessel (תשמיש קדושה), forbidden for mundane use.
Rava initially thought a curtain used for a Torah scroll is merely a secondary vessel.
Upon seeing that the curtain is folded and a Torah scroll placed on it, Rava deems it a sacred vessel, forbidden for mundane use.
Rava rules that a worn-out chest may be made into a small chest (permitted) but not into a chair (forbidden).
Rava rules that a worn-out curtain may be used for books (permitted) but not for chumashim (forbidden).

items.text: Rava's ruling on baskets and bags for sacred books
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on baskets and bags for sacred books
items.desc_en: Rava states that baskets for chumashim and bags for books are sacred and must be hidden. The Gemara notes this is obvious, but it teaches that even though they are made only for protection, they still have sanctity.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that baskets for chumashim and bags for books are sacred items that must be hidden.
The Gemara objects that Rava's ruling is obvious.
The Gemara explains that Rava's statement is necessary to counter the assumption that since these items are only for protection, they lack sanctity.

items.text: Rava's solution for a synagogue near a corpse
items.text_en: Rava's solution for a synagogue near a corpse
items.desc_en: A synagogue in Rome was open to a courtyard where a corpse was kept, preventing priests from entering. Rava advises placing a chest there, which, as a wooden vessel used for resting, does not contract impurity and blocks the impurity. The rabbis object that when a Torah scroll is placed on it, it becomes movable, but Rava says that is impossible.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a synagogue in Rome was open to a courtyard where a corpse was kept, preventing priests from entering, and they came to ask Rava.
Rava advises placing a chest there, which, as a wooden vessel used for resting, does not contract impurity and blocks the impurity.
The rabbis object that when a Torah scroll is placed on it, it becomes movable and thus susceptible to impurity.
Rava rejects the objection, stating that if that were the case, it is impossible (i.e., the scenario does not apply).

items.text: Mar Zutra's ruling on worn-out Torah mantles
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's ruling on worn-out Torah mantles
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra rules that worn-out Torah mantles may be made into shrouds for a met mitzvah (an unattended corpse), and that is their proper genizah.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra rules that worn-out Torah mantles may be made into shrouds for a met mitzvah (an unattended corpse), and that is their proper genizah.

items.text: Rava's ruling on burying a worn-out Torah scroll
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on burying a worn-out Torah scroll
items.desc_en: Rava says a worn-out Torah scroll should be buried near a Torah scholar, even one who only knows halakhot. Rav Acha bar Yaakov adds that it must be in an earthenware vessel, as per Jeremiah 32:14.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that a worn-out Torah scroll should be buried near a Torah scholar, even one who only knows halakhot.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov adds that the scroll must be placed in an earthenware vessel, citing Jeremiah 32:14.

items.text: Dispute about moving sanctity from synagogue to study hall
items.text_en: Dispute about moving sanctity from synagogue to study hall
items.desc_en: Rav Papi reports in Rava's name that moving a synagogue's sanctity to a study hall is permitted, but the reverse is forbidden. Rav Pappa reports the opposite in Rava's name. Rav Acha then comments.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papi reports in Rava's name that moving sanctity from a synagogue (בית כנסת) to a study hall (בית רבנן) is permitted, but the reverse is forbidden.
Rav Pappa cites the opposite ruling in Rava's name: moving sanctity from a study hall to a synagogue is permitted, but the reverse is forbidden.
Rav Acha begins a comment (the text is cut off here, likely introducing a resolution or further discussion).

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi regarding upgrading a synagogue to a study hall
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi regarding upgrading a synagogue to a study hall
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's statement that a synagogue may be made into a study hall that one may upgrade a Torah scroll by selling an old one for a new one. Bar Kappara's exposition of a verse is cited, with a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi about whether 'beit gadol' refers to a place where Torah or prayer is magnified. The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds it refers to Torah, supporting the inference.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that it stands to reason to rule like Rav Pappi, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling that a synagogue may be made into a study hall, and concludes that this supports Rav Pappi.

Bar Kappara interprets the verse about 'beit gadol' (great house), and Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi dispute whether it refers to a place where Torah is magnified or a place where prayer is magnified.

The Gemara explains the scriptural proofs for each opinion: the one who says Torah cites the verse 'יגדיל תורה ויאדיר' (He will magnify Torah), and the one who says prayer cites the verse about Elisha's great deeds through prayer.

The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi is the one who said 'beit gadol' refers to a place where Torah is magnified, based on his ruling that a synagogue may be made into a study hall, and confirms this inference.

items.text: Question about selling an old Torah scroll for a new one
items.text_en: Question about selling an old Torah scroll for a new one
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: may one sell an old Torah scroll to purchase a new one? The doubt is whether it is prohibited because it is not an upgrade, or permitted since there is no other way to upgrade.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: may one sell an old Torah scroll to purchase a new one, considering whether it is prohibited because it is not an upgrade or permitted since no higher upgrade is possible.

items.text: First attempted proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: First attempted proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that selling a Torah scroll for another Torah scroll is permitted, since the Mishnah only prohibits buying other books with the proceeds, implying Torah for Torah is fine. However, this is rejected as the Mishnah speaks after the fact, not ab initio.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that selling a Torah scroll for another Torah scroll is permitted, since the Mishnah only prohibits buying other books with the proceeds, implying Torah for Torah is fine; however, this is rejected as the Mishnah speaks after the fact, not לכתחילה (the ideal standard).

items.text: Second attempted proof from the laws of rolling Torah scrolls
items.text_en: Second attempted proof from the laws of rolling Torah scrolls
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about rolling a Torah scroll with mantles of Chumashim, but not Chumashim with mantles of a Torah scroll. The inference is that a Torah scroll may be used for another Torah scroll, but this is refuted because the baraita's end shows the opposite inference, so no proof can be drawn.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about rolling a Torah scroll with mantles of Chumashim, inferring that a Torah scroll may be used for another Torah scroll.
The Gemara refutes the proof by pointing to the baraita's end, which implies the opposite, concluding that no inference can be drawn from this baraita.

items.text: Third attempted proof from placing scrolls and its refutation
items.text_en: Third attempted proof from placing scrolls and its refutation
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the rule of placing a Torah scroll on top of another Torah scroll that selling for an upgrade is permitted. This is refuted because placement is unavoidable, unlike sale which is optional.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that selling a Torah scroll for an upgrade is permitted by citing the rule that one may place a Torah scroll on top of another Torah scroll, implying a hierarchy of sanctity that allows upgrading.
The Gemara refutes the proof by distinguishing placement (הנחה), which is unavoidable, from sale, which is optional, and therefore the permission for placement does not extend to sale.

items.text: Fourth attempted proof from Rabbi Yochanan and final rejection
items.text_en: Fourth attempted proof from Rabbi Yochanan and final rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that one may not sell an old Torah scroll for a new one due to negligence. The Gemara then asks about a case where one writes and sets aside for redemption. Another citation from Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir permits selling only for Torah study or marriage, but the Gemara rejects the proof because those cases have special reasons.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita in the name of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that one may not sell an old Torah scroll to buy a new one.

The Gemara distinguishes the case of selling an old scroll for a new one from the baraita, suggesting the baraita's prohibition is due to negligence, and asks about a case where one writes and sets aside for redemption.
The Gemara brings another citation from Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir, permitting selling a Torah scroll only for Torah study or marriage.

The Gemara rejects the proof, arguing that Torah study and marriage have special reasons (study leads to action, marriage fulfills creation), but selling a Torah scroll for another Torah scroll is not permitted.

items.text: Baraita on selling a Torah scroll and the dispute between Rava and Abaye
items.text_en: Baraita on selling a Torah scroll and the dispute between Rava and Abaye
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one should not sell a Torah scroll even if not needed, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that even if one has no food, selling a Torah scroll or his daughter brings no blessing. Rava distinguishes between selling and leftover funds versus collecting and leftover funds. Abaye challenges with a baraita about stipulation, and the Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to selling with a stipulation by the seven town leaders.

sub.text: Baraita (Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel)
sub.text_en: Baraita (Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel)
sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that one may not sell a Torah scroll even if not needed, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that selling a Torah scroll or his daughter brings no blessing.
Rava distinguishes between selling and having leftover funds (forbidden) versus collecting and having leftover funds (permitted).
Abaye objects with a baraita that permits even using leftover funds for a duchsusia (town parade) if a stipulation was made.
The Gemara questions the scenario: if it refers to selling with leftover funds, stipulation is irrelevant; if it refers to collecting with leftover funds, it contradicts Rava.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to selling with leftover funds, but the stipulation is by the seven town leaders (שבעה טובי העיר) in the presence of the townspeople, which permits even a duchsusia.

items.text: Explanation of 'duchsusia' and a lesson for scholars
items.text_en: Explanation of 'duchsusia' and a lesson for scholars
items.desc_en: Abaye asks a rabbi who arranges mishnayot before Rav Sheshet about the meaning of 'duchsusia', and Rav Sheshet explains it means the town's commander. Abaye then derives a lesson: a scholar who hears a term and does not know its meaning should ask someone who frequents the rabbis, as it is likely known from a great man.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks a rabbi who arranges mishnayot before Rav Sheshet what 'duchsusia' means.

sub.text: Rav Sheshet's answer via the rabbi
sub.text_en: Rav Sheshet's answer via the rabbi
sub.desc_en: The rabbi reports that Rav Sheshet explained 'duchsusia' means the town's commander (פָּרָשָׁא דְמָתָא).
Abaye derives a lesson: a scholar who hears a term and does not know its meaning should ask someone who frequents the rabbis, as it is likely known from a great man.

items.text: Laws of charity collected by travelers
items.text_en: Laws of charity collected by travelers
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir rules that townspeople who travel to another city and pledge charity there give it, and when they return, they bring it to support their own poor. A baraita adds that an individual who pledges gives to the poor of that city. A story about Rav Huna and Rav Chana bar Chanilai illustrates the application: when they wanted to take the charity back to their town, Rav Huna initially objected based on the baraita, but the text is cut off.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir rules that townspeople who travel to another city and pledge charity there give it, and when they return, they bring it to support their own poor.
A baraita supports the rule for townspeople and adds that an individual who pledges gives to the poor of that city.

sub.text: Story about Rav Huna and Rav Chana bar Chanilai
sub.text_en: Story about Rav Huna and Rav Chana bar Chanilai
sub.desc_en: A story about Rav Huna and Rav Chana bar Chanilai illustrates the application: when they wanted to take the charity back to their town, they asked Rav Huna for permission.
Rav Huna objects based on the baraita, stating that the rule applies only when there are no poor in the other city, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Conclusion of previous Mishnah
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the discussion from the previous Mishnah regarding the distribution of charity funds, stating that if there is a local sage, the funds are given to him, and the poor rely on him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that if there is a local sage (חבר עיר), the charity funds are given to him, and the poor rely on him.

items.text: Mishnah: Selling communal property
items.text_en: Mishnah: Selling communal property
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not sell communal property to an individual because it lowers its sanctity, according to Rabbi Meir. The Sages said to him: If so, one should also not sell from a large city to a small city.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that one may not sell communal property to an individual because it lowers its sanctity.
The Mishnah attributes the ruling to Rabbi Meir.
The Sages object to Rabbi Meir: if so, one should also not sell from a large city to a small city.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Sages' objection to Rabbi Meir, explaining that Rabbi Meir distinguishes between selling to an individual (which removes sanctity) and selling to a smaller city (which retains sanctity). The Sages counter that there is still a concern due to the principle 'In a multitude of people is the king's glory.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Meir can defend his position against the Sages' objection.
Rabbi Meir explains that selling from a large city to a small city retains sanctity since the object remains in a communal context, but selling to an individual removes sanctity entirely.
The Sages counter that even in the case of a large city to a small city, there is a concern due to the principle 'In a multitude of people is the king's glory' (משלי י״ד:כ״ח).

items.text: Mishnah: Selling a synagogue with conditions
items.text_en: Mishnah: Selling a synagogue with conditions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses selling a synagogue: Rabbi Meir says it can only be sold on condition that it can be redeemed; the Sages say it can be sold permanently except for four uses (bathhouse, tannery, immersion, and toilet); Rabbi Yehuda says it can be sold as a courtyard and the buyer may do as he pleases.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three positions on selling a synagogue: Rabbi Meir requires a redemption condition, the Sages permit permanent sale except for four degrading uses, and Rabbi Yehuda allows sale as a courtyard with full buyer discretion.

items.text: Gemara: Usury concern in Rabbi Meir's condition
items.text_en: Gemara: Usury concern in Rabbi Meir's condition
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Meir's condition (that the buyer can return the synagogue) is not usury, since the buyer pays for use of the building. Rabbi Yochanan explains that Rabbi Meir follows Rabbi Yehuda's view that 'one-sided usury' is permitted. A baraita is cited to illustrate the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages regarding usury. Rava offers an alternative explanation: the dispute is about 'usury on condition of return.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Meir's conditional sale avoids the prohibition of usury (ריבית), since the buyer pays for use of the building.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that Rabbi Meir follows Rabbi Yehuda's view that 'one-sided usury' (צד אחד בריבית) is permitted.
A baraita is cited illustrating the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages regarding one-sided usury in a sale arrangement.
The Gemara clarifies that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages is specifically about whether one-sided usury (צד אחד בריבית) is permitted or forbidden.
Rava offers an alternative explanation: the dispute is about 'usury on condition of return' (ריבית על מנת להחזיר), not one-sided usury.

items.text: Gemara: Urinating within four cubits of prayer
items.text_en: Gemara: Urinating within four cubits of prayer
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the ruling of the Sages that a synagogue can be sold permanently except for certain uses. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel says it is permitted to urinate within four cubits of prayer. Rav Yosef questions this, citing the Mishnah that a synagogue can be sold for any use. A baraita is taught before Rav Nachman about distancing for prayer and urination, leading to a discussion about waiting four cubits between prayer and urination due to sparks and the prayer being fresh in one's mouth.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that it is permitted to urinate within four cubits of prayer.
Rav Yosef questions what new teaching Shmuel is conveying, citing the Mishnah that Rabbi Yehuda permits selling a synagogue for any use, implying even urination.
Rav Yosef explains that even the Sages, who restrict selling a synagogue, only do so because its sanctity is fixed, but four cubits of prayer have no fixed sanctity, so Shmuel's ruling is novel.
A baraita taught before Rav Nachman states that one who prays must distance four cubits before urinating, and one who urinates must distance four cubits before praying.
Rav Nachman objects that the second clause (urinator distances before praying) is already known from a Mishnah about distancing from feces, so the baraita seems redundant.

Rav Nachman questions why the baraita requires the one who prays to distance before urinating, noting that if taken literally it would sanctify all paths of Nehardea, and the baraita is corrected to say 'wait' rather than 'distance'.
The Gemara explains that the urinator must wait four cubits because of sparks of urine, but questions why the one who prays must wait.
Rav Ashi answers that within four cubits after prayer, the prayer is still arranged in his mouth and his lips are murmuring, so he must wait to avoid disrespect.

items.text: Siman: Zalfan
items.text_en: Siman: Zalfan
items.desc_en: A mnemonic sign 'Zalfan' is given to indicate the following stories.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides the mnemonic sign 'Zalfan' to indicate the following stories.

items.text: Stories of longevity and piety
items.text_en: Stories of longevity and piety
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts stories of Rabbi Zakkai, Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua, and Rabbi Perida, who were asked by their students how they merited long life. They attributed it to various pious practices, including not urinating within four cubits of prayer, not calling others by nicknames, not neglecting Kiddush HaYom, not making a synagogue a shortcut, not stepping over people's heads, and not raising hands without a blessing. The story of Rav Huna's poverty and subsequent wealth is also told.

sub.desc_en: The students ask Rabbi Zakkai how he merited long life.

Rabbi Zakkai lists his pious practices: not urinating within four cubits of prayer, not calling others by nicknames, and not neglecting Kiddush HaYom, illustrated by his mother selling her headdress to provide wine for Kiddush.
A baraita reports that Rabbi Zakkai's mother left him 300 barrels of wine, and he left his sons 3,000 barrels, showing the reward for honoring Kiddush HaYom.

sub.text: Story of Rav Huna and Rav
sub.text_en: Story of Rav Huna and Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna, standing before Rav with a rope around his neck, explains he pawned his belt for Kiddush wine, and Rav blesses him to be filled with silk.
At Rav Huna's son's wedding, his daughters and daughters-in-law cover him with silk garments, fulfilling Rav's blessing, but Rav is upset that Rav Huna did not reciprocate the blessing.

sub.text: Students' question to Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua
sub.text_en: Students' question to Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua
sub.desc_en: The students ask Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua how he merited long life.
Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua lists his pious practices: not making a synagogue a shortcut, not stepping over people's heads, and not raising his hands for the priestly blessing without a blessing.
The students ask Rabbi Perida how he merited long life.
Rabbi Perida begins his answer, stating that no one ever preceded him to the study hall.

items.text: Additional practice: not eating from an animal whose priestly gifts were not removed
items.text_en: Additional practice: not eating from an animal whose priestly gifts were not removed
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the statement in the Mishnah about not eating from an animal whose gifts were not removed, citing Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that it is forbidden, and that one who does so is like one who eats tevel. The Gemara concludes that the halakha does not follow this view.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the practice of not eating from an animal whose priestly gifts were not removed.
Rabbi Yitzchak reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that eating from such an animal is forbidden and is like eating tevel (untithed produce).
The Gemara concludes that the halakha does not follow Rabbi Yitzchak's view.

items.text: Clarification: blessing before a priest
items.text_en: Clarification: blessing before a priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the statement about not blessing before a priest, citing Rabbi Yochanan that a Torah scholar who blesses before an ignorant priest, even a High Priest, is liable to death. The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers to equals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara quotes the Mishnah's statement that the speaker never blessed before a priest, and questions whether this is a praiseworthy act.

The Gemara objects by citing Rabbi Yochanan that a Torah scholar who blesses before an ignorant priest, even a High Priest, is liable to death, implying that blessing before a priest is not praiseworthy.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's statement refers to equals, where the speaker and the priest are both Torah scholars, so blessing before the priest is not problematic.

items.text: Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana's practices for long life
items.text_en: Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana's practices for long life
items.desc_en: Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana tells his students that he never honored himself through his friend's shame, never went to bed with a curse from his friend, and was lenient with his money. The Gemara provides examples for each: Rav Huna refusing to let another carry his burden, Mar Zutra forgiving all who troubled him, and Iyov leaving a coin for a shopkeeper.

sub.text: Students' question to Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana
sub.text_en: Students' question to Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana
sub.desc_en: The students ask Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana how he merited long life, and he lists three practices: never honoring himself through a friend's shame, never going to bed with a friend's curse, and being lenient with his money.

sub.text: Gemara's example for 'never honored himself through a friend's shame'
sub.text_en: Gemara's example for 'never honored himself through a friend's shame'
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the case of Rav Huna carrying a hoe on his shoulder; when Rav Chana bar Chanilai tried to take it from him, Rav Huna refused, saying he would not be honored through his friend's shame.

sub.text: Gemara's example for 'never went to bed with a friend's curse'
sub.text_en: Gemara's example for 'never went to bed with a friend's curse'
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Mar Zutra who, when going to bed, would forgive anyone who had troubled him.

sub.text: Gemara's example for 'lenient with his money'
sub.text_en: Gemara's example for 'lenient with his money'
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Mar's statement that Iyov was lenient with his money, leaving a coin for the shopkeeper from his own funds.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's question to Rabbi Nechunya HaGadol
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's question to Rabbi Nechunya HaGadol
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva asks Rabbi Nechunya HaGadol about his longevity. After a brief interruption, Rabbi Nechunya explains that he never accepted gifts, never stood on his rights, and was lenient with his money. The Gemara provides examples: Rabbi Elazar refusing gifts from the Patriarch's house, Rabbi Zeira accepting invitations but not gifts, and Rava's teaching that one who forgoes his rights has his sins forgiven.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva asks Rabbi Nechunya HaGadol about the merit for his longevity.
Guards come to strike Rabbi Akiva, but Rabbi Nechunya intervenes, recognizing him as a Torah scholar.

sub.text: Rabbi Nechunya's answer to the interruption
sub.text_en: Rabbi Nechunya's answer to the interruption
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Nechunya explains the verse 'one lamb' means the unique one of the flock.

sub.text: Rabbi Nechunya's answer to Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: Rabbi Nechunya's answer to Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Nechunya lists three merits: never accepting gifts, never insisting on his rights, and being lenient with his money.

sub.text: Supporting baraita for not accepting gifts
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for not accepting gifts
sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides examples of Rabbi Elazar refusing gifts and Rabbi Zeira accepting invitations but not gifts.
Rava teaches that one who forgoes his rights has all his sins forgiven, citing the verse 'נושא עון ועובר על פשע' (He bears iniquity and passes over transgression).

items.text: Rabbi's question to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha and the danger of looking at a wicked person
items.text_en: Rabbi's question to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha and the danger of looking at a wicked person
items.desc_en: Rabbi asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha about his longevity. He replies that he never looked at the image of a wicked person, citing Rabbi Yochanan that it is forbidden. The Gemara discusses the cause of Isaac's blindness, attributing it to looking at Esau, but also to the curse of Avimelech. Rava cites a verse that it is not good to show favor to a wicked person.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha about the secret of his longevity, and Rabbi Yehoshua initially rebuffs him but then accepts the question as Torah study.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha answers that he never looked at the image of a wicked person, citing Rabbi Yochanan's prohibition with a proof from the verse about Yehoram.
Rabbi Elazar supports the idea by noting that Isaac's eyes dimmed because he looked at the wicked Esau.
The Gemara objects that Isaac's blindness was caused by Avimelech's curse on Sarah, not by looking at Esau, citing Rabbi Yitzchak's principle that a commoner's curse is not trivial.
Rava resolves that both causes contributed to Isaac's blindness, and cites a verse that it is not good to show favor to a wicked person.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's blessing to Rabbi
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's blessing to Rabbi
items.desc_en: At his death, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha blesses Rabbi that he should reach half his days. When Rabbi questions why not all his days, he explains that the future generations would be left like animals without a leader.

sub.desc_en: At the time of his death, Rabbi asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha to bless him.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha blesses Rabbi that he should reach half his days.
Rabbi questions why the blessing is only for half his days and not all of them.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha explains that if Rabbi lived all his days, the future generations would be left like animals without a leader.

items.text: Additional practices for long life: avoiding Gentiles and Torah study
items.text_en: Additional practices for long life: avoiding Gentiles and Torah study
items.desc_en: Two sages attribute their longevity to not looking at a Gentile and not partnering with a Gentile. Rabbi Zeira tells his students that he never was angry at home, never walked before a greater person, never thought about Torah in filthy alleys, never walked four cubits without Torah and tefillin, never slept in the study hall, never rejoiced at his friend's downfall, and never called his friend by a derogatory nickname.

sub.text: Avuh bar Ihi and Minyamin bar Ihi
sub.text_en: Avuh bar Ihi and Minyamin bar Ihi
sub.desc_en: Two sages each attribute their longevity to a different practice: one to never looking at a Gentile, the other to never partnering with a Gentile.

Rabbi Zeira lists multiple practices that he attributes to his longevity, including never being angry at home, never walking before a greater person, never thinking about Torah in filthy alleys, never walking four cubits without Torah and tefillin, never sleeping in the study hall, never rejoicing at his friend's downfall, and never calling his friend by a derogatory nickname.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: laws of a ruined synagogue
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: laws of a ruined synagogue
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a ruined synagogue may not be used for eulogies, rope-making, spreading nets, drying fruit, or as a shortcut, because its sanctity remains even in ruin. Weeds may not be uprooted due to anguish. The Gemara adds that synagogues may not be treated with frivolity, and one may not eat or drink in them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists activities forbidden in a ruined synagogue: eulogies, rope-making, spreading nets, drying fruit, and using it as a shortcut.
The Mishnah cites the verse 'וַהֲשִׁמּוֹתִי אֶת מִקְדְּשֵׁיכֶם' (I will desolate your sanctuaries) to prove that their sanctity remains even in ruin.
The Mishnah rules that if weeds grow in the ruined synagogue, one may not uproot them, because it would cause anguish (over the desolation).
The Gemara cites a baraita that synagogues may not be treated with frivolity, and one may not eat or drink in them.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Prohibited and permitted uses of synagogues
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Prohibited and permitted uses of synagogues
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists prohibited uses of synagogues (e.g., entering for shelter from sun or rain, eulogizing an individual) and permitted uses (reading, studying, eulogizing a community). Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between when the synagogue is inhabited and when it is in ruins.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists prohibited uses of synagogues (shelter, eulogizing an individual) and permitted uses (reading, studying, eulogizing a community), and Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between when the synagogue is inhabited and when it is in ruins.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of Rabbi Yehuda's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of Rabbi Yehuda's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the mention of weeds in Rabbi Yehuda's statement, suggesting a missing clause about sweeping and watering to prevent weeds, and then rephrases Rabbi Yehuda's ruling accordingly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehuda mentions weeds, since they are not relevant to the original ruling.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah is missing a clause: one must sweep and water the synagogues to prevent weeds from growing.
Rabbi Yehuda's ruling is rephrased: in inhabited synagogues one sweeps and waters, but in ruined ones one leaves weeds and does not uproot them due to anguish.

items.text: Rav Asi on synagogues in Babylonia and the consequence of treating them lightly
items.text_en: Rav Asi on synagogues in Babylonia and the consequence of treating them lightly
items.desc_en: Rav Asi states that synagogues in Babylonia are built conditionally, yet one should not treat them lightly by doing calculations there. He adds that a synagogue used for calculations will eventually house a corpse (a mitzvah corpse).

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi states that synagogues in Babylonia are built conditionally, yet one should not treat them lightly by doing calculations there.
The Gemara objects that the phrase 'they will lodge a corpse there' is impossible, since a corpse cannot be left overnight in a synagogue.
The Gemara resolves that the statement means that eventually a mitzvah corpse (with no one to bury it) will be brought there for lodging.

items.text: Rava permits scholars to benefit from synagogues
items.text_en: Rava permits scholars to benefit from synagogues
items.desc_en: Rava explains that scholars and their students are permitted to benefit from synagogues, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's interpretation of 'beit rabbanan' as the house of the rabbis.

sub.desc_en: Rava permits scholars and their students to benefit from synagogues, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's interpretation of 'beit rabbanan' as the house of the rabbis.

items.text: Entering a synagogue for shelter: the case of Ravina and Rav Adda bar Mattana
items.text_en: Entering a synagogue for shelter: the case of Ravina and Rav Adda bar Mattana
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Ravina and Rav Adda bar Mattana entered a synagogue to escape rain while asking a question of Rava, but they justified it as needing a cool place for the halakhic discussion, not for shelter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Ravina and Rav Adda bar Mattana entered a synagogue to escape rain while asking a question of Rava.

sub.text: Ravina and Rav Adda bar Mattana's justification
sub.text_en: Ravina and Rav Adda bar Mattana's justification
sub.desc_en: They justified entering the synagogue not for shelter from rain but because the halakhic discussion required a cool place like a summer day.

items.text: Calling someone out of a synagogue: how to avoid disrespect
items.text_en: Calling someone out of a synagogue: how to avoid disrespect
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi how to call someone out of a synagogue without disrespect. Rav Ashi advises that if the person is a scholar, one should say a halakha; if a Tanna, a mishna; if a reader, a verse; otherwise, ask a child to recite a verse, or wait a bit and leave.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi how to call a person out of a synagogue without disrespect.
Rav Ashi advises that depending on the person's status, one should say a halakha, a mishna, a verse, or have a child recite a verse, or wait a bit and leave.

items.text: Definition of a eulogy for the community and examples
items.text_en: Definition of a eulogy for the community and examples
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines a eulogy for the community as one attended by a great scholar like Rav Sheshet or Rav Chisda. It then recounts eulogies by Rafram, Rabbi Zeira, and Resh Lakish for various individuals, and Rav Nachman's refusal to eulogize a scholar who only knew texts without understanding.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constitutes a eulogy for the community (הספד של רבים) that may be held in a synagogue.
Rav Chisda defines a community eulogy as one attended by Rav Sheshet.
Rav Sheshet defines a community eulogy as one attended by Rav Chisda.
Rafram eulogized his daughter-in-law in the synagogue, explaining that the entire community came due to his honor and the honor of the deceased.
Rabbi Zeira eulogized a certain rabbinic scholar in the synagogue, stating that the entire community came either for his own honor or for the honor of the deceased.
Resh Lakish eulogized a rabbinic scholar in the land of Israel who taught halachot in twenty-four rows, lamenting the loss of a great man.
Rav Nachman refused to eulogize a scholar who only knew texts (Sifra, Sifrei, Tosefta) without understanding, asking rhetorically what use is a basket full of books that is lacking.

items.text: Transition: contrast between the powerful of Eretz Yisrael and the pious of Babylonia
items.text_en: Transition: contrast between the powerful of Eretz Yisrael and the pious of Babylonia
items.desc_en: A brief statement introducing a contrast between the strong figures of Eretz Yisrael and the pious ones of Babylonia, leading into the next section.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a contrast between the powerful figures of Eretz Yisrael and the pious ones of Babylonia.

items.text: The importance of studying halakhot and the warning against using Torah for personal benefit
items.text_en: The importance of studying halakhot and the warning against using Torah for personal benefit
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the mishna about using the crown (tag), which Resh Lakish interprets as using a scholar who studies halakhot. Ulla distinguishes between one who studies four orders of Mishnah and one who only repeats them. A story illustrates Resh Lakish's disdain for one who studied but did not internalize.
