The section concludes with a baraita from the school of Eliyahu promising that one who studies halakhot is assured a place in the World to Come.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's rule that one who uses the crown (tag) will pass away.
Resh Lakish teaches that the 'crown' refers to one who uses a person who studies halakhot (הלכות), which is the crown of Torah.
Ulla rules that one may use a person who has studied (תָּנֵי) four orders of Mishnah, but not one who merely repeats them (מַתְנֵי) without internalizing.

A story illustrates Resh Lakish's disdain: a man who carried him across a river claimed to have studied four orders of Mishnah, so Resh Lakish threw him into the water for presuming to carry a Torah scholar without true mastery.

sub.text: The man's plea and Resh Lakish's teaching
sub.text_en: The man's plea and Resh Lakish's teaching
sub.desc_en: The man begged to learn from Resh Lakish, who then taught him Rabbi Zeira's ruling that Jewish women have adopted the stringency of counting seven clean days even for a drop of blood the size of a mustard seed.

sub.text: Baraita from the school of Eliyahu
sub.text_en: Baraita from the school of Eliyahu
sub.desc_en: A baraita from the school of Eliyahu promises that one who studies halakhot (הלכות) is assured a place in the World to Come, based on the verse 'הליכות עולם לו' (the ways of the world are His), read as 'הלכות' (halakhot).

items.text: Beginning of a new baraita
items.text_en: Beginning of a new baraita
items.desc_en: The daf ends with the opening of a new baraita introduced by 'Tanu rabbanan', which will continue on the next amud.

sub.desc_en: The baraita begins with the standard formula 'תנו רבנן' (the Sages taught), introducing a new teaching that will continue on the next amud.

items.text: Interrupting Torah study for a funeral or wedding
items.text_en: Interrupting Torah study for a funeral or wedding
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one interrupts Torah study to attend to a funeral or a wedding procession. The Gemara clarifies that this applies only when there is not a sufficient quorum; Rav Shmuel bar Inya defines the quorum as 12,000 men and 6,000 shofar blowers, while Ulla describes it as a line of people from the gate to the cemetery. Rav Sheshet compares the taking of the Torah to its giving, requiring 600,000 for those who read and repeat, but for one who teaches, there is no limit.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one interrupts Torah study for a funeral or wedding, but only when there is not a sufficient quorum.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Inya quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Inya quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Inya in the name of Rav defines the quorum as 12,000 men and 6,000 shofar blowers.
Ulla describes the quorum as a line of people from the gate to the cemetery.
Rav Sheshet compares the taking of the Torah to its giving, requiring 600,000 for those who read and repeat, but for one who teaches, there is no limit.

items.text: The Shekhinah accompanies Israel in exile
items.text_en: The Shekhinah accompanies Israel in exile
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai teaches that the Shekhinah is with Israel wherever they are exiled, citing verses for Egypt, Babylonia, and the future redemption. Abaye identifies the synagogues of Hutzal and Shaf veYativ in Neharde'a as places where the Shekhinah resides. A story is told about Rav Sheshet who did not flee from the Shekhinah, and the ministering angels sought to frighten him, but God told them to leave him alone.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai teaches that the Shekhinah accompanies Israel in all their exiles, citing verses for Egypt, Babylonia, and the future redemption.
The Gemara asks where in Babylonia the Shekhinah resides.
Abaye identifies the synagogues of Hutzal and Shaf veYativ in Neharde'a as places where the Shekhinah resides, and notes that he himself enters them to pray when nearby.

sub.text: Story about Samuel's father and Levi
sub.text_en: Story about Samuel's father and Levi
sub.desc_en: A story is told that Samuel's father and Levi were sitting in the Shaf veYativ synagogue, heard the sound of the Shekhinah's arrival, and fled.
Rav Sheshet did not flee from the Shekhinah, and when ministering angels sought to frighten him, God told them to leave him alone.

items.text: Synagogues and study halls as a 'minor sanctuary'
items.text_en: Synagogues and study halls as a 'minor sanctuary'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak interprets 'a minor sanctuary' as referring to the synagogues and study halls in Babylonia, while Rabbi Elazar says it refers to the house of our master in Babylonia. Rava expounds on the verse 'Hashem, You have been a dwelling place for us' as referring to these institutions. Abaye relates that he used to study at home and pray in the synagogue, but after hearing David's verse, he began to study in the synagogue.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak interprets the verse 'וָאֱהִי לָהֶם לְמִקְדָּשׁ מְעַט' (I was for them a minor sanctuary) as referring to the synagogues and study halls in Babylonia.
Rabbi Elazar offers an alternative interpretation, identifying the 'minor sanctuary' as the house of our master in Babylonia.
Rava expounds the verse 'ה׳ מָעוֹן אַתָּה הָיִיתָ לָּנוּ' (Hashem, You have been a dwelling place for us) as referring to synagogues and study halls.

Abaye relates that he initially studied at home and prayed in the synagogue, but after hearing David's verse 'ה׳ אָהַבְתִּי מְעוֹן בֵּיתֶךָ' (Hashem, I love the dwelling of Your house), he began to study in the synagogue.

items.text: Future establishment of Babylonian synagogues in Israel
items.text_en: Future establishment of Babylonian synagogues in Israel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar teaches that the synagogues and study halls of Babylonia will eventually be established in the Land of Israel, using a kal vachomer from Mount Tabor and Mount Carmel. Bar Kappara expounds on a verse about mountains, concluding that a haughty person is like a blemished animal.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar teaches that Babylonian synagogues and study halls will be established in the Land of Israel, using a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from Mount Tabor and Mount Carmel.
Bar Kappara expounds on a verse about mountains, concluding that a haughty person is like a blemished animal, and Rav Ashi affirms this.

items.text: Using a synagogue as a shortcut (kappendarya)
items.text_en: Using a synagogue as a shortcut (kappendarya)
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one should not make a synagogue into a kappendarya (a shortcut). Rava explains the term as meaning 'as I go around the houses, I will enter through this one.' Rabbi Avahu rules that if there was a path from the beginning, it is permitted. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says that if one enters with the intention not to make it a shortcut, it is permitted to do so. Rabbi Chelbo quoting Rav Huna says that one who enters to pray may use it as a shortcut, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one should not make a synagogue into a kappendarya, and the Gemara asks what this term means.
Rava explains that kappendarya means using the synagogue as a shortcut, as one says 'as I go around the houses, I will enter through this one.'
Rabbi Avahu rules that if there was a path through the synagogue from the beginning, it is permitted to use it as a shortcut.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rules that if one enters with the intention not to make it a shortcut, it is permitted to do so.

Rabbi Chelbo quoting Rav Huna rules that one who enters to pray may use it as a shortcut, citing the verse 'and when the people of the land come before the Lord... he who enters through the north gate to bow down shall exit through the south gate.'

items.text: Weeds in a synagogue and cemetery conduct
items.text_en: Weeds in a synagogue and cemetery conduct
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if weeds grow in a synagogue, one should not uproot them due to anguish. A baraisa permits uprooting and leaving them, but not feeding them to animals. The Gemara resolves the contradiction by saying the Mishnah refers to uprooting and feeding. A baraisa teaches that a cemetery must be treated with respect: no grazing, no water channels, no gathering herbs; if gathered, they are burned in place. The Gemara clarifies that the prohibition of burning applies to the first clause (respect), not the latter (burning).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if weeds grow in a synagogue, one should not uproot them because of the anguish it would cause.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraisa that permits uprooting and leaving the weeds, contradicting the Mishnah's prohibition.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah refers specifically to uprooting and feeding to animals, which is prohibited, while the baraisa permits uprooting and leaving.
A baraisa teaches that a cemetery must be treated with respect: no grazing, no water channels, no gathering herbs; if gathered, they are burned in place.
The Gemara asks which clause of the baraisa the burning applies to, questioning whether it could be the latter clause about gathering herbs.
The Gemara clarifies that the burning applies to the first clause (the prohibition of disrespectful conduct), not the latter clause about gathering herbs.

items.text: The four special Shabbatot and the order of readings
items.text_en: The four special Shabbatot and the order of readings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the special Torah readings for the four Shabbatot surrounding Purim and Passover: Shekalim, Zachor, Parah, HaChodesh, and then returning to the regular cycle. It also states that one interrupts the regular reading for Rosh Chodesh, Chanukah, Purim, fasts, ma'amadot, and Yom Kippur. The Gemara begins with a reference to the Mishnah in Shekalim about announcing the shekalim on the first of Adar.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the rule for Rosh Chodesh Adar that falls on Shabbat: one reads the portion of Shekalim, and if it falls during the week, one advances to the previous Shabbat and interrupts for the next one.
The Mishnah lists the remaining special Shabbatot: the second for Zachor, third for Parah, fourth for HaChodesh, and the fifth returns to the regular cycle.
The Mishnah states that one interrupts the regular reading for all occasions: Rosh Chodesh, Chanukah, Purim, fasts, ma'amadot, and Yom Kippur.
The Gemara begins by referencing the Mishnah in Shekalim about announcing the shekalim on the first of Adar.

items.text: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the four parashiyot read before Passover, including Parashat Shekalim.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the portion about forbidden mixtures (כלאים) is read before Passover.

items.text: Gemara's question on the source for reading Parashat Shekalim
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the source for reading Parashat Shekalim
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why we read about shekalim on the first of Adar, and Rabbi Tavi cites a verse to derive that the new year's offering must come from new terumah. The Gemara then explains that we read early to collect shekalim for the Temple, and notes that this view disagrees with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who requires only two weeks before Passover.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: the reading about kilayim is understandable because it's planting season, but what is the source for reading about shekalim?
Rabbi Tavi in the name of Rabbi Yoshiya cites the verse 'זֹאת עוֹלַת חוֹדֶשׁ בְּחׇדְשׁוֹ' to derive that the new year's offering must come from new תרומה (priestly portion).
Since the offering must come from new תרומה in Nisan, we read early on the first of Adar so that shekalim can be collected for the Temple.
The Gemara notes that this view disagrees with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who holds that questions about Passover are asked only two weeks before the holiday.
Even according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, since the tables for collecting shekalim sit on the 15th in the provinces and the 25th in the Temple, we read early because of the tables.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel over which parashah is read
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel over which parashah is read
items.desc_en: Rav says Parashat Shekalim is 'Tzav et Bnei Yisrael' (the korbanot section), while Shmuel says it is 'Ki Tisa'. The Gemara explains each opinion: Shmuel's has explicit shekalim, while Rav's relies on Rabbi Tavi's teaching about korbanot. A baraita of Rav Yosef about three terumot supports the connection.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the portion of Shekalim? Rav says it is 'צַו אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל' (Command the children of Israel...), and Shmuel says it is 'כִּי תִשָּׂא' (When you take a census).
Rav identifies Parashat Shekalim as the section beginning with 'צו את בני ישראל' (Command the children of Israel) about the daily offerings.
Shmuel identifies Parashat Shekalim as the section 'כי תשא' (When you take a census) which explicitly mentions shekalim.
The Gemara explains that Shmuel's identification is straightforward because the word 'שקלים' (shekels) appears in that portion.
The Gemara objects that the word 'שקלים' does not appear in Rav's chosen portion.
The Gemara resolves that Rav's opinion follows Rabbi Tavi's teaching that the korbanot section relates to the new terumah for the altar, which is funded by shekalim.
Rav Yosef's baraita distinguishes three types of terumot (contributions): for the altar, for the sockets, and for the Temple maintenance, supporting the connection between korbanot and shekalim.

items.text: Why Rosh Chodesh Adar differs from other Roshei Chodashim
items.text_en: Why Rosh Chodesh Adar differs from other Roshei Chodashim
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the uniqueness of Rosh Chodesh Adar: according to Shmuel, it is because we read 'Ki Tisa', while according to Rav, it is because we read all six aliyot from the Rosh Chodesh portion instead of the usual one. The discussion considers both those who follow the order of parashiyot and those who follow the order of haftarot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Shmuel who says the parsha is 'כי תשא', the name 'Parshat Shekalim' fits because shekalim are written there; but according to Rav who says 'את קרבני לחמי', where are shekalim written there?
The Gemara answers: yes, the reason is like Rabbi Tavi's teaching that the Torah said to renew and bring a korban from the new תרומה (priestly portion).

The Gemara asks: according to Rav who says 'צו את בני ישראל', korbanot are written there, fitting Rabbi Tavi's reason; but according to Shmuel who says 'כי תשא', are korbanot written there? Shekalim for the sockets are written there!
Rav Yosef teaches a baraita that there are three types of תרומות (donations): for the altar, for the sockets, and for the Temple maintenance.
The Gemara asks: according to Shmuel who says 'כי תשא', it is clear why this Rosh Chodesh differs from other Roshei Chodashim; but according to Rav who says 'צו את קרבני', what is different?

The Gemara answers: it is different because on other Roshei Chodashim they read six aliyot from the day's topic and one from the Rosh Chodesh portion, but here all six are from the Rosh Chodesh portion.
The Gemara notes: this works well for the one who says the cycle follows the order of parashiyot.
The Gemara asks: but according to the one who says the cycle follows the order of haftarot, and we read the weekly parsha, what is different about this Rosh Chodesh?

The Gemara answers: it is different because on other Roshei Chodashim they read six from the day's topic and one from Rosh Chodesh, but here they read three from the day's topic and four from Rosh Chodesh.

items.text: Support for Shmuel from a baraita and other sources
items.text_en: Support for Shmuel from a baraita and other sources
items.desc_en: A baraita states that when Rosh Chodesh Adar falls on Shabbat, we read Parashat Shekalim and the haftarah from Yehoiada the priest. This supports Shmuel because the haftarah relates to shekalim. Another baraita discusses when Rosh Chodesh falls in the adjacent parashah, and a Tosefta explicitly supports Shmuel's view that we read 'Ki Tisa'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that when Rosh Chodesh Adar falls on Shabbat, we read Parashat Shekalim and the haftarah from Yehoiada the priest.
The gemara notes that the haftarah fits Shmuel's view that Parashat Shekalim is 'כי תשא' (Ki Tisa), but questions how it fits Rav's view that it is 'את קרבני לחמי' (Et Korbani Lachmi).
The gemara resolves that even for Rav, the haftarah is appropriate because of Rabbi Tavi's teaching linking shekalim to the new terumah.
Another baraita is cited: when Rosh Chodesh Adar falls in the adjacent parashah, we read that parashah and repeat it.
The gemara notes that this baraita supports Shmuel because 'כי תשא' (Ki Tisa) can occur at that time in the regular cycle.
The gemara resolves that even for Rav, the baraita works for the Westerners who complete the Torah in three years.
A Tosefta is cited that explicitly supports Shmuel's view: when Rosh Chodesh Adar falls on Shabbat, we read 'כי תשא' (Ki Tisa) and the haftarah from Yehoiada.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha's ruling on Rosh Chodesh Adar on Shabbat
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha's ruling on Rosh Chodesh Adar on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha rules that when Rosh Chodesh Adar falls on Shabbat, three Torah scrolls are taken out, and one reads from each: the weekly portion, the Rosh Chodesh portion, and 'Ki Tisa'. The Gemara notes that this implies he follows Shmuel, and that the same applies to Rosh Chodesh Tevet on Shabbat with Chanukah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha rules that when Rosh Chodesh Adar falls on Shabbat, three Torah scrolls are taken out and read from: the weekly portion, the Rosh Chodesh portion, and 'Ki Tisa'; similarly for Rosh Chodesh Tevet on Shabbat with Chanukah.

The Gemara explains why both rulings were necessary: without the second, one might think Rabbi Yitzchak follows Rav (who requires only two scrolls for Adar), so the second case teaches that he requires three even for Tevet.
The Gemara resolves that one ruling was stated as a corollary of the other, so both were needed to avoid redundancy.

items.text: Dispute about Rosh Chodesh Tevet on a weekday
items.text_en: Dispute about Rosh Chodesh Tevet on a weekday
items.desc_en: When Rosh Chodesh Tevet falls on a weekday, Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha says three aliyot are for Rosh Chodesh and one for Chanukah, while Rav Dimi of Haifa says three for Chanukah and one for Rosh Chodesh. Rabbi Mani supports Rabbi Yitzchak because the frequent (tadir) takes precedence, while Rabbi Avin supports Rav Dimi because Rosh Chodesh causes the fourth reader. The Gemara concludes that we do not consider Chanukah, and Rosh Chodesh is primary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: when Rosh Chodesh Tevet falls on a weekday, Rabbi Yitzchak says three aliyot are for Rosh Chodesh and one for Chanukah, while Rav Dimi of Haifa says three for Chanukah and one for Rosh Chodesh.
Rabbi Mani supports Rabbi Yitzchak because the frequent (תדיר, the regular) takes precedence over the infrequent.
Rabbi Avin supports Rav Dimi, arguing that Rosh Chodesh causes the fourth reader to come, so the fourth aliyah should be for Rosh Chodesh.

The Gemara concludes the dispute: Rav Yosef says we do not consider Rosh Chodesh (i.e., Chanukah is primary), Rabbah says we do not consider Chanukah, and the final ruling is that we do not consider Chanukah and Rosh Chodesh is primary.

items.text: Reading when Rosh Chodesh falls in 'Ve'atah Tetzaveh'
items.text_en: Reading when Rosh Chodesh falls in 'Ve'atah Tetzaveh'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha rules that when Rosh Chodesh Adar falls in the parashah of 'Ve'atah Tetzaveh', six aliyot are read from that parashah until 'Ki Tisa', and one from 'Ki Tisa' until 'Ve'asita'. Abaye begins to comment.

sub.desc_en: It was stated: if Rosh Chodesh Adar falls on the portion 'וְאַתָּה תְּצַוֶּה', Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha says they read six from 'וְאַתָּה תְּצַוֶּה' until 'כִּי תִשָּׂא', and one from 'כִּי תִשָּׂא' until 'וְעָשִׂיתָ'; Abaye says:

items.text: Abaye's resolution for the reading when Rosh Chodesh Adar falls on Shabbat
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution for the reading when Rosh Chodesh Adar falls on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that when Rosh Chodesh Adar falls on Shabbat, six people read from 'Ve'atah Tetzaveh' to 'Ve'asita', and one reads from 'Ki Tisa' to 'Ve'asita', resolving the earlier dispute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the earlier resolution merely establishes a fixed reading arrangement.
Abaye resolves that six read from 'Ve'atah Tetzaveh' to 'Ve'asita' and one reads from 'Ki Tisa' to 'Ve'asita'.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and resolution for Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and resolution for Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if Rosh Chodesh falls in the adjacent parashah, they read it and repeat it. This challenges Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha, but he responds that Abaye's view also has difficulty with the case of 'after it'. The Gemara resolves that the repetition applies to Shabbatot, and here too they repeat it on Shabbatot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: if Rosh Chodesh falls in the adjacent parashah, they read it and repeat it.
The Gemara notes that the baraita is consistent with Abaye's view but poses a difficulty for Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha.
Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha retorts that even Abaye's view is not consistent, because the baraita's case of 'after it' is difficult to find.
The Gemara resolves that the repetition applies to Shabbatot, and here too they repeat it on Shabbatot.

items.text: Reading when Rosh Chodesh falls in 'Ki Tisa' itself
items.text_en: Reading when Rosh Chodesh falls in 'Ki Tisa' itself
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha says six read from 'Ve'asita' to 'Vayakhel' and one reads from 'Ki Tisa' to 'Ve'asita'. Abaye objects that this would mean reading backwards, and instead says six read until 'Vayakhel' and one reads from 'Ki Tisa' to 'Ve'asita'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha states the reading arrangement when Rosh Chodesh falls in the 'Ki Tisa' portion itself: six read from 'Ve'asita' to 'Vayakhel' and one reads from 'Ki Tisa' to 'Ve'asita'.
Abaye objects that Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha's proposal would mean reading the Torah backwards (למפרע).
Abaye proposes an alternative: six read until 'Vayakhel' and one reads from 'Ki Tisa' to 'Ve'asita', avoiding the backward reading.

items.text: Baraita supporting Abaye
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Abaye
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Abaye's view: when Rosh Chodesh falls in 'Ki Tisa' itself, they read it and repeat it.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Abaye's view: when Rosh Chodesh falls in 'Ki Tisa' itself, they read it and repeat it.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding Rosh Chodesh Adar on Friday
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding Rosh Chodesh Adar on Friday
items.desc_en: If Rosh Chodesh Adar falls on Friday, Rav says to advance the reading to the previous Shabbat, while Shmuel says to postpone it. The Gemara brings a baraita that seems to support Rav, but Shmuel interprets it as referring to when Rosh Chodesh falls within the Shabbat itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute: if Rosh Chodesh Adar falls on Friday, Rav says to advance the reading to the previous Shabbat, while Shmuel says to postpone it.

Rav explains that advancing is necessary so that the days of the 'shulchanot' (the collection for the poor) are not reduced; Shmuel counters that since the fifteenth of Adar will still fall on Friday, the poor will not go out until Sunday, so postponing is better.
The Gemara cites a baraita that seems to support Rav, but then rejects the inference, saying the baraita refers specifically to when Rosh Chodesh falls within the Shabbat itself, not on Friday.

The Gemara brings another baraita that defines the first Shabbat as one where Rosh Chodesh Adar falls within it, even on Friday, and argues that just as within the Shabbat one advances, so too on Friday one advances.
Shmuel responds that the baraita refers to when Rosh Chodesh falls within the Shabbat itself, and the school of Shmuel also teaches this interpretation.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute about serugin for Shabbatot
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute about serugin for Shabbatot
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says they interweave the readings for the Shabbatot, while Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says they do not. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar explains that when Rosh Chodesh falls on Friday, they do not interweave, but when it falls within the Shabbat, they advance and read from the previous Shabbat even though it is Shevat.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rules that they interweave the readings for the Shabbatot.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar disagrees and says they do not interweave.

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar clarifies that when Rosh Chodesh falls on Friday they do not interweave, but when it falls within the Shabbat they advance and read from the previous Shabbat even though it is Shevat.

items.text: Dispute about reading Parashat Zachor when Purim falls on Friday
items.text_en: Dispute about reading Parashat Zachor when Purim falls on Friday
items.desc_en: Rav says to advance Parashat Zachor to the previous Shabbat, while Shmuel says to postpone it. The Gemara brings a baraita that seems to support Rav, but Shmuel interprets it as referring to when Purim falls within the Shabbat itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding when to read Parashat Zachor when Purim falls on Friday.
Rav explains that the reading should be advanced so that the act of fulfilling the mitzvah of Purim (עשייה) does not precede the remembrance of Amalek (זכירה).
Shmuel argues that since those in walled cities observe Purim on the 15th, the act and the remembrance occur simultaneously, so there is no need to advance the reading.

The Gemara challenges Rav and Shmuel from the Mishnah, which states that when Rosh Chodesh Adar falls on Shabbat, Parashat Zachor is read on the second Shabbat, implying that Purim falls on Friday and the reading is not advanced.
Rav Pappa resolves the objection by explaining that 'second' in the Mishnah refers to the second Shabbat after the interruption, not the second of the month.
A baraita is brought that defines the second Shabbat as one when Purim falls within it, even on Friday, and the Gemara infers that this supports advancing the reading.
Shmuel rejects the inference, stating that the baraita refers specifically to when Purim falls within the Shabbat itself, not on Friday.

items.text: Dispute about Purim falling on Shabbat itself
items.text_en: Dispute about Purim falling on Shabbat itself
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says that according to all opinions, they do not advance the reading of Zachor, while Rav Nachman says the dispute still stands. A supporting statement from Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rav says that if Purim falls on Shabbat, they advance and read Zachor on the previous Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents the dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Nachman regarding whether the reading of Zachor is advanced when Purim falls on Shabbat itself.

sub.text: Supporting statement from Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Supporting statement from Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports in the name of Rav that when Purim falls on Shabbat, one advances and reads Zachor on the previous Shabbat.

items.text: Definition of the third Shabbat (Parah)
items.text_en: Definition of the third Shabbat (Parah)
items.desc_en: The rabbis taught that the third Shabbat is the one adjacent to Purim from after it. Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina says it is the Shabbat adjacent to Rosh Chodesh Nisan. The Gemara resolves that they do not disagree: one refers to when Rosh Chodesh Nisan falls on Shabbat, the other when it falls during the week.

sub.desc_en: The baraita defines the third Shabbat as the one adjacent to Purim from after it.
Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina offers an alternative definition: the Shabbat adjacent to Rosh Chodesh Nisan.
The Gemara resolves that the two definitions do not disagree: one applies when Rosh Chodesh Nisan falls on Shabbat, the other when it falls during the week.

items.text: Summary of the four special Shabbatot and their readings
items.text_en: Summary of the four special Shabbatot and their readings
items.desc_en: The baraita details the Torah and haftarah readings for the four Shabbatot: first (Rosh Chodesh Adar), second (Zachor), third (Parah), and fourth (HaChodesh), with definitions for each Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists the Torah and haftarah readings for the four special Shabbatot: Shekalim, Zachor, Parah, and HaChodesh, defining each Shabbat by its proximity to Purim or Rosh Chodesh.

items.text: Definition of the fourth Sabbath
items.text_en: Definition of the fourth Sabbath
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines the fourth Sabbath as one that includes Rosh Chodesh Nisan, even if it falls on Friday.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines the fourth Sabbath as one that includes Rosh Chodesh Nisan, even if it falls on Friday.

items.text: Debate on returning to the order
items.text_en: Debate on returning to the order
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what 'returning to the order' means. Rabbi Ami says it refers to the order of Torah portions, while Rabbi Yirmiyah says it refers to the order of haftarot. Abaye supports Rabbi Ami from a Mishnah listing interruptions, and the Gemara resolves the objection regarding haftarot on weekdays.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'returning to the order' refers to.
Rabbi Ami says it refers to the order of Torah portions.
Rabbi Yirmiyah says it refers to the order of haftarot.
Abaye supports Rabbi Ami by citing a Mishnah that lists interruptions, implying Torah portions exist on weekdays.
The Gemara objects that according to Rabbi Yirmiyah, there is no haftarah on weekdays to interrupt.
The Gemara resolves that each opinion refers to its own context: Torah portions for weekdays and haftarot for Shabbat.

items.text: Reading schedule for fast days
items.text_en: Reading schedule for fast days
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why fast days require an interruption, suggesting one could read the day's topic in the morning and the fast in the afternoon. It supports Rav Huna's view that the morning is for eulogizing. Abaye then describes the practice: morning for town matters, afternoon for reading and supplication, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why fast days require an interruption in the reading schedule, suggesting one could read the day's topic in the morning and the fast in the afternoon.
The Gemara supports Rav Huna's view that the morning is designated for eulogizing, implying the reading schedule must be interrupted.
Abaye describes the practice: morning for town matters, afternoon for reading and supplication, citing a verse.
The Gemara rejects the possibility of reversing the order, citing verses that show the afternoon is for prayer and supplication.

items.text: Mishnah: Readings for festivals
items.text_en: Mishnah: Readings for festivals
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the Torah readings for Passover, Shavuot, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Sukkot, Chanukah, Purim, Rosh Chodesh, Ma'amadot, and fast days.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the Torah readings for all festivals, including Passover, Shavuot, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Sukkot, Chanukah, Purim, Rosh Chodesh, Ma'amadot, and fast days.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: General rules for festival readings
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: General rules for festival readings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the blessings and curses are read without interruption, and that on Monday, Thursday, and Shabbat Mincha the readings follow their order but do not count toward the annual cycle, citing a verse from Leviticus.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the blessings and curses are read without interruption, and that on Monday, Thursday, and Shabbat Mincha the readings follow their order but do not count toward the annual cycle, citing a verse from Leviticus.

items.text: Gemara: Readings for Passover
items.text_en: Gemara: Readings for Passover
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states the readings for Passover: on the first day from Parashat Mo'edot with a Haftarah from the Passover of Gilgal, and for the two-day diaspora, the first day from Gilgal and the second from Josiah. For the intermediate days, Rav Pappa says to read from the section beginning with the mnemonic אפ״ו. Abaye notes the contemporary custom to read from the sections beginning with the words משך תורא, קדש בכספא, פסל במדברא, and שלח בוכרא.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the Torah and Haftarah readings for Passover: on the first day from Parashat Mo'edot with a Haftarah from the Passover of Gilgal, and for the two-day diaspora, the first day from Gilgal and the second from Josiah.
The Gemara asks what specific Torah readings are used for the intermediate days of Passover.
Rav Pappa answers that one reads from the sections beginning with the mnemonic אפ״ו (Ephod).
The baraita specifies the readings for the last day of Passover and the following day (the two-day diaspora).
Abaye notes that the contemporary custom is to read from the sections beginning with the words משך תורא, קדש בכספא, פסל במדברא, and שלח בוכרא.

items.text: Readings for Shavuot
items.text_en: Readings for Shavuot
items.desc_en: The baraita presents two opinions for Shavuot: one reads 'Seven Weeks' with a Haftarah from Habakkuk, and others read 'In the Third Month' with a Haftarah from the Chariot. The Gemara notes that in the diaspora with two days, we do both in reverse order.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the first opinion: on Shavuot one reads 'Seven Weeks' (Deuteronomy 16:9) and the Haftarah from Habakkuk.
Acherim gives an alternative opinion: read 'In the Third Month' (Exodus 19:1) with the Haftarah of the Chariot (Ezekiel 1).
The Gemara rules that in the diaspora, where two days are observed, we follow both opinions in reverse order.

items.text: Readings for Rosh Hashanah
items.text_en: Readings for Rosh Hashanah
items.desc_en: The baraita gives two traditions for Rosh Hashanah: one reads 'In the Seventh Month' with a Haftarah from 'Is Ephraim a dear son', and others read 'And the Lord remembered Sarah' with a Haftarah from Hannah. For the two-day diaspora, the first day follows the 'others' and the second day reads 'And God tested Abraham' with the Haftarah 'Is Ephraim a dear son'.

sub.desc_en: Tanna Kamma states that on Rosh Hashanah they read the portion 'In the Seventh Month' and the Haftarah 'Is Ephraim a dear son'.
Yesh Omrim (some say) propose an alternative: they read 'And the Lord remembered Sarah' and the Haftarah from Hannah.
The Gemara rules that nowadays in the Diaspora with two days, the first day follows Yesh Omrim, and the second day reads 'And God tested Abraham' with the Haftarah 'Is Ephraim a dear son'.

items.text: Readings for Yom Kippur and a homily by Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Readings for Yom Kippur and a homily by Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: For Yom Kippur, the Torah reading is 'After the Death' and the Haftarah is 'For thus says the High and Lofty One'; for Mincha, the reading is from the forbidden relations and the Haftarah is Jonah. Rabbi Yochanan then expounds that wherever you find God's might, you find His humility, citing verses from Torah, Prophets, and Writings that juxtapose God's greatness with His care for the orphan and widow.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the Torah and Haftarah readings for Yom Kippur: the Torah reading is 'After the Death' (Leviticus 16) and the Haftarah is 'For thus says the High and Lofty One' (Isaiah 57:14–58:14); for Mincha, the Torah reading is from the forbidden relations (Leviticus 18) and the Haftarah is Jonah.
Rabbi Yochanan states a general principle: wherever you find God's might, you find His humility, and this is written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, and stated a third time in the Writings.

Rabbi Yochanan supports his principle with three sets of verses: from the Torah (Deuteronomy 10:17–18), from the Prophets (Isaiah 57:15), and from the Writings (Psalms 68:5–6), each juxtaposing God's greatness with His care for the orphan, widow, and humble.

items.text: Readings for Sukkot
items.text_en: Readings for Sukkot
items.desc_en: For the first day of Sukkot, the reading is from Parashat Mo'edot in Leviticus with a Haftarah from 'Behold the day is coming'. For the two-day diaspora, the second day reads the same Torah portion but with a Haftarah from 'And they assembled to King Solomon'. The intermediate days read from the festival offerings. The last day reads 'All the firstborn' with a Haftarah from 'And it was when Solomon finished'. The next day reads 'And this is the blessing' with a Haftarah from 'And Solomon stood'.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states the Torah reading and Haftarah for the first day of Sukkot.
The Gemara explains the current practice for the second day of Sukkot in the diaspora: the same Torah portion is read, but the Haftarah is from 'And they assembled to King Solomon'.

The Tanna Kamma states that on the intermediate days of Sukkot, the reading is from the festival offerings, and on the last day, the reading is 'All the firstborn' with a Haftarah from 'And it was when Solomon finished'.
The Tanna Kamma states that on the day after Sukkot (Shemini Atzeret), the reading is 'And this is the blessing' with a Haftarah from 'And Solomon stood'.

items.text: Readings for Shabbat Chol HaMoed, Chanukah, Purim, and Rosh Chodesh
items.text_en: Readings for Shabbat Chol HaMoed, Chanukah, Purim, and Rosh Chodesh
items.desc_en: Rav Huna quoting Rav states that for Shabbat during Chol HaMoed of Passover or Sukkot, the Torah reading is 'Re'eh Atta' with a Haftarah from 'The dry bones' for Passover and 'On the day of Gog' for Sukkot. For Chanukah, the reading is from the princes with a Haftarah from Zechariah's menorah; if two Shabbatot occur, the first uses Zechariah and the second uses Solomon's menorah. For Purim, the reading is 'And Amalek came'. For Rosh Chodesh, the reading is 'And on your new moons'; if it falls on Shabbat, the Haftarah is 'And it shall be from new moon'; if on Sunday, the Haftarah from the previous day is 'And Jonathan said to him, tomorrow is the new moon'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna in the name of Rav states the Torah reading and Haftarah for Shabbat during Chol HaMoed of Passover and Sukkot.
Rav Huna in the name of Rav specifies the readings for Chanukah, including the Torah portion of the princes and the Haftarah from Zechariah, with a rule for two Shabbatot.
Rav Huna in the name of Rav specifies the readings for Purim and Rosh Chodesh, including the Haftarah for Rosh Chodesh falling on Shabbat or Sunday.

items.text: Beginning of Rav Huna's next statement
items.text_en: Beginning of Rav Huna's next statement
items.desc_en: The daf ends with the beginning of another statement by Rav Huna, which is cut off and continues on the next amud.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna begins a statement that is cut off at the end of the daf.

items.text: Haftarah for Rosh Chodesh Av falling on Shabbat
items.text_en: Haftarah for Rosh Chodesh Av falling on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the haftarah for Rosh Chodesh Av when it falls on Shabbat, citing the verse 'Your new moons and your appointed seasons My soul hates' and interpreting God's complaint that Israel not only sins but also burdens Him to know what harsh decree to bring upon them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the rule: when Rosh Chodesh Av falls on Shabbat, the haftarah is from Isaiah 1:14, 'Your new moons and your appointed seasons My soul hates; they are a burden to Me.'
The Gemara asks: what does the phrase 'they are a burden to Me' mean?
God explains: not only do Israel sin before Me, but they burden Me to know what harsh decree I will bring upon them.

items.text: Haftarah for Tisha B'Av itself
items.text_en: Haftarah for Tisha B'Av itself
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what haftarah is read on Tisha B'Av itself. Rav says 'How the faithful city has become a harlot', and other opinions are cited: 'And if you will not listen to Me', 'How long will this people despise Me', and 'How long shall I bear with this evil congregation'. Abaye reports the current custom to read 'When you beget children' and the haftarah 'I will utterly consume them'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what haftarah is read on Tisha B'Av itself.
Rav answers that the haftarah is 'How the faithful city has become a harlot' (Isaiah 1:21).
A baraita cites Acherim who say the haftarah is 'And if you will not listen to Me' (Leviticus 26:14).
Rabbi Natan bar Yosef says the haftarah is 'How long will this people despise Me' (Numbers 14:11).
Yesh Omrim say the haftarah is 'How long shall I bear with this evil congregation' (Numbers 14:27).
Abaye reports the current custom to read 'When you beget children' (Deuteronomy 4:25) as the Torah portion and 'I will utterly consume them' (Jeremiah 8:13) as the haftarah.

items.text: The institution of ma'amadot
items.text_en: The institution of ma'amadot
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the source for ma'amadot, the groups of Israelites who would stand by during the Temple service. Rabbi Ami says that without ma'amadot, heaven and earth would not endure, citing Jeremiah 33:25. Abraham's dialogue with God about Israel's fate is recounted, where God promises that the reading of the order of sacrifices is considered as if they were offered, and He forgives their sins.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the institution of ma'amadot (מעמדות).
Rabbi Ami answers that without ma'amadot (מעמדות) heaven and earth would not endure, citing Jeremiah 33:25.
The Gemara recounts Abraham's dialogue with God, where Abraham fears that Israel might sin and be destroyed like the generation of the flood, and God reassures him that this will not happen.
God promises Abraham that when the Temple is not standing, the reading of the order of sacrifices (סדר קרבנות) is considered as if they were offered, and He forgives all their sins.

items.text: No pausing between curses in the Torah reading
items.text_en: No pausing between curses in the Torah reading
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the rule that one does not pause between the curses in the Torah reading. Rabbi Chiyya bar Gammada in the name of Rabbi Asi derives this from Proverbs 3:11. Reish Lakish says it is because one does not recite a blessing over calamity; instead, one begins with the verse before the curses and ends with the verse after them. Abaye distinguishes between the curses in Leviticus (said in plural, from God's mouth) where one does not pause, and those in Deuteronomy (said in singular, from Moses' own mouth) where one may pause. A story with Levi bar Butei illustrates this.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on fast days one reads the blessings and curses, and one does not pause between the curses.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of this rule.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Gammada in the name of Rabbi Asi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Gammada in the name of Rabbi Asi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Gammada in the name of Rabbi Asi derives the rule from Proverbs 3:11, 'Do not despise the discipline of the Lord.'
Reish Lakish gives a different reason: one does not recite a blessing over calamity; instead, one begins with the verse before the curses and ends with the verse after them.

Abaye distinguishes between the curses in Leviticus (said in plural, from God's mouth) where one does not pause, and those in Deuteronomy (said in singular, from Moses' own mouth) where one may pause.

sub.text: Story with Levi bar Butei and Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Story with Levi bar Butei and Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: A story with Levi bar Butei illustrates the rule: when he hesitated over the curses in Leviticus, Rav Huna rebuked him, confirming that one does not pause there, but may pause in Deuteronomy.

items.text: Ezra's enactment to read curses before Shavuot and before Rosh Hashanah
items.text_en: Ezra's enactment to read curses before Shavuot and before Rosh Hashanah
items.desc_en: A beraita states that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says Ezra enacted that the curses in Leviticus be read before Shavuot and those in Deuteronomy before Rosh Hashanah, so that the year and its curses end. The Gemara questions why Shavuot is considered a new year, and answers that Shavuot is the new year for the fruit of the tree, as taught in a mishnah.

sub.text: Beraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Beraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: The beraita states that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says Ezra enacted reading the curses of Leviticus before Shavuot and those of Deuteronomy before Rosh Hashanah.
Abaye (or alternatively Reish Lakish) explains the reason: so that the year and its curses end together.
The Gemara questions: for Deuteronomy it makes sense, but is Shavuot considered a new year?
The Gemara answers that Shavuot is indeed a new year for the fruit of the tree, as taught in a mishnah.

items.text: The principle of listening to elders over youth
items.text_en: The principle of listening to elders over youth
items.desc_en: A beraita cites Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's teaching that if elders say 'destroy' and youth say 'build', one should destroy and not build, because the destruction of elders is constructive and the building of youth is destructive, with the sign being Rehoboam son of Solomon.

sub.text: Beraita citing Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Beraita citing Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: A beraita teaches that if elders say 'destroy' and youth say 'build', one should destroy and not build, because the destruction of elders is constructive and the building of youth is destructive, with the sign being Rehoboam son of Solomon.

items.text: Dispute about where to resume reading on different days
items.text_en: Dispute about where to resume reading on different days
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda about where one resumes reading on Shabbat Mincha, Monday, Thursday, and the next Shabbat. Rabbi Meir says one resumes at the place where one stopped on Shabbat morning for Mincha, and similarly for subsequent days. Rabbi Yehuda says one resumes at the same place for Mincha, Monday, Thursday, and the next Shabbat. Rabbi Zeira rules the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi Meir holds that the reading place advances each time (Shabbat morning → Mincha → Monday → Thursday → next Shabbat), while Rabbi Yehuda holds that all subsequent readings (Mincha, Monday, Thursday, next Shabbat) resume at the same place where Shabbat morning stopped.
Rabbi Zeira rules the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda's position, and the Gemara notes that he could have simply said 'the halakha is like Rabbi Yehuda'.

items.text: Reason for the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Reason for the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda about whether to roll the Torah scroll before the blessing is due to the concern that people might think blessings are written in the Torah, similar to Ulla's reasoning about the translator.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the dispute is because people might invert the order, thinking blessings are written in the Torah.

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda about the procedure for reading
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda about the procedure for reading
items.desc_en: A baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi Meir says one opens, sees, rolls, blesses, and then opens again to read; Rabbi Yehuda says one opens, sees, blesses, and reads without rolling. The Gemara explains their reasoning: Rabbi Meir follows Ulla's concern that people might think blessings are written in the Torah, while Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between translation (which could be mistaken) and blessings (which cannot).

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi Meir says one opens, sees, rolls, blesses, and then opens again to read; Rabbi Yehuda says one opens, sees, blesses, and reads without rolling.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Meir's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Meir's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir follows Ulla's concern: just as the reader does not assist the translator lest people think translation is written in the Torah, so too one rolls the scroll before blessing lest people think blessings are written in the Torah.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between translation, which could be mistaken for Torah text, and blessings, which cannot be mistaken, so no rolling is needed.

items.text: Rav Matna's ruling in favor of Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Rav Matna's ruling in favor of Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rav Matna rules that the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda's view: one opens, sees, blesses, and reads. The Gemara notes that this is stated without explicitly saying it follows Rabbi Yehuda, because the earlier explanation already reversed the names.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav Mattana rules the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda, but the Gemara notes that the statement was phrased indirectly to avoid the concern of inversion.
The Gemara asks why Rav Matna did not explicitly say 'the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda'.
The Gemara answers that the explicit attribution was omitted because the earlier baraita had already reversed the names of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: The status of lecterns and platforms
items.text_en: The status of lecterns and platforms
items.desc_en: Rav Matna states that lecterns and platforms (used for Torah reading) do not possess inherent sanctity.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav Mattana states that the wooden tablets (for Torah scrolls) and platforms (bimot) have no inherent sanctity.

items.text: Laws of rolling a Torah scroll
items.text_en: Laws of rolling a Torah scroll
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan gives three rulings: one must roll the scroll so it rests on the seam; one rolls it from the outside, not the inside; and when tightening it, one does so from the inside, not the outside.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one rolling a Torah scroll must position it so it rests on the seam.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that one rolls the scroll from the outside, not the inside.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that when tightening the scroll, one does so from the inside, not the outside.

items.text: The reward of the one who rolls the Torah scroll
items.text_en: The reward of the one who rolls the Torah scroll
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says that among ten readers, the one who rolls the Torah scroll receives reward equivalent to all of them, as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi taught. The Gemara clarifies that he receives reward corresponding to all, not the reward of all.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shefatya in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules that when ten read from the Torah, the greatest among them rolls the scroll, and the Gemara clarifies that the roller receives reward equivalent to all of them, not their actual reward.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that the one who rolls the Torah scroll receives the reward of all the readers.
The Gemara objects: can it enter your mind that he receives the reward of all of them (as if he performed all their mitzvot)?
The Gemara resolves: rather say he receives reward corresponding to all of them (equivalent in value, not the identical reward).

items.text: Using a bat kol (heavenly voice)
items.text_en: Using a bat kol (heavenly voice)
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan derives from Isaiah 30:21 that one may rely on a bat kol, but only under specific conditions: hearing a man's voice in the city or a woman's voice in the field, and when the voice says 'yes yes' or 'no no'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shefatya in the name of Rabbi Yochanan derives from a verse that one may rely on a בת קול (heavenly echo) under certain conditions: hearing a man's voice in town or a woman's voice in the field, and the echo says 'yes yes' or 'no no'.

items.text: The verse about reading without pleasantness
items.text_en: The verse about reading without pleasantness
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says that one who reads without pleasantness or recites without melody is subject to the verse 'I gave them statutes that are not good.' Abaye objects that this cannot be the meaning, and instead explains it as referring to two Torah scholars who do not show each other courtesy in halacha.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shefatya in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that one who reads without pleasantness or studies without melody is subject to the verse 'I gave them bad statutes'.

Abaye objects: because one cannot sweeten one's voice, does the verse 'judgments by which they shall not live' apply? Rather, the verse applies as Rav Mesharshiya explained: to two Torah scholars in one city who do not treat each other pleasantly in halacha.
Rav Mesharshiya explains that the verse refers to two Torah scholars who do not show each other courtesy in halacha.

items.text: Holding a Torah scroll uncovered
items.text_en: Holding a Torah scroll uncovered
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says that one who holds a Torah scroll uncovered is buried uncovered. The Gemara clarifies that this means buried without mitzvot, and Abaye further explains it means without that specific mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Parnakh in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says one who holds a Torah scroll naked is buried naked, and Abaye clarifies: buried naked without that mitzvah (of holding the Torah scroll).
The Gemara objects that literal naked burial is impossible, and reinterprets 'uncovered' as buried without mitzvot (commandments).
Abaye further clarifies that the punishment is being buried without that specific mitzvah (the honor of the Torah scroll), not all mitzvot.

items.text: Preference for using a cloth for the Torah scroll
items.text_en: Preference for using a cloth for the Torah scroll
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai says it is better that the cloth (used to cover the Torah) be rolled rather than the Torah scroll itself be rolled.

sub.text: Rabbi Yannai quoting Rabbi Yannai the Elder
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yannai quoting Rabbi Yannai the Elder
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai in the name of Rabbi Yannai the Elder says it is better that the cloth cover be rolled than the Torah scroll itself.

items.text: Moses' institution of reading about the festivals in their season
items.text_en: Moses' institution of reading about the festivals in their season
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that Moses instituted that Israel should inquire and expound on the laws of each festival during its time: Passover laws on Passover, Shavuot laws on Shavuot, and Sukkot laws on Sukkot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse and a baraita: Moses instituted that Israel should inquire and expound on the topic of the day — halachot of Passover on Passover, of Shavuot on Shavuot, of Sukkot on Sukkot.
